metadata.title: Claude Certified Architect – Foundations Practice Question Bank
metadata.source: Built from the official Anthropic Claude Certified Architect – Foundations Exam Guide (task statements, sample questions, and the 6 official exam scenarios). Independent study resource — not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

questions[].task_statement: string, the exam guide task statement or 'Mixed / Scenario-Integration Questions' this question targets
questions[].scenario: string, one of the 6 official exam scenario names (shortened)
questions[].question: string, the question stem
questions[].options: object with keys A, B, C, D, each a string answer choice
questions[].rationale: string, explanation of why the correct answer is right (and often why others are wrong)

metadata.version: 2.0 — expanded Domain 1 coverage + general-knowledge question set (added 69 questions)

questions.question: Your agent's control loop checks whether the assistant's response contains the word "done" to decide whether to stop calling tools. In testing, the loop sometimes stops prematurely when Claude mentions "I'm done with step 1" mid-task. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Use a more specific keyword like "TASK_COMPLETE" instead of "done", since a different keyword would avoid this same class of false trigger
options.B: Replace the keyword check with logic that terminates on `stop_reason == "end_turn"` and continues on `"tool_use"`
options.C: Add a confirmation step asking Claude to verify it meant to stop, layering an extra check onto the same unreliable keyword-based approach
options.D: Increase the iteration cap so premature stops matter less, masking the underlying detection problem rather than fixing it

questions.rationale: Natural-language keyword parsing is inherently unreliable regardless of which keyword is chosen (A is the same anti-pattern with extra steps). The `stop_reason` field is the structured, deterministic signal designed for this purpose.

questions.question: After each tool call, your implementation discards the tool's result once it has been used to construct the next prompt, keeping only a short natural-language summary in history. What problem is this most likely to cause?

options.A: Increased token costs from redundant data, since discarding tool results after use should only ever reduce token usage
options.B: The model losing access to precise data it may need to reason about in later turns
options.C: Slower agentic loop execution, since summarizing tool results into natural language adds meaningful processing overhead per turn
options.D: Violation of MCP protocol requirements, which mandate that raw tool results be preserved verbatim in conversation history

questions.rationale: Tool results should be appended to conversation history in full (or with only irrelevant fields trimmed) so the model can reason over them in subsequent iterations; summarizing away precision risks the model missing details it needs later.

questions.question: Which of the following is a legitimate use of an iteration cap in an agentic loop?

options.A: As the primary mechanism for deciding when the agent is finished, replacing `stop_reason` as the main termination signal
options.B: As a safety net to prevent runaway loops, while `stop_reason` remains the primary termination signal
options.C: As a way to avoid checking `stop_reason` on every turn, since the cap alone can substitute for that check
options.D: As a substitute for tool result validation, using the iteration count in place of actually checking tool outputs

questions.rationale: Iteration caps are a reasonable safety net but become an anti-pattern when used as the *primary* stopping mechanism instead of `stop_reason`.

questions.question: Your agent occasionally calls a tool, receives a result, and then calls the exact same tool with identical arguments again on the very next turn without using the new information. What does this most likely indicate?

options.A: A hardware issue with the API, since repeated identical tool calls typically indicate an infrastructure-level fault
options.B: The tool result was not properly appended to conversation history before the next request was sent
options.C: The tool_choice parameter is misconfigured, forcing the same tool to be selected repeatedly regardless of context
options.D: The model has exceeded its context window, causing it to lose track of having already made the call

questions.rationale: If the model doesn't have the prior tool result in its visible context, it has no way to know it already has the answer, and may re-issue the same call.

questions.question: A teammate proposes that instead of an agentic loop, the coordinator should use a fixed, pre-written sequence of tool calls (search → analyze → synthesize) with no model-driven branching, arguing this is simpler and more predictable. What is the main tradeoff being introduced?

options.A: None — this is functionally identical to an agentic loop, since both approaches ultimately call the same three tools in some order
options.B: The system becomes a decision tree rather than agentic, losing the model's ability to adapt tool selection to what it discovers along the way
options.C: It will use more tokens than an agentic loop, since a fixed sequence requires more verbose prompting to specify each step in advance
options.D: It will be unable to call any tools at all, since a fixed sequence removes the model's ability to initiate any tool call

questions.rationale: A pre-configured tool sequence is not model-driven decision-making; it's scripted automation, which trades adaptability for predictability. This is a valid engineering choice in some cases, but it's important to recognize it isn't "agentic" in the tested sense.

questions.question: In an automated review agent, you notice the loop checks `if response.content` (i.e., whether any text was returned) to decide whether the review is complete. What issue does this create?

options.A: It works correctly in all cases, since the presence of any text reliably indicates the model has finished its reasoning for that turn
options.B: A response can contain text alongside a tool_use block, or no text while still being mid-loop, so text-presence is not a reliable completion signal
options.C: It will always terminate too early, since checking for text content causes the loop to stop before any tool calls can be made
options.D: It is only a problem when using the Batches API, since the standard Messages API guarantees text only appears on the final turn

questions.rationale: Checking for assistant text content as a completion indicator is explicitly called out as an anti-pattern; `stop_reason` is the correct signal.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly describes one full iteration of the agentic loop when Claude decides to use a tool?

options.A: Send request → receive `stop_reason: "end_turn"` → execute tool → terminate, since `end_turn` is what signals a tool call is pending
options.B: Send request → receive `stop_reason: "tool_use"` → execute requested tool(s) → append tool result to history → send updated request
options.C: Execute tool → send request → check `stop_reason` → discard result, running the tool before the model has actually requested it
options.D: Send request → append assistant text to a log file → terminate, treating any assistant text as the end of the interaction

questions.rationale: This is the correct lifecycle: request, inspect `stop_reason`, execute on `"tool_use"`, append results, loop again.

questions.question: True or False framing: "An agentic loop should treat `stop_reason: 'tool_use'` as a terminal state requiring no further action." Which best describes why this is incorrect?

options.A: It's correct — `tool_use` always means the task is finished, since the model has already produced its final response by that point
options.B: `tool_use` means Claude wants to call a tool and expects a result back; the loop must execute the tool and continue, not stop
options.C: `tool_use` should be treated the same as an error state, halting the loop and surfacing a failure to the calling application
options.D: `tool_use` only appears when the agent has failed, indicating something went wrong with the model's reasoning process

questions.rationale: `"tool_use"` is a signal to continue the loop by executing the requested tool(s), not a terminal signal.

questions.question: A coordinator delegates research on "renewable energy adoption trends" by spawning subagents for "solar panel costs" and "wind turbine efficiency" only. The final report omits any discussion of policy incentives, storage technology, or grid infrastructure — areas clearly relevant to "adoption trends." Each subagent completed its assigned work correctly. What is the root cause?

options.A: The synthesis agent failed to combine the findings properly, mishandling correctly-scoped subagent output during aggregation
options.B: The coordinator's task decomposition was too narrow, omitting whole relevant subtopics from the outset
options.C: The web search subagent used outdated data, returning stale information about solar costs and turbine efficiency
options.D: The document analysis agent applied overly strict filtering, discarding relevant sources within its assigned subtopics

questions.rationale: When every subagent executes correctly but coverage is still incomplete, the defect is in what they were assigned, not how they executed it — a decomposition problem, not an execution problem.

questions.question: In a hub-and-spoke architecture, which statement is accurate?

options.A: Subagents communicate directly with each other for efficiency, bypassing the coordinator to reduce round trips
options.B: All inter-subagent communication, error handling, and routing flows through the coordinator
options.C: Subagents share a single conversation history with the coordinator automatically, without any explicit context passing
options.D: The coordinator only handles the final aggregation step, not error handling, leaving failures to be dealt with elsewhere

questions.rationale: Hub-and-spoke means the coordinator is the sole router of information and errors between subagents, supporting observability and consistent error handling.

questions.question: A support coordinator is designed to always invoke all four available subagents (billing, shipping, technical, and account) on every customer request, regardless of what the request is about. What is the main downside of this design?

options.A: It guarantees the most thorough possible response every time, so this is actually the recommended design regardless of query complexity
options.B: It adds unnecessary latency and cost, and risks irrelevant subagents contributing noise, when the coordinator should dynamically select subagents based on query complexity and relevance
options.C: It is required by the MCP protocol, which mandates that all available subagents be invoked on every incoming request
options.D: It prevents the coordinator from ever escalating to a human, since invoking every subagent removes any need for human involvement

questions.rationale: Coordinators should analyze query requirements and dynamically select which subagents to invoke, not always route through the full pipeline regardless of need.

questions.question: After an initial research pass, the coordinator evaluates the synthesis output and finds a gap in coverage of a subtopic. What is the best next step?

options.A: Publish the report as-is, noting the limitation in a footnote, without attempting to close the identified coverage gap
options.B: Re-delegate to search/analysis subagents with a targeted query addressing the gap, then re-invoke synthesis
options.C: Terminate the workflow since the initial pass is complete, treating the first synthesis attempt as final regardless of gaps found
options.D: Ask the synthesis agent to invent plausible content to fill the gap, fabricating material rather than gathering real findings

questions.rationale: Iterative refinement loops, where the coordinator evaluates for gaps and re-delegates with targeted follow-up queries before re-synthesizing, is the correct pattern.

questions.question: In a multi-agent coding assistant, a "documentation subagent" starts making direct calls to a separate "refactoring subagent" to save a round trip through the coordinator. What principle does this violate?

options.A: None — this improves efficiency and is the recommended pattern, since direct subagent-to-subagent calls reduce unnecessary round trips
options.B: The hub-and-spoke principle that all subagent communication should route through the coordinator for observability and controlled information flow
options.C: The requirement that only the coordinator can use the Task tool, since a documentation subagent calling another subagent directly violates that restriction
options.D: The MCP resource specification, which prohibits any subagent from initiating a request to another subagent under any circumstances

questions.rationale: Direct subagent-to-subagent communication bypasses the coordinator's routing, error handling, and observability — this breaks the hub-and-spoke pattern.

questions.question: Which of the following is a legitimate reason for a coordinator to invoke only 2 of its 4 available subagents for a given query?

options.A: The coordinator has assessed that the query's complexity doesn't require the full pipeline
options.B: Subagents can only be invoked in pairs, making 2-of-4 the only valid subset size regardless of query complexity
options.C: The Task tool has a hard limit of 2 concurrent subagents, preventing more than two from being spawned at once
options.D: Coordinators are not permitted to selectively invoke subagents, and must always invoke the full available set

questions.rationale: Dynamic subagent selection based on query complexity is an explicit best practice, not a limitation to work around.

questions.question: A coordinator handling billing disputes routes error messages from subagents directly to the customer without any processing. A subagent returns a raw internal exception trace. What does this scenario primarily illustrate the failure to do?

options.A: Use the Task tool correctly, since raw exceptions being passed through indicate the coordinator's `allowedTools` configuration is missing "Task"
options.B: Have the coordinator normalize/handle errors consistently rather than passing raw failures straight through
options.C: Spawn subagents in parallel, since sequential subagent execution is what causes unprocessed errors to reach the customer directly
options.D: Use `fork_session`, since branching the coordinator's session would have caught the raw exception before it reached the customer

questions.rationale: Centralized, consistent error handling by the coordinator (not raw pass-through) is a core responsibility in the hub-and-spoke pattern.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: A coordinator attempts to spawn a subagent using the Task tool, but the call fails. Investigation shows the coordinator's `allowedTools` list includes `WebSearch` and `Read` but not `Task`. What is the issue?

options.A: The Task tool requires a separate API key, distinct from the one used for the coordinator's other tool calls
options.B: `allowedTools` must explicitly include `"Task"` for the coordinator to be able to spawn subagents at all
options.C: Subagents can only be spawned via MCP servers, not the Task tool, which is reserved for a different purpose entirely
options.D: The coordinator needs `fork_session` enabled first, since session forking is a prerequisite for using the Task tool

questions.rationale: Without `"Task"` in `allowedTools`, the coordinator has no ability to spawn subagents, regardless of other tool access.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: A synthesis subagent produces a report with no citations, even though the web search subagent found and returned several well-sourced articles earlier in the session. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The synthesis subagent has a bug in its output formatting that strips citation markers before the report is finalized
options.B: The coordinator did not explicitly include the prior findings (with source metadata) in the synthesis subagent's prompt, since subagents don't automatically inherit context
options.C: The Task tool strips citations by default whenever content is passed from one subagent to another during delegation
options.D: Citations require a separate MCP resource, and without one configured, no subagent is able to include source attribution in its output

questions.rationale: Subagents have isolated context; if source findings weren't explicitly passed into the synthesis subagent's prompt, it has no way to know they exist.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: Which approach best preserves source attribution when passing findings from a document-analysis subagent to a synthesis subagent?

options.A: Concatenate all findings into a single unstructured paragraph, blending claims and sourcing details together with no separation
options.B: Use structured data that separates claim content from metadata (source URL, document name, page number)
options.C: Have the synthesis subagent re-fetch each source itself to verify, redundantly repeating work the document-analysis subagent already did
options.D: Omit metadata to keep the prompt shorter, dropping source attribution in favor of a more compact context payload

questions.rationale: Structured formats that separate content from metadata preserve attribution as data moves between agents.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: A coordinator needs to research three independent subtopics as quickly as possible. Which approach achieves true parallel execution?

options.A: Emit three separate Task tool calls within a single coordinator response
options.B: Emit one Task tool call per coordinator turn, across three separate turns, executing each subagent one after another
options.C: Use `fork_session` three times sequentially, branching the coordinator's session once per subtopic
options.D: Increase the iteration cap to allow more turns, giving the loop more room without changing how subagents are invoked

questions.rationale: Multiple Task tool calls emitted within a single response run in parallel; spawning across separate turns serializes execution and adds latency.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: A coordinator's prompt to a "test-writing" subagent reads: "Step 1: open the file. Step 2: identify all exported functions. Step 3: for each function, write exactly one test using the following template: [rigid template]." What is a downside of this approach compared to a goal-oriented prompt?

options.A: None — highly procedural prompts always produce better subagent results, since removing ambiguity guarantees more consistent output
options.B: It reduces the subagent's ability to adapt when it encounters cases the fixed procedure didn't anticipate (e.g., functions needing multiple tests, or none)
options.C: It violates the AgentDefinition schema, since step-by-step instructions are not a valid format for a subagent's system prompt
options.D: It prevents the subagent from using any tools, since a rigid procedural template overrides the subagent's configured tool access

questions.rationale: Coordinator prompts that specify goals and quality criteria (rather than rigid step-by-step procedures) enable better subagent adaptability to real, varied cases.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: You want to compare two different synthesis strategies starting from the same completed research baseline, without redoing the research. What is the appropriate mechanism?

options.A: `--resume` with the same session name twice, reopening the identical session state for each comparison attempt
options.B: `fork_session` to branch into independent explorations from the shared baseline
options.C: Re-run the entire coordinator workflow twice from scratch, redoing the shared research baseline for each strategy
options.D: Use two separate Task tool calls to the same subagent simultaneously, spawning duplicate instances of one subagent

questions.rationale: `fork_session` is specifically for branching into divergent approaches from a shared analysis baseline without redoing the shared groundwork.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: An `AgentDefinition` for a "code review subagent" includes a description, a system prompt, and a tool restriction limiting it to `Read` and `Grep` only. What is the primary purpose of the tool restriction here?

options.A: To reduce API costs only, since restricting a subagent's available tools has no bearing on the actions it's able to take
options.B: To scope the subagent to its role and prevent it from taking actions (like `Write` or `Bash`) outside its intended responsibility
options.C: To comply with a licensing requirement, since certain built-in tools like `Write` and `Bash` require separate licensing for subagent use
options.D: Tool restrictions are not part of AgentDefinition, since tool access for subagents is instead configured globally at the session level

questions.rationale: Restricting tools per AgentDefinition enforces role scoping, consistent with least-privilege tool distribution principles.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.4 — Multi-Step Workflow Enforcement and Handoff
questions.question: Your system prompt states "Always call get_customer and confirm identity before calling process_refund." Logs still show occasional refunds processed without prior identity confirmation. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Reword the instruction to be more emphatic, since a stronger phrasing of the same prompt-based rule will close the remaining gap
options.B: Add a programmatic prerequisite gate that blocks `process_refund` from executing until `get_customer` has returned a verified customer ID
options.C: Add three more few-shot examples showing correct ordering, since additional demonstrations will eventually drive compliance to 100%
options.D: Increase the model's temperature to improve instruction-following, since more randomness in generation improves adherence to stated rules

questions.rationale: When deterministic ordering is required for a financially consequential action, only programmatic enforcement (not prompt wording, however emphatic) guarantees it.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.4 — Multi-Step Workflow Enforcement and Handoff
questions.question: A customer message reads: "My order #4521 arrived damaged AND I was charged twice for it." What is the best way for the agent to handle this?

options.A: Address only the first issue mentioned and ask the customer to submit a separate request for the second concern
options.B: Decompose the message into its distinct concerns, investigate each using shared context, then synthesize one unified response
options.C: Escalate immediately since the message mentions multiple issues, treating any multi-concern message as automatically too complex
options.D: Pick whichever issue seems easier to resolve and ignore the other, addressing only part of what the customer raised

questions.rationale: Multi-concern requests should be decomposed into distinct items, each investigated (in parallel where possible), then synthesized into a single coherent resolution.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.4 — Multi-Step Workflow Enforcement and Handoff
questions.question: When escalating a case to a human agent, which handoff summary is most appropriate?

options.A: "Escalating case #8891, please review.", giving the human agent an identifier but no actual context to act on
options.B: A structured summary including customer details, root cause analysis, and a recommended action
options.C: The full raw conversation transcript with no summary, requiring the human to read through the entire history unassisted
options.D: Just the customer's original message, unedited, omitting everything the agent discovered during its own investigation

questions.rationale: Since human agents won't have access to the full conversation transcript, a structured handoff (customer details, root cause, recommended action) prevents them from having to re-investigate from scratch.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.4 — Multi-Step Workflow Enforcement and Handoff
questions.question: Which scenario correctly calls for programmatic enforcement rather than prompt-based guidance?

options.A: Preferring a friendly tone in responses, a stylistic preference well suited to flexible, probabilistic prompt guidance
options.B: Blocking a refund above $500 until a human has approved it
options.C: Choosing which greeting to use based on time of day, a low-stakes stylistic decision with no compliance implications
options.D: Deciding whether to use bullet points or prose in a summary, a formatting choice with no financial or compliance risk

questions.rationale: Financially consequential, compliance-critical actions need deterministic enforcement; stylistic choices are appropriate for prompt-based guidance.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.4 — Multi-Step Workflow Enforcement and Handoff
questions.question: True or False: "Prompt instructions alone, if written clearly enough, can achieve the same reliability as a programmatic prerequisite gate." Which is correct?

options.A: True, if enough few-shot examples are included, since sufficiently detailed examples can bring prompt-based compliance to the same reliability level
options.B: False — prompt-based compliance is probabilistic and has a non-zero failure rate no matter how well written, whereas a programmatic gate is deterministic
options.C: True, but only for text-generation agents, since agents that don't call tools have no compliance risk to begin with
options.D: False, because prompts cannot reference tool names, which is why programmatic gates are the only mechanism capable of enforcing order

questions.rationale: This is a foundational distinction in the exam guide: prompt guidance is always probabilistic to some degree; only code-level gates are deterministic.

questions.question: Different backend MCP tools return timestamps in different formats: one uses Unix epoch, another ISO 8601, another a custom string. What is the best fix?

options.A: Instruct the model in the system prompt to "interpret timestamps carefully", relying on the model to correctly infer each format at read time
options.B: Implement a PostToolUse hook that normalizes all timestamp formats into one consistent format before the agent processes the result
options.C: Ignore timestamp fields entirely, removing them from consideration rather than resolving the underlying inconsistency
options.D: Ask the customer to specify dates manually every time, shifting the burden of format normalization onto the end user

questions.rationale: PostToolUse hooks are the correct mechanism for normalizing heterogeneous data formats from different tools before the model reasons over them.

questions.question: You need to guarantee that no refund over $500 is ever processed without human approval, with zero tolerance for the agent bypassing this rule. What should you implement?

options.A: A strongly worded system prompt rule, since sufficiently forceful language in the prompt is what guarantees zero-tolerance compliance
options.B: A tool-call interception hook that blocks any `process_refund` call exceeding $500 and redirects to a human escalation workflow
options.C: A few-shot example showing the agent declining large refunds, since a single demonstration is enough to establish a hard compliance boundary
options.D: A confidence threshold check performed by the model itself, since self-assessed certainty reliably predicts whether a refund should proceed

questions.rationale: "Zero tolerance" / guaranteed compliance is the defining signal for a hook-based interception rather than any prompt-based approach.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between using a hook versus a prompt instruction to enforce a business rule?

options.A: Hooks are faster but less accurate, trading response time for a higher chance of incorrect enforcement decisions
options.B: Hooks provide deterministic guarantees; prompts provide probabilistic compliance
options.C: Prompts can only be used with the Batches API, restricting prompt-based enforcement to asynchronous workflows
options.D: There is no meaningful distinction, since both mechanisms provide the same reliability guarantee in practice

questions.rationale: This is the central theme repeated across Domain 1 and 2: hooks guarantee, prompts guide.

questions.question: A PostToolUse hook is attached to a web-search tool to strip tracking parameters from returned URLs before the model sees them. What category of hook use case does this represent?

options.A: Tool-call interception for compliance, since stripping parameters before the model sees them functions as a business-rule enforcement mechanism
options.B: Data normalization/transformation of tool results before the agent processes them
options.C: Session forking, since modifying tool output before the model processes it is functionally equivalent to branching the session
options.D: Escalation routing, since altering the URL content is a way of redirecting the request toward a different downstream handler

questions.rationale: This is a data transformation/normalization use case for PostToolUse hooks, distinct from compliance interception (which blocks outgoing calls).

questions.question: Your CI review agent needs to check every file in a PR against the same fixed set of criteria (security, style, test coverage), then run one final pass checking cross-file consistency. What decomposition strategy fits best?

options.A: Dynamic/adaptive decomposition, since PRs vary enough that a fixed sequence can't reliably apply across different pull requests
options.B: Prompt chaining — a fixed sequential pipeline of per-file analysis followed by one integration pass
options.C: A single subagent handling everything in one giant pass, since consolidating the work avoids any coordination overhead
options.D: Random task assignment across available subagents, distributing files without regard to which subagent is best suited for which check

questions.rationale: This is a predictable, multi-aspect, known-shape task — the textbook case for prompt chaining (sequential steps: per-file passes, then a cross-file integration pass).

questions.question: A developer asks the agent to "add comprehensive tests to this legacy codebase we've never touched before." What decomposition strategy is most appropriate?

options.A: A fixed pipeline: test file 1, then file 2, then file 3, in filename order, applied uniformly regardless of what's discovered along the way
options.B: Dynamic decomposition: first map the codebase structure, identify high-impact areas, then build a plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered
options.C: Prompt chaining using a rigid, pre-defined template for every file, regardless of how each file's testing needs actually differ
options.D: Immediately writing tests for every function without any exploration phase, relying on the codebase already being well understood

questions.rationale: Open-ended, unfamiliar-codebase tasks require adaptive decomposition since the right subtasks can't be known until exploration reveals them.

questions.question: A single-pass review of a 14-file PR produces inconsistent depth across files and contradictory findings (approving a pattern in one file, flagging it in another). What restructuring addresses this?

options.A: Switch to a bigger context window model and keep the single pass, assuming capacity alone resolves attention dilution
options.B: Split into per-file local analysis passes, plus a separate cross-file integration pass
options.C: Randomly sample 5 of the 14 files to review, reducing coverage rather than restructuring how the review is conducted
options.D: Have three different developers review manually instead, replacing the automated review entirely rather than fixing it

questions.rationale: This is the direct fix for attention dilution: separate per-file passes for consistent local depth, plus one dedicated cross-file pass for integration issues.

questions.question: Which factor should determine whether you use prompt chaining versus dynamic decomposition for a given workflow?

options.A: The number of available subagents, since more subagents always call for dynamic decomposition regardless of the task's predictability
options.B: Whether the task has a known, predictable shape (chaining) or requires exploration where next steps depend on what's discovered (dynamic)
options.C: The size of the context window alone, since a larger window makes dynamic decomposition unnecessary regardless of task shape
options.D: Whether the task involves customer data, since data sensitivity — not task predictability — determines the appropriate decomposition strategy

questions.rationale: This is the core decision criterion: predictability of task shape, not agent count or context size.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.7 — Session State, Resumption, and Forking
questions.question: A developer resumes a named session from yesterday to continue investigating a bug, but doesn't mention that they've since modified two of the files the agent had already analyzed. What risk does this create?

options.A: None — resumed sessions automatically re-scan all files for changes before continuing any investigation
options.B: The agent may reason from a stale understanding of those files since it isn't automatically aware of changes made outside the session
options.C: The session will fail to resume entirely, since file modifications outside the session invalidate the saved session state
options.D: `fork_session` will be triggered automatically whenever the agent detects a discrepancy between its memory and the file system

questions.rationale: When resuming, you must explicitly inform the agent about file changes; it won't automatically detect modifications made since the last session.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.7 — Session State, Resumption, and Forking
questions.question: A long investigation session's tool results (e.g., file contents, API responses) are known to have become stale since the session was last active. What is the more reliable approach?

options.A: Resume with `--resume` and proceed as normal, since resumed sessions always re-verify tool results before continuing
options.B: Start a new session with a structured summary of key findings injected as initial context, rather than resuming with stale tool results
options.C: Use `fork_session` to duplicate the stale session, since forking automatically refreshes any outdated tool results in the process
options.D: Simply ask the agent if anything has changed, since the agent can independently detect external file modifications without being told

questions.rationale: When prior tool results are stale, starting fresh with an injected summary is more reliable than resuming, which would re-anchor the agent to outdated data.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.7 — Session State, Resumption, and Forking
questions.question: What is the primary use case for `fork_session`?

options.A: Recovering from a crashed session, restoring exactly the state that existed at the moment of failure
options.B: Creating independent branches from a shared analysis baseline to explore divergent approaches
options.C: Merging two unrelated sessions into one, combining their separate conversation histories into a single thread
options.D: Permanently deleting a session's history, clearing all prior conversation state beyond recovery

questions.rationale: `fork_session` branches from a shared baseline to explore different approaches independently, e.g., comparing two refactoring strategies.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.7 — Session State, Resumption, and Forking
questions.question: When is `--resume <session-name>` the better choice over starting a fresh session?

options.A: When the prior session's context and tool results are still mostly valid
options.B: Whenever more than one day has passed, using elapsed time alone as the deciding factor regardless of context validity
options.C: Only when working with MCP servers, restricting `--resume` to sessions that happen to use MCP configuration
options.D: Never — starting fresh is always safer, treating any session resumption as inherently riskier than beginning again

questions.rationale: Resumption is appropriate specifically when prior context remains valid; if it's stale, starting fresh with a summary is preferred (see Q37).

questions.question: A coordinator for the support agent needs to (1) verify identity, (2) look up the order, (3) process a refund only if eligible. Which combination of techniques from Domain 1 best ensures this sequence is followed reliably every time, even under adversarial or unusual customer phrasing?

options.A: A single well-written system prompt describing the sequence, since sufficiently clear prose instructions guarantee compliance under any phrasing
options.B: A programmatic prerequisite gate enforcing step order, combined with structured error handling for each step's failure modes
options.C: Increasing the temperature parameter, since more randomness in generation improves the model's ability to follow a strict multi-step sequence
options.D: A `fork_session` for each customer interaction, since branching sessions is what enforces step-by-step ordering across a conversation

questions.rationale: Programmatic enforcement (from 1.4) combined with proper structured error handling (from Domain 2, but tested here in context) is what guarantees reliability regardless of how the request is phrased.

questions.question: Which of the following best demonstrates *dynamic* coordinator behavior as opposed to a fixed pipeline?

options.A: The coordinator always invokes web search, then document analysis, then synthesis, in that exact order, for every query
options.B: The coordinator analyzes the query, decides two subagents are sufficient this time, invokes them in parallel, evaluates the synthesis for gaps, and re-delegates only if needed
options.C: The coordinator has a hardcoded switch statement mapping keywords to subagents, applied identically regardless of query content
options.D: The coordinator ignores subagent outputs and always returns the same templated report, regardless of what was actually found

questions.rationale: Dynamic subagent selection, parallel invocation where appropriate, and gap-driven re-delegation together represent genuinely adaptive, model-driven orchestration.

questions.question: A CI review agent's coordinator spawns a "security reviewer" subagent and a "style reviewer" subagent in parallel for the same PR. The security subagent times out. What should happen next, based on Domain 1 principles (assume standard error propagation applies)?

options.A: The entire review process should terminate immediately, since a single subagent timeout means the overall PR review cannot be trusted
options.B: The coordinator should receive structured context about the failure and can proceed with the style review results, annotating that security review is incomplete
options.C: The style subagent's results should also be discarded to keep things consistent, even though it completed successfully
options.D: The coordinator should silently mark the security review as "passed", since a timeout shouldn't block the PR from proceeding

questions.rationale: Consistent with error propagation principles, partial results should proceed with clear annotation of the gap rather than total termination or silent suppression.

questions.question: A coordinator building developer tools spawns an "Explore" subagent to investigate an unfamiliar module before making changes. What is the main benefit of this pattern?

options.A: It reduces the number of tools available, since spawning a dedicated Explore subagent removes the need for general-purpose tools in the main session
options.B: It isolates the (often verbose) discovery process from the main conversation, returning a summary and preserving the main session's context budget
options.C: It automatically writes the final code, since the Explore subagent's findings are directly committed once discovery is complete
options.D: It replaces the need for plan mode entirely, since exploration alone provides sufficient investigation before any change is made

questions.rationale: The Explore subagent pattern exists specifically to isolate verbose discovery output while the main agent stays high-level.

questions.question: A coordinator prompt tells a synthesis subagent: "Your goal is to produce a comprehensive, well-cited report on the research topic, resolving any conflicting findings with clear attribution." This is an example of:

options.A: Rigid procedural instruction, specifying an exact fixed sequence of steps the subagent must follow with no room to adapt
options.B: Goal- and quality-criteria-based prompting that allows the subagent to adapt its approach
options.C: A prompt that violates hub-and-spoke principles, since instructing a subagent this way bypasses the coordinator's routing role
options.D: An instruction that should instead be enforced via a hook, since goal-oriented guidance like this requires deterministic enforcement

questions.rationale: This is exactly the recommended style: specifying goals and quality criteria rather than rigid steps.

questions.question: Which of these is an anti-pattern for a coordinator's loop termination logic?

options.A: Checking `stop_reason == "end_turn"`, which is the correct, structured signal for loop termination
options.B: Scanning the assistant's final text for the phrase "issue resolved" as the signal to stop
options.C: Continuing the loop when `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, which correctly reflects that a requested tool still needs to be executed
options.D: Appending tool results to history before the next iteration, which is the correct way to carry forward new information

questions.rationale: Natural-language phrase matching for loop termination is the classic anti-pattern; the others are correct practices.

questions.question: A coordinator's error-handling logic catches a subagent failure and simply logs it internally, returning an empty (but unmarked) result to the synthesis step as if the subagent had succeeded with no findings. What is wrong with this?

options.A: Nothing — this is the correct behavior, since presenting a clean, unmarked result avoids introducing unnecessary complexity downstream
options.B: It silently suppresses the failure, hiding it from downstream reasoning that could have accounted for the gap
options.C: It should instead terminate the whole workflow, since any subagent failure — however handled — should halt the entire process
options.D: It violates the Task tool's schema, since `Task` requires every subagent response to include an explicit success or failure flag

questions.rationale: Silently suppressing errors as if they were valid empty results is an explicit anti-pattern; it should be surfaced with structured context instead.

questions.question: In a coding assistant using built-in tools plus MCP servers, the coordinator's `allowedTools` is set to include `Task`, `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, and three MCP tools. What does including `Task` specifically enable?

options.A: The ability to read files, which is instead provided by the `Read` tool already listed separately
options.B: The ability to spawn subagents
options.C: The ability to search file contents, which is instead provided by the `Grep` tool already listed separately
options.D: The ability to connect to MCP servers, which is configured independently of the `Task` tool

questions.rationale: `Task` is specifically the mechanism for subagent spawning, distinct from file/search tools or MCP server connections.

questions.question: A support coordinator escalates to a human but the handoff message only says "Complex case, please assist." The human agent then has to spend 10 minutes re-reading the entire transcript. Which Domain 1 principle was violated?

options.A: Programmatic enforcement of prerequisite steps, since the handoff message itself represents a missing prerequisite gate
options.B: The requirement for structured handoff protocols including customer details, root cause, and recommended action
options.C: The Task tool's `allowedTools` requirement, since a vague handoff indicates the coordinator lacked permission to invoke the escalation tool
options.D: `fork_session` usage, since a properly forked session would have automatically generated a more detailed handoff summary

questions.rationale: This is a direct failure of the structured handoff pattern designed to prevent exactly this kind of redundant re-investigation.

questions.question: Two subagents (web search and document analysis) both return findings to the coordinator. The coordinator merges and forwards everything to synthesis without adding any relevance filtering or organization. What Domain 1 concern does this raise, most directly?

options.A: Task tool misconfiguration, since the coordinator's `allowedTools` list must not include "Task" if it's forwarding subagent output without processing
options.B: Failure to properly manage the coordinator's aggregation responsibility, potentially overwhelming the synthesis subagent's context with unfiltered material
options.C: A violation of the `stop_reason` protocol, since forwarding unfiltered content between agents means the loop never properly reaches `end_turn`
options.D: An MCP resource scoping issue, since the coordinator should have exposed the raw findings as a resource rather than passing them directly in a prompt

questions.rationale: Result aggregation is an explicit coordinator responsibility; passing everything through unfiltered defeats the purpose of having a coordinating layer at all.

questions.question: Which best summarizes the core lesson of Domain 1 as tested across the exam's scenarios?

options.A: Agentic systems work best with the fewest possible rules, since minimal constraints let the model make the most contextually appropriate decisions
options.B: Reliability in agentic systems comes from combining model-driven adaptability with deterministic enforcement exactly where mistakes are costly, plus explicit context passing between isolated agents
options.C: All orchestration should be hardcoded for predictability, since deterministic sequences eliminate the risk of the model choosing an unexpected action
options.D: Subagents should always have full access to the coordinator's tools, since broader access improves their ability to complete any assigned task

questions.rationale: This synthesizes the domain's throughline: adaptability where safe, hard guarantees where costly, and explicit (never assumed) context passing.

questions.question: Two tools, `get_customer` ("Retrieves customer information") and `lookup_order` ("Retrieves order details"), are frequently confused by the agent when a customer provides an order number. What is the most effective *first* fix?

options.A: Merge the two tools into one generic `lookup` tool, since consolidating overlapping functionality is the most effective first step
options.B: Expand both descriptions with input formats, example queries, and explicit boundaries distinguishing when to use each
options.C: Add a routing classifier ahead of the agent, since a separate model deciding which tool to call resolves the ambiguity most directly
options.D: Add five few-shot examples showing correct routing, since demonstrations alone are a more effective first fix than improving the descriptions

questions.rationale: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism for tool selection; the lowest-effort, highest-leverage fix is improving them before considering heavier architectural changes.

questions.question: A tool named `analyze_content` is used inconsistently — sometimes for web pages, sometimes for uploaded PDFs, sometimes for raw text. What is a reasonable next step if description improvements alone haven't fully resolved ambiguity?

options.A: Delete the tool entirely, since removing it forces callers to use a different, already-unambiguous tool instead
options.B: Split it into purpose-specific tools (e.g., `extract_web_results`, `extract_pdf_content`) each with a tightly scoped description
options.C: Rename it to something shorter, since a more concise name is what actually drives reliable tool selection, not the description's specificity
options.D: Disable tool_choice entirely, since forcing tool selection is what's causing the model to apply the tool inconsistently

questions.rationale: Splitting an overly generic tool into purpose-specific tools with defined input/output contracts resolves ambiguity that description tweaks alone can't fix.

questions.question: A system prompt for a review agent says: "Always prioritize checking documentation before making any claims." The agent now over-relies on a `read_docs` tool even for questions clearly suited to a `check_syntax` tool. What is happening?

options.A: The `check_syntax` tool is broken, causing the agent to avoid it in favor of the `read_docs` tool as a fallback
options.B: Keyword-sensitive system prompt wording is creating an unintended bias in tool selection
options.C: This is expected and requires no fix, since prioritizing documentation is generally sound guidance for a review agent
options.D: The Task tool needs to be added, since spawning a subagent would resolve the bias toward `read_docs`

questions.rationale: System prompt wording can create unintended keyword associations that override otherwise well-written tool descriptions; the fix is reviewing and adjusting that wording.

questions.question: Which tool description is best written?

options.A: "Extracts data from documents using built-in heuristics to automatically determine document type and apply the appropriate parsing rules."
options.B: "Extracts invoice line items (description, quantity, unit price) from PDF or scanned invoice images; use for invoice documents only, not for receipts or purchase orders, which have different structures — see extract_receipt_data for those."
options.C: "A tool for documents that intelligently determines the correct extraction approach based on the file's content and structure."
options.D: "Handles all document types by dynamically selecting the best extraction method for invoices, receipts, and purchase orders alike."

questions.rationale: Includes input format, scope, explicit boundary against a similar tool, and enough specificity for reliable selection.

questions.question: After improving tool descriptions doesn't fully resolve confusion between two overlapping tools, what is a reasonable escalation of effort?

options.A: Give up and route all requests to a human, abandoning the automated tool-selection approach entirely
options.B: Rename tools to eliminate functional overlap, or split a generic tool into purpose-specific tools with clear contracts
options.C: Remove one of the two tools without replacement, eliminating functionality rather than resolving the underlying ambiguity
options.D: Disable the confused tool and hardcode its logic into the system prompt, moving the functionality out of tool-based execution altogether

questions.rationale: This is the correct next-tier fix after description improvements, per the guide's escalation path.

questions.task_statement: Task 2.2 — Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools
questions.question: A `lookup_order` tool returns `{"isError": true, "message": "Operation failed"}` for every kind of failure — timeouts, invalid order numbers, and permission issues alike. What problem does this cause?

options.A: None — `isError: true` is sufficient information, since the agent only needs to know that the call didn't succeed
options.B: The agent cannot distinguish retryable from non-retryable failures, or select an appropriate recovery action, because the error category isn't communicated
options.C: It will cause the MCP server to crash, since returning the same generic message for every failure type creates a resource leak
options.D: It prevents the tool from being called again, since a generic failure message triggers a cooldown before the tool can be retried

questions.rationale: Uniform error responses prevent the agent from making appropriate recovery decisions; structured metadata (category, retryability) is needed.

questions.task_statement: Task 2.2 — Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools
questions.question: Which error response is best structured for agent consumption?

options.A: `{"isError": true, "message": "failed"}`, since a boolean flag plus a short message gives the agent enough information to decide how to proceed
options.B: `{"isError": true, "errorCategory": "validation", "isRetryable": false, "description": "Document is missing a required field: invoice_number"}`
options.C: `{"isError": true}`, since the presence of the flag alone is sufficient for the agent to trigger appropriate recovery behavior
options.D: `{"success": false}`, since inverting the field name provides equivalent structured information to an explicit error category

questions.rationale: Includes category, retryability, and a human-readable description — exactly the metadata that enables intelligent agent decisions.

questions.task_statement: Task 2.2 — Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools
questions.question: A `lookup_order` call for order #99999 (which doesn't exist) returns an empty array with `isError: false`. A separate call times out due to a network issue and also returns an empty array with `isError: false`. What is the problem?

options.A: There is no problem — both are legitimately "no data" cases, since an empty array always represents the same underlying condition
options.B: A valid empty result (order doesn't exist) is being conflated with an access failure (timeout), preventing the agent from making an appropriate retry/recovery decision
options.C: `isError` should never be false, since any tool call that doesn't return a fully populated result should be flagged as an error
options.D: Empty arrays should never be returned by MCP tools, since a missing or invalid identifier should always raise an explicit exception instead

questions.rationale: Distinguishing access failures from valid empty results is essential; conflating them means the agent can't tell "genuinely nothing found" from "something went wrong."

questions.task_statement: Task 2.2 — Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools
questions.question: A subagent encounters a transient network error while calling a search tool. What should happen before this is escalated to the coordinator?

options.A: Immediately propagate the raw exception to the coordinator, since subagents should never attempt to handle errors on their own
options.B: The subagent should attempt local recovery (e.g., a retry) for the transient failure, only escalating if it cannot resolve it locally, including partial results and what was attempted
options.C: The subagent should silently return success with no data, since an empty but successful-looking result is safer than surfacing an error
options.D: The entire multi-agent workflow should be terminated, since any tool-level error indicates the whole system is in an unrecoverable state

questions.rationale: Local recovery for transient failures before escalation, with structured context if escalation is needed, is the correct pattern.

questions.task_statement: Task 2.2 — Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools
questions.question: A `process_refund` tool call fails because the requested refund exceeds a policy limit. Which error category and retryability best fits?

options.A: `errorCategory: "transient"`, `isRetryable: true`, treating a policy-limit violation as a temporary condition worth retrying
options.B: `errorCategory: "business"`, `isRetryable: false`, with a customer-friendly explanation
options.C: `errorCategory: "permission"`, `isRetryable: true`, misclassifying a business-rule violation as an access-control issue
options.D: No error category is needed since this isn't a real failure, treating a legitimate policy rejection as if nothing went wrong

questions.rationale: A policy-limit violation is a business rule error, not retryable by simply trying again, and should include an explanation the agent can relay appropriately.

questions.task_statement: Task 2.2 — Structured Error Responses for MCP Tools
questions.question: Why is `isRetryable: false` on a validation error useful, beyond just describing the error?

options.A: It has no practical use beyond documentation, since the agent's retry behavior is unaffected by whatever the field's value is set to
options.B: It prevents the agent from wasting cycles retrying something that will never succeed without a different input
options.C: It automatically fixes the validation issue, triggering the tool to self-correct the malformed input before returning a final result
options.D: It disables the tool permanently, preventing any further calls to that tool for the remainder of the session

questions.rationale: Retryability metadata directly prevents wasted retry attempts on errors that retrying alone cannot fix.

questions.question: A synthesis subagent is given access to 18 tools "just in case it needs them," including several web search and database tools clearly intended for other subagents. What is the most likely consequence?

options.A: Improved synthesis quality due to flexibility, since having more tools available gives the subagent more ways to verify its conclusions
options.B: Degraded tool selection reliability, and a tendency to misuse tools outside its specialization (e.g., attempting web searches itself)
options.C: No effect, since more tools are always better regardless of whether they fall within the subagent's intended role
options.D: The subagent will automatically ignore irrelevant tools, since the model filters out tools that don't match its system prompt

questions.rationale: Both effects (degraded selection reliability with too many tools, and cross-specialization misuse) are explicitly called out risks of over-provisioning tool access.

questions.question: The synthesis subagent frequently needs simple fact verification (85% of cases) but occasionally needs deeper investigation (15%). What is the best-scoped solution?

options.A: Give the synthesis subagent full web search tool access for all cases, since broad access ensures every verification need is covered directly
options.B: Give it a scoped `verify_fact` tool for simple lookups, while complex verifications continue to route through the coordinator to the search subagent
options.C: Route 100% of verification needs through the coordinator regardless of complexity, since centralizing every request improves consistency
options.D: Remove verification capability from synthesis entirely, forcing every fact-check, however small, through a separate dedicated pipeline

questions.rationale: This applies least-privilege scoping matched to the actual frequency distribution of needs, without over-provisioning for the common case or under-provisioning for the rare one.

questions.question: You have three different extraction schemas for three different document types, and you don't know in advance which type a given document is. You need to guarantee the model calls *some* extraction tool rather than returning free text. Which `tool_choice` setting is correct?

options.A: `"auto"`, since letting the model freely decide whether to call a tool best fits an unknown document type
options.B: `"any"`
options.C: A forced call to one specific tool, which would incorrectly commit to a single schema before the type is known
options.D: No `tool_choice` needed, relying on default model behavior to guarantee a tool call happens

questions.rationale: `"any"` guarantees a tool call while letting the model choose which of the multiple valid schemas fits, appropriate when the document type is unknown in advance.

questions.question: You need `extract_metadata` to run before any enrichment tools are considered, in a specific required first step. Which `tool_choice` setting enforces this?

options.A: `"auto"`, which allows the model to skip tool use entirely and cannot guarantee the required first step runs
options.B: `"any"`, which guarantees a tool call but not specifically the `extract_metadata` tool as the required first step
options.C: `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}`
options.D: Tool choice cannot enforce ordering, so this requirement would need to be handled entirely through prompt wording instead

questions.rationale: Forced tool selection guarantees a specific tool runs, which is the mechanism for enforcing that a particular step happens first (with subsequent steps handled in follow-up turns).

questions.question: What is the main risk of giving every subagent in a 4-subagent pipeline access to all 15 tools available across the whole system?

options.A: Increased latency only, with no accuracy impact, since more available tools simply add processing time without affecting selection quality
options.B: Increased decision complexity per agent, degrading reliable tool selection, and increased risk of role-inappropriate tool use
options.C: MCP servers will refuse the connection, since there's a hard limit on how many tools a single agent can be connected to
options.D: The Task tool will be disabled, since exceeding a certain tool count automatically restricts subagent-spawning capability

questions.rationale: This is the direct restatement of the "too many tools degrades selection reliability" principle at a system level.

questions.question: When should `tool_choice: "auto"` be used?

options.A: When you need to guarantee a tool call happens every time, which is instead the purpose of `tool_choice: "any"`
options.B: When the model should be free to either call a tool or return conversational text, based on the situation
options.C: When forcing a specific extraction tool, which is instead the purpose of named forced tool selection
options.D: Only in batch processing workflows, since `"auto"` behaves identically but is restricted to asynchronous requests

questions.rationale: `"auto"` is the default, flexible mode where the model may or may not call a tool, appropriate when conversational responses are also valid outcomes.

questions.question: A team wants a Jira MCP server available to every developer who clones the repository, using a token stored securely without being committed to version control. What configuration approach fits?

options.A: Hardcode the token directly in `.mcp.json` and commit it, embedding the literal secret value into version control
options.B: Configure the server in project-scoped `.mcp.json` using environment variable expansion (e.g., `${JIRA_TOKEN}`)
options.C: Configure it only in each developer's personal `~/.claude.json`, requiring every developer to set up the server manually with no shared configuration
options.D: Store the token in a code comment, placing the credential in a source file rather than an environment variable

questions.rationale: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` provides team-wide shared config, and environment variable expansion keeps credentials out of version control.

questions.question: A developer wants to experiment with a new, unstable MCP server without affecting teammates. Where should they configure it?

options.A: In the project's `.mcp.json`, which is shared via version control and would expose the unstable server to the whole team
options.B: In their personal `~/.claude.json`
options.C: In `CLAUDE.md`, which is a configuration file for instructions, not a location for registering MCP servers
options.D: In `.claude/rules/`, which is used for path-scoped conventions, not for MCP server configuration

questions.rationale: User-scoped `~/.claude.json` is for personal/experimental servers not shared with the team.

questions.question: A project has both a project-scoped MCP server (in `.mcp.json`) and a developer's personal experimental server (in `~/.claude.json`) configured. What happens when the developer starts a session?

options.A: Only the project-scoped server's tools are available, with the developer's personal server excluded from that session
options.B: Only the personal server's tools are available, with the project-scoped server excluded from that session
options.C: Tools from all configured MCP servers are discovered at connection time and are simultaneously available
options.D: The developer must manually choose which server to activate each session, selecting one over the other explicitly

questions.rationale: All configured servers' tools become available simultaneously upon connection, regardless of scope.

questions.question: The agent has both `Grep` (built-in) and a more capable MCP-provided code-search tool available, but keeps defaulting to `Grep` even in cases where the MCP tool would perform better. What is the most likely fix?

options.A: Remove `Grep` entirely, since eliminating the competing built-in tool is the most direct way to force correct tool selection
options.B: Enhance the MCP tool's description to more clearly explain its capabilities and outputs, since minimal descriptions bias selection toward familiar built-ins
options.C: This is unfixable and expected behavior, since models will always default to familiar built-in tools over MCP-provided ones regardless of description quality
options.D: Switch the MCP server to project scope, since scope — not description quality — is what determines how reliably a tool gets selected

questions.rationale: Improving the MCP tool's description addresses the root cause: the model isn't choosing it because it doesn't understand what it offers.

questions.question: A coordinator repeatedly makes exploratory tool calls just to discover what data sources and schemas are available before it can plan its research. What MCP feature could reduce this overhead?

options.A: A better system prompt only, since instructing the coordinator to remember available schemas removes the need for any structural change
options.B: MCP resources exposing content catalogs (e.g., available schemas, document hierarchies) so the agent has visibility without exploratory calls
options.C: A larger `allowedTools` list, since giving the coordinator access to more tools directly reduces the number of exploratory calls needed
options.D: `fork_session`, since branching into parallel exploration paths would let the coordinator discover data sources faster

questions.rationale: MCP resources exist specifically to expose browsable catalogs of available content, reducing the need for exploratory tool calls just to learn what exists.

questions.question: Your team needs standard Jira integration. Should you build a custom MCP server for this?

options.A: Yes, always build custom servers for full control, since relying on community-maintained integrations introduces unacceptable risk
options.B: No — prefer existing community MCP servers for standard integrations like Jira, reserving custom servers for genuinely team-specific workflows
options.C: Custom servers are required by MCP specification for any third-party tool, regardless of whether a standard integration already exists
options.D: It doesn't matter either way, since custom and community servers are functionally interchangeable in every case

questions.rationale: The guide explicitly recommends using existing community servers for standard integrations and reserving custom development effort for team-specific needs.

questions.question: A developer wants to find every file matching the pattern `**/*.test.tsx` across a large repository. Which built-in tool is appropriate?

options.A: `Grep`, which searches file contents for patterns rather than matching file paths by name
options.B: `Glob`
options.C: `Read`, which loads the contents of a specific known file rather than discovering files by pattern
options.D: `Bash` with no other option, since a dedicated built-in tool exists specifically for this kind of path matching

questions.rationale: `Glob` is for file *path/name* pattern matching; `Grep` is for searching file *contents*.

questions.question: A developer wants to find every place in the codebase where a specific function name is called. Which tool is appropriate?

options.A: `Glob`, which matches file paths by name or pattern rather than searching the contents of files
options.B: `Grep`
options.C: `Write`, which creates or overwrites file contents rather than searching for existing usages
options.D: `Edit`, which modifies existing file content rather than searching across the codebase for usages

questions.rationale: `Grep` searches file contents for patterns like function names, which is exactly this use case.

questions.question: An `Edit` call fails because the anchor text it's trying to match appears in three different places in the file, none of which are unique. What is the recommended fallback?

options.A: Keep retrying `Edit` with the same text, since repeating the identical call will eventually resolve the non-unique match
options.B: Use `Read` to load the full file, then `Write` to save it back with the change applied
options.C: Delete the file and recreate it from scratch, discarding the rest of its contents just to make one targeted change
options.D: Switch to a different file, abandoning the intended edit rather than resolving the non-unique anchor text issue

questions.rationale: Read + Write is the documented fallback for non-unique `Edit` matches, since it doesn't depend on finding unique anchor text.

questions.question: A developer exploring an unfamiliar codebase wants to understand how a module works. What is the recommended incremental approach?

options.A: Read every file in the repository upfront before doing anything else, building a complete mental model before starting the investigation
options.B: Start with `Grep` to find entry points, then `Read` to follow imports and trace flow, building understanding incrementally
options.C: Use `Write` to annotate every file with comments first, documenting the module before attempting to understand how it works
options.D: Ask the user to describe the entire codebase manually, relying on the user's own explanation instead of direct exploration

questions.rationale: This incremental Grep-then-Read approach avoids wasting context budget on reading everything upfront.

questions.question: A function `formatDate` is re-exported under the alias `fmtDate` through a wrapper module. A developer greps only for `formatDate` to find all usages. What will they miss?

options.A: Nothing — grep finds all references regardless of aliasing, since it can resolve import and export relationships automatically
options.B: Usages that reference the function only by its re-exported alias `fmtDate`
options.C: All usages, since grep doesn't work on wrapper modules, failing to find even the original `formatDate` references
options.D: Only usages in test files, since re-exported aliases are conventionally only used in test code

questions.rationale: Tracing usage across re-exports requires first identifying all exported names (including aliases), then searching for each — a single grep on the original name misses aliased call sites.

questions.question: A support agent has `get_customer`, `lookup_order`, `process_refund`, and `escalate_to_human` — each with detailed, differentiated descriptions and appropriate error handling. What Domain 2 principle does this exemplify well?

options.A: Over-provisioning for flexibility, giving the agent broader access than its role strictly requires in case future needs arise
options.B: Purpose-scoped tool design with clear boundaries, appropriate to a small, well-defined toolset
options.C: The anti-pattern of too few tools, since four tools is an unusually small set for a production customer support agent
options.D: A violation of MCP resource specifications, which require a minimum number of exposed tools per agent role

questions.rationale: A small, clearly-scoped, well-described toolset (4-5 tools) is exactly the recommended pattern for reliable tool selection.

questions.question: An extraction pipeline's tool schema marks every field as required, including "discount_percentage," which is often genuinely absent from source invoices. What problem results?

options.A: No problem — required fields ensure completeness, since marking every field required guarantees nothing important is ever missed
options.B: The model may fabricate a value (e.g., inventing "0%") to satisfy the schema, since it can't return null for a required field
options.C: The pipeline will fail to run entirely, since a required field with no source value always causes a hard validation error
options.D: This only matters for optional fields, since required fields are populated correctly by definition

questions.rationale: This is the classic Domain 4 concept applied here: required fields for genuinely-absent data push the model toward fabrication; nullable fields prevent this. (Cross-referenced with Domain 4 Task 4.3.)

questions.question: A web search subagent's tool returns a `503 Service Unavailable` error. Its MCP tool response correctly sets `isError: true`, `errorCategory: "transient"`, `isRetryable: true`. What should the subagent do?

options.A: Immediately propagate this to the coordinator without any local handling, since transient errors should always bypass local recovery
options.B: Attempt local recovery (e.g., retry with backoff) since it's marked transient/retryable, escalating only if retries are exhausted
options.C: Treat it as a permanent failure and abandon the task, since a `503` response indicates the underlying service is unrecoverable
options.D: Ignore the error and return an empty result marked as success, since presenting a clean result avoids unnecessary coordinator involvement

questions.rationale: Structured retryability metadata is precisely what enables the subagent to make this local-recovery decision correctly.

questions.question: A CI review agent is configured with `Read`, `Grep`, `Glob`, and one custom MCP tool for posting PR comments — but not `Bash` or `Write`. What principle does this reflect?

options.A: A configuration mistake that should be fixed by adding all tools, since a review agent benefits from maximum available capability
options.B: Least-privilege tool distribution — a review agent needs to read and analyze, not modify files or execute arbitrary commands
options.C: A violation of the built-in tools specification, which requires every agent to have access to `Bash` and `Write` by default
options.D: This setup cannot post comments at all, since the omission of `Bash` and `Write` also disables any custom MCP tool access

questions.rationale: Scoping a review agent's tools to only what its role requires (read/search/comment, not write/execute) is the correct least-privilege pattern.

questions.question: Which best distinguishes an MCP "tool" from an MCP "resource"?

options.A: They are functionally identical, since both tools and resources are exposed to the agent through the same MCP interface
options.B: Tools represent actions/queries the agent invokes; resources expose browsable content catalogs the agent can reference without an active call
options.C: Resources can only be used by subagents, not coordinators, since coordinators are restricted to tool-based interactions only
options.D: Tools are always faster than resources, since resources require an additional network round trip that tools do not

questions.rationale: This is the defining distinction: tools = actions, resources = content visibility.

questions.question: A `lookup_order` tool call returns 40+ fields (warehouse internal IDs, shipping carrier codes, etc.) when only 5 are relevant to a return request. Besides the Domain 5 context-budget concern, what Domain 2 principle is also relevant here?

options.A: None — this is purely a Domain 5 issue, since Domain 2 principles only apply to how tools are described, not what they return
options.B: Well-designed tool responses (or a PostToolUse hook trimming them) reduce noise the agent has to sift through, complementing good tool interface design
options.C: This means the tool must be split into 8 separate tools, since each irrelevant field group requires its own dedicated tool
options.D: This is a tool_choice misconfiguration, since forcing a narrower tool selection would have reduced the number of fields returned

questions.rationale: While the context-budget angle is Domain 5, tool/response design and hook-based trimming (Domain 1/2) are complementary levers on the same underlying problem.

questions.question: A coordinator gives the "web search" subagent tools for search, browsing, and also database queries (intended for the "document analysis" subagent). The search subagent begins occasionally querying the database when it shouldn't. What two Domain 2 principles were violated?

options.A: MCP resource scoping and `fork_session` usage, since resources and session forking govern how tools are distributed between subagents
options.B: Least-privilege tool distribution per role, and prevention of out-of-specialization tool access/misuse
options.C: `tool_choice` configuration and `Glob` usage, since forcing a specific tool selection is what would have prevented the database queries
options.D: None — this is a Domain 1 issue only, since it concerns which subagent was invoked rather than which tools it has access to

questions.rationale: Both principles (scope tools to role, avoid giving agents tools outside their specialization) were violated together here.

questions.question: An extraction tool schema includes a `document_type` enum field with only three fixed values: `invoice`, `receipt`, `purchase_order`. A genuinely novel document type appears. What schema design would have handled this more gracefully?

options.A: No changes needed — the model will guess the closest match, and an approximate category is acceptable for downstream use
options.B: Include an `"other"` enum value paired with a free-text detail field to handle extensible/unanticipated categories
options.C: Remove the enum entirely and use free text for everything, sacrificing the reliability benefits of constrained categories across the board
options.D: Reject any document that isn't one of the three types, discarding genuinely novel documents rather than processing them

questions.rationale: The `"other"` + detail-string pattern is the recommended way to keep enums extensible without forcing false precision.

questions.question: Which is the best justification for keeping `process_refund` and `lookup_order` as two separate tools rather than merging them into one flexible `handle_order` tool?

options.A: Merging tools is always better for flexibility, since a single tool that can do more gives the model more options to choose from
