options.B: Separate, purpose-specific tools with clear, non-overlapping descriptions are more reliably selected than one overloaded generic tool
options.C: MCP requires a minimum of 4 tools per agent, so keeping `process_refund` and `lookup_order` separate simply satisfies that requirement
options.D: There is no meaningful difference, since tool selection reliability is unaffected by whether functionality is merged or split

questions.rationale: This reflects the general principle that purpose-specific tools with clear contracts outperform generic, overloaded ones for selection reliability.

questions.question: A skill's description says merely "Helps with code." Developers report Claude rarely invokes it even when clearly relevant. What is the most likely cause, applying Domain 2 tool-description principles by analogy?

options.A: Skills are not affected by description quality, since Claude invokes skills based on explicit user commands rather than description matching
options.B: Like tools, minimal/vague descriptions provide insufficient signal for reliable selection — the description needs specifics on when and how to use it
options.C: The skill file is corrupted, since a vague one-line description like this typically indicates a parsing or formatting error in SKILL.md
options.D: Skills cannot have descriptions, since only the skill's name and frontmatter configuration are considered during invocation

questions.rationale: The same "descriptions drive selection" principle that governs MCP tools applies to skill invocation as well.

questions.question: A pipeline processes both structured invoices (consistent format) and messy scanned receipts (inconsistent format) using the same single extraction tool with one rigid schema. What tool/schema design issue does this likely cause?

options.A: None — one tool should always handle all document types, since maintaining a single tool is simpler than managing multiple type-specific ones
options.B: A single rigid tool/schema struggling to serve fundamentally different input structures — splitting into type-specific tools/schemas (as in Q2/Q36) would likely improve reliability
options.C: This is purely a batch-processing issue and would not occur if the pipeline instead used the standard, real-time Messages API
options.D: This can only be solved with a bigger model, since model capacity — not tool or schema design — determines extraction reliability across formats

questions.rationale: This connects back to the "split overly generic tools into purpose-specific ones" principle applied to extraction schemas.

questions.question: A CI pipeline's review tool posts every finding as a separate, unstructured comment string on the PR. Reviewers ask for the ability to filter by severity programmatically. What's the underlying Domain 2/4 crossover issue?

options.A: The MCP server is down, since inability to filter findings programmatically typically indicates a connectivity or availability issue
options.B: Output isn't structured (e.g., via `tool_use`/JSON schema with a severity field), preventing downstream systems from filtering or processing it programmatically
options.C: This requires the Batches API, since only asynchronous processing supports structured, filterable output fields
options.D: `Grep` should be used instead of the review tool, since built-in tools inherently produce more structured output than MCP-based ones

questions.rationale: Unstructured text output can't be reliably filtered downstream; structured output (Domain 4 territory) resolves this, and is worth recognizing as connected to tool/interface design here.

questions.question: A `verify_fact` tool given to the synthesis subagent (per Q13) returns `isError: true` with `errorCategory: "validation"` when given a malformed claim string. What should the synthesis subagent do?

options.A: Retry the exact same malformed input repeatedly, since persistence with the same request will eventually produce a valid result
options.B: Not retry blindly — a validation error signals the input itself needs correction, not that persistence will eventually succeed
options.C: Escalate to a human immediately, since any validation error from a tool call warrants pausing the entire research task for review
options.D: Terminate the entire research task, since a single malformed claim string indicates the underlying data source cannot be trusted

questions.rationale: Validation errors indicate an input problem, not a transient one; retrying identical input won't help (contrast with retryable transient errors).

questions.question: Which best describes why `escalate_to_human` should have its own clearly bounded tool description rather than being folded into a generic `respond` tool?

options.A: It doesn't matter, since escalation happens rarely enough that tool selection reliability isn't a meaningful concern for it
options.B: A dedicated, clearly described escalation tool makes it easier for the model to reliably recognize and select the escalation path when appropriate, versus burying it in an overloaded generic tool
options.C: MCP prohibits generic multi-purpose response tools, so a dedicated escalation tool is required by the protocol itself
options.D: This would violate `tool_choice: "any"`, which requires exactly one tool to be available to the model at any given time

questions.rationale: Consistent with the general "specific > generic, clearly described" principle for reliable tool selection.

questions.question: A `.mcp.json` file includes `"env": {"GITHUB_TOKEN": "${GITHUB_TOKEN}"}`. What does this achieve?

options.A: It hardcodes a fixed token value for all developers, embedding the literal secret directly into the committed `.mcp.json` file
options.B: It expands the value from each developer's own environment variable at runtime, avoiding committing the actual secret to version control
options.C: It disables authentication entirely, treating the `GITHUB_TOKEN` variable as an optional field the server can ignore
options.D: It only works for user-scoped configuration, never project-scoped, since environment variable expansion isn't supported at the project level

questions.rationale: Environment variable expansion is exactly this mechanism: reference, not hardcode, credentials.

questions.question: An extraction schema is technically valid (passes JSON schema validation) but the extracted `line_item_total` values don't sum to the extracted `invoice_total`. What kind of error is this?

options.A: A syntax error that `tool_use` should have prevented, since schema-compliant output is supposed to guarantee internally consistent values
options.B: A semantic error — schema enforcement via `tool_use` prevents syntax errors but not this kind of logical/semantic inconsistency
options.C: An MCP transport error, since a mismatch between related numeric fields typically indicates a problem in how the tool response was transmitted
options.D: A permission error, since the extraction tool likely lacks sufficient access to compute the correct invoice total

questions.rationale: This is the key limitation of schema-enforced structured output: syntactic validity is guaranteed, semantic correctness is not.

questions.question: Why might exposing a database schema as an MCP *resource* (rather than requiring a tool call to discover it) improve a research agent's efficiency?

options.A: Resources execute faster than tools at the network level, since resource requests bypass the standard MCP transport layer entirely
options.B: It gives the agent visibility into what's queryable without spending a tool-call round trip just to explore/discover structure
options.C: Resources bypass the coordinator's hub-and-spoke routing, letting subagents communicate with each other directly through shared resources
options.D: It removes the need for any tools at all, since exposing a resource makes every subsequent action available without a tool call

questions.rationale: This is the core value proposition of MCP resources: browsable visibility without exploratory tool-call overhead.

questions.question: Should a code-review MCP tool used in CI include `Bash` execution access to "just run the tests to be thorough"?

options.A: Yes, always maximize capability — a code-review tool benefits from being as capable as possible, and restricting access would limit its ability to catch issues
options.B: Not necessarily — this should be a deliberate scoping decision weighed against least-privilege principles; broad execution access on an automated review path carries more risk than a read/analyze-scoped toolset
options.C: MCP requires all agents used in CI to include `Bash` execution access as part of the protocol specification
options.D: This has no bearing on tool design — scoping decisions like this only matter for customer-facing agents, not internal CI/CD tooling

questions.rationale: This tests judgment: broadening scope should be a deliberate tradeoff, not a default "more is better," especially for automated pipeline agents.

questions.question: A `get_customer` tool returns multiple matching customer records for a common name search. What should the agent do?

options.A: Pick the first result returned, using return order as a heuristic to resolve the ambiguity automatically
options.B: Ask the customer for an additional identifier to disambiguate rather than guessing via a heuristic
options.C: Merge all matching records into one response, combining potentially unrelated customer accounts into a single working record
options.D: Escalate immediately without attempting clarification, bypassing the simple identifier request that could resolve this directly

questions.rationale: Multiple ambiguous matches call for requesting an additional identifier, not heuristic guessing (this connects directly to Domain 5.2 as well).

questions.question: A batch of 200 documents is processed with an extraction tool. 12 fail with `errorCategory: "validation"` due to a date-format edge case; the rest succeed. What's the appropriate remediation?

options.A: Resubmit all 200 documents, since resubmitting the full batch is simpler than isolating and reprocessing just the 12 that failed
options.B: Resubmit only the 12 failed documents (via their `custom_id`s), potentially after adjusting the prompt/schema to handle the date-format edge case
options.C: Discard the 12 failures permanently with no further action, since a 6% failure rate is within acceptable tolerance for any extraction pipeline
options.D: Switch the entire pipeline to `tool_choice: "auto"`, since forced tool selection is what caused the date-format validation failures

questions.rationale: Structured errors with correlation IDs allow targeted resubmission of only the failures, not the whole batch (also ties to Domain 4.5).

questions.question: Which combination reflects best practice for a 4-subagent research pipeline's tool design overall?

options.A: Every subagent has access to every tool for maximum flexibility, since broader access only ever improves a subagent's ability to complete its task
options.B: Each subagent has a small, role-scoped toolset with clear descriptions; a few high-frequency cross-role needs get narrow, dedicated tools; complex cross-role needs route through the coordinator
options.C: Only the coordinator has any tools; subagents have none, since centralizing all execution capability in one place is the safest design
options.D: Tool descriptions are optional as long as tool names are self-explanatory, since a clear name alone gives the model everything it needs for selection

questions.rationale: This combines Domain 2's key principles: scoping, clear descriptions, and coordinator-routed complexity — all in one coherent picture.

questions.question: Overall, which statement best captures the throughline of Domain 2?

options.A: More tools and broader access always improve outcomes, since giving every agent maximum capability removes any risk of task failure
options.B: Reliable multi-tool systems depend on clear, differentiated tool descriptions, structured (not generic) error responses, and disciplined, role-scoped tool distribution
options.C: MCP servers should always be built custom rather than reused, since community-maintained servers can't be trusted for production use
options.D: Error handling is optional if tool descriptions are good enough, since well-written descriptions alone prevent all categories of tool failure

questions.rationale: This synthesizes the domain: description clarity, structured errors, and scoped distribution are the three pillars tested throughout.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.1 — CLAUDE.md Hierarchy and Modular Organization
questions.question: A new hire joins the team, clones the repo, and runs Claude Code — but it doesn't follow the team's established coding conventions, even though a senior developer's sessions do follow them correctly. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The conventions are in the senior developer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, which is user-scoped and never propagated via git
options.B: The new hire has an outdated version of Claude Code, which is missing support for reading CLAUDE.md files correctly
options.C: `CLAUDE.md` files expire after 30 days, requiring periodic manual renewal to remain active for any team member
options.D: The conventions must be re-typed by every new team member manually, since CLAUDE.md is not something Claude Code loads automatically

questions.rationale: This is the classic hierarchy-misplacement diagnostic: user-level config isn't shared, so if only the senior dev's personal config has the conventions, new team members won't inherit them.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.1 — CLAUDE.md Hierarchy and Modular Organization
questions.question: Where should universal, team-wide coding standards that every contributor must follow be placed?

options.A: `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, since user-scoped configuration is the standard place for conventions the whole team must follow
options.B: Project-level `.claude/CLAUDE.md` or root `CLAUDE.md`, checked into version control
options.C: A private Slack message to each developer, communicating the standards outside of any file Claude Code actually loads
options.D: A comment in the main entry-point file, embedding conventions as inline documentation rather than structured configuration

questions.rationale: Project-level CLAUDE.md, version-controlled, is what ensures universal application across the team.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.1 — CLAUDE.md Hierarchy and Modular Organization
questions.question: A large monorepo has packages with very different domain knowledge needs. What lets each package's CLAUDE.md include only the standards relevant to it, without duplicating a giant shared file?

options.A: `.claude/rules/` only, since glob-pattern rule files alone can scope conventions to individual packages without any other mechanism
options.B: `@import` syntax to selectively reference relevant external standards files per package
options.C: Multiple root-level CLAUDE.md files, placing several competing top-level files at the repository root
options.D: Renaming CLAUDE.md to package-specific names, relying on filename alone to signal which conventions apply where

questions.rationale: `@import` is specifically designed for this kind of modular, selective inclusion.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.1 — CLAUDE.md Hierarchy and Modular Organization
questions.question: A team's CLAUDE.md has grown to several thousand lines covering testing, API conventions, and deployment, and it's become hard to maintain. What's a better structural alternative?

options.A: Delete the file and rely on default behavior, since Claude Code performs reasonably well without any project-specific configuration
options.B: Split it into focused topic-specific files under `.claude/rules/` (e.g., `testing.md`, `api-conventions.md`, `deployment.md`)
options.C: Compress it by removing all comments and whitespace, since reducing file size is what actually improves maintainability at scale
options.D: Move it to `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, since user-level configuration is easier to maintain than project-level configuration

questions.rationale: `.claude/rules/` with topic-specific files is the documented alternative to one monolithic CLAUDE.md.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.1 — CLAUDE.md Hierarchy and Modular Organization
questions.question: A developer is confused about why Claude Code isn't behaving consistently with their teammate's setup, despite both claiming to have "the same CLAUDE.md." What command helps diagnose this?

options.A: `/compact`, since reducing context usage would reveal whether the two developers' sessions have diverged in behavior
options.B: `/memory`, to verify which memory files are actually loaded in the session
options.C: `--resume`, since resuming a named session surfaces which CLAUDE.md files were active when that session was originally started
options.D: `fork_session`, since branching a session exposes any differences in the underlying configuration between two developers

questions.rationale: `/memory` is the documented diagnostic tool for verifying which memory files are actually loaded.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.1 — CLAUDE.md Hierarchy and Modular Organization
questions.question: Which statement about the CLAUDE.md hierarchy is correct?

options.A: Directory-level CLAUDE.md files override and disable project-level ones entirely, replacing rather than supplementing them
options.B: There are three conceptual levels — user, project, and directory — each with different scope and sharing characteristics
options.C: Only one CLAUDE.md file is allowed per repository, with any additional files at other levels simply being ignored
options.D: User-level CLAUDE.md is automatically shared with the team via git, propagating personal settings to every collaborator

questions.rationale: Correctly describes the three-level hierarchy; D is the classic wrong-answer trap (user-level is never auto-shared).

questions.task_statement: Task 3.1 — CLAUDE.md Hierarchy and Modular Organization
questions.question: A subdirectory `packages/payments/CLAUDE.md` contains payment-specific conventions. What is its scope?

options.A: It applies to the entire repository, overriding conventions defined anywhere else regardless of directory
options.B: It applies only to that subtree/directory
options.C: It applies only to the developer who created it, functioning as a personal rather than shared configuration
options.D: It requires `@import` to take effect at all, remaining inactive unless explicitly imported from another file

questions.rationale: Directory-level CLAUDE.md files affect only their own subtree, unlike project-level files.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.1 — CLAUDE.md Hierarchy and Modular Organization
questions.question: Why might a team prefer `.claude/rules/` files over subdirectory-level CLAUDE.md files for conventions that apply to test files scattered throughout many directories?

options.A: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files are deprecated and no longer supported in current versions of Claude Code
options.B: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md is directory-bound and can't cleanly apply to files spread across many directories; `.claude/rules/` with glob patterns can match by file type regardless of location
options.C: `.claude/rules/` files load faster than CLAUDE.md files, which is the primary reason they're preferred for scattered conventions
options.D: There's no meaningful difference between the two approaches; either can be used interchangeably regardless of how conventions are distributed

questions.rationale: This is the direct rationale for preferring glob-based rules over directory-bound files for cross-cutting, file-type-based conventions (elaborated further in 3.3).

questions.task_statement: Task 3.1 — CLAUDE.md Hierarchy and Modular Organization
questions.question: A CLAUDE.md file references `@import ./standards/testing-standards.md`. What does this accomplish?

options.A: It copies the contents of testing-standards.md into CLAUDE.md permanently on disk, merging the two files into one
options.B: It references the external file so its content is included when CLAUDE.md loads, keeping the main file modular
options.C: It creates a symbolic link at the OS level, establishing a filesystem-level link rather than a configuration-time reference
options.D: It disables testing-standards.md from being read elsewhere, restricting that file to being loaded only through this one reference

questions.rationale: This describes the functional effect of `@import`: modular inclusion without maintaining one giant file.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.2 — Custom Slash Commands and Skills
questions.question: The team wants a `/review` slash command available to every developer automatically when they clone the repo. Where should it live?

options.A: `~/.claude/commands/`, which is personal and scoped to the individual developer's home directory, not shared via git
options.B: `.claude/commands/` in the project repository
options.C: `CLAUDE.md`, which holds project instructions and context rather than reusable slash command definitions
options.D: A `.claude/config.json` commands array, a configuration format that isn't how Claude Code defines slash commands

questions.rationale: Project-scoped commands directory, version-controlled and shared automatically on clone.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.2 — Custom Slash Commands and Skills
questions.question: A developer wants a personal `/my-shortcut` command just for their own workflow, without affecting teammates. Where should it be created?

options.A: `.claude/commands/`, which is version-controlled and shared with the whole team rather than kept personal
options.B: `~/.claude/commands/`
options.C: `.claude/skills/`, which is intended for on-demand task workflows rather than personal slash-command shortcuts
options.D: `.claude/rules/`, which is used for path-scoped conventions rather than defining custom slash commands

questions.rationale: User-scoped commands directory, personal and not version-controlled.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.2 — Custom Slash Commands and Skills
questions.question: A skill produces very verbose intermediate output during a deep codebase analysis. The team wants this output kept out of the main conversation, with only a summary returned. What frontmatter option achieves this?

options.A: `allowed-tools`, which restricts which tools a skill can use, rather than isolating its output from the main conversation
options.B: `context: fork`
options.C: `argument-hint`, which prompts for missing parameters rather than controlling where the skill's output is surfaced
options.D: There is no way to achieve this, when a dedicated frontmatter option exists specifically for this purpose

questions.rationale: `context: fork` runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context specifically to prevent output pollution of the main session.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.2 — Custom Slash Commands and Skills
questions.question: A skill should only be allowed to write files, never execute shell commands, to reduce the risk of destructive actions. What frontmatter option enforces this?

options.A: `context: fork`, which isolates a skill's output from the main conversation rather than restricting which tools it can use
options.B: `allowed-tools`
options.C: `argument-hint`, which prompts for missing parameters rather than restricting a skill's available tool access
options.D: This cannot be enforced via frontmatter, when a dedicated option exists specifically for restricting tool access

questions.rationale: `allowed-tools` restricts which tools a skill can use during execution.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.2 — Custom Slash Commands and Skills
questions.question: A developer invokes a skill without providing any arguments, and it's unclear what parameters are expected. What frontmatter option helps here?

options.A: `context: fork`, which isolates a skill's output from the main session rather than clarifying its expected parameters
options.B: `allowed-tools`, which restricts a skill's available tools rather than prompting for missing arguments
options.C: `argument-hint`
options.D: `paths`, which scopes a rule file to matching files rather than clarifying a skill's expected parameters

questions.rationale: `argument-hint` prompts the developer for required parameters when invoked without arguments.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.2 — Custom Slash Commands and Skills
questions.question: A developer wants to tweak a shared project skill's behavior for their own personal use, without changing it for teammates. What's the recommended approach?

options.A: Directly edit the shared skill file in `.claude/skills/`, which would change the behavior for every teammate as well
options.B: Create a personal variant under a different name in `~/.claude/skills/`
options.C: Delete the shared skill and replace it, removing the version teammates rely on rather than creating a personal variant
options.D: This is not possible — skills cannot be personalized, when a personal-variant mechanism exists specifically for this case

questions.rationale: Personal skill customization via a differently-named variant in the user-scoped skills directory avoids affecting teammates.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.2 — Custom Slash Commands and Skills
questions.question: When should you use a skill instead of putting instructions in CLAUDE.md?

options.A: When the instructions should always be loaded for every interaction, which is instead the intended use case for CLAUDE.md
options.B: When the workflow is on-demand/task-specific, rather than a universal standard that should always apply
options.C: Skills and CLAUDE.md are interchangeable in all cases, with no meaningful distinction in when each should be used
options.D: Skills can only be used for testing tasks, and aren't a general-purpose mechanism for on-demand workflows

questions.rationale: Skills are for on-demand invocation; CLAUDE.md is for always-loaded universal standards. This is the key decision criterion.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.2 — Custom Slash Commands and Skills
questions.question: A skill for "brainstorm alternative refactoring approaches" tends to produce long, exploratory, sometimes-meandering output. Which frontmatter setting is most appropriate and why?

options.A: `argument-hint`, to clarify inputs, since this frontmatter option is meant for parameter guidance, not output isolation
options.B: `context: fork`, to isolate the exploratory output from polluting the main session
options.C: `allowed-tools`, to speed up execution, since restricting tool access affects capability, not how output is isolated
options.D: None — this output should always be shown inline, regardless of how exploratory or meandering it tends to be

questions.rationale: Exploratory/brainstorming content is a named example use case for `context: fork` isolation.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.2 — Custom Slash Commands and Skills
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches scope to sharing behavior?

options.A: `.claude/commands/` = personal; `~/.claude/commands/` = shared, reversing the actual scoping of the two locations
options.B: `.claude/commands/` = shared via version control; `~/.claude/commands/` = personal
options.C: Both are always shared, disregarding the distinction between project-scoped and user-scoped command locations
options.D: Both are always personal, disregarding that `.claude/commands/` is checked into version control and shared with the team

questions.rationale: This is the reverse of the common trap (A); project-scoped is shared, user-scoped is personal.

questions.question: Test files (`*.test.tsx`) are scattered throughout the codebase, each sitting next to the component it tests, rather than being grouped in one directory. The team wants consistent testing conventions applied regardless of location. What's the best approach?

options.A: Create a CLAUDE.md in every subdirectory that contains a test file, requiring a separate file wherever a test happens to live
options.B: Create a `.claude/rules/testing.md` file with YAML frontmatter `paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"]`
options.C: Put all testing conventions in the root CLAUDE.md and hope Claude infers relevance, relying on inference rather than explicit matching
options.D: Rename all test files to live in one central `/tests` directory, restructuring the codebase rather than using path-scoped rules

questions.rationale: Glob-pattern path scoping applies by file type regardless of location — exactly suited to this scattered-file scenario.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of path-scoped rules over always-loaded CLAUDE.md content?

options.A: Path-scoped rules load faster over the network, since their file size is generally smaller than a full CLAUDE.md
options.B: They reduce irrelevant context and token usage by only loading when editing matching files
options.C: Path-scoped rules support more formatting options, offering richer markdown syntax than a standard CLAUDE.md file
options.D: There is no meaningful benefit, since always-loaded CLAUDE.md content and path-scoped rules behave identically in practice

questions.rationale: Conditional loading based on file match is specifically about reducing unnecessary context/token usage.

questions.question: A `.claude/rules/terraform.md` file has frontmatter `paths: ["terraform/**/*"]`. When does this rule's content get loaded into context?

options.A: Always, for every session regardless of what's being edited, ignoring the `paths` frontmatter entirely
options.B: Only when editing files matching the `terraform/**/*` glob pattern
options.C: Only once per day, reloading on a fixed schedule rather than in response to which files are being edited
options.D: Never — frontmatter paths are decorative only, having no actual effect on when the rule's content loads

questions.rationale: This is the functional behavior of path-scoped conditional rule loading.

questions.question: Why might glob-pattern rules be preferable to directory-level CLAUDE.md files even when conventions happen to mostly align with directory structure?

options.A: They never actually differ in outcome, since both mechanisms apply conventions identically regardless of how the codebase evolves
options.B: Glob patterns generalize better if the codebase structure changes or if similar file types appear in new locations later, without requiring new CLAUDE.md files to be created
options.C: Directory-level CLAUDE.md files are being deprecated by Anthropic in favor of `.claude/rules/` as the only supported configuration mechanism
options.D: Glob patterns support encryption, which directory-level CLAUDE.md files lack, making them the more secure choice for sensitive conventions

questions.rationale: This reflects the general resilience of type-based over location-based rule scoping, though directory-level CLAUDE.md remains valid when structure genuinely matches convention boundaries.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.4 — Plan Mode vs. Direct Execution
questions.question: A developer needs to restructure a monolithic application into microservices, affecting 45+ files and requiring decisions about service boundaries. What approach should they take?

options.A: Direct execution, making changes incrementally to discover boundaries as they go, risking costly rework once dependencies surface
options.B: Plan mode, to explore the codebase, understand dependencies, and design an approach before making any changes
options.C: Direct execution with an extremely long, detailed upfront prompt specifying everything exactly, assuming the boundaries are already known
options.D: Begin in direct execution and switch to plan mode only if unexpected complexity arises, when the complexity is already evident upfront

questions.rationale: This is exactly the profile plan mode is designed for: large-scale, multi-file, architecturally consequential change with multiple valid approaches.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.4 — Plan Mode vs. Direct Execution
questions.question: A developer needs to add a single null-check to one function, with a clear stack trace showing exactly where the bug is. What approach fits best?

options.A: Plan mode, to be thorough, even though the fix is already clearly scoped with an obvious cause and location
options.B: Direct execution — this is a simple, well-scoped change with an obvious fix
options.C: Spawning three subagents to investigate in parallel, over-provisioning coordination for a single, well-understood fix
options.D: `fork_session` to explore multiple fix strategies, branching unnecessarily when only one clear fix is needed

questions.rationale: Simple, well-understood, single-file changes are the direct-execution use case; plan mode would be overhead here.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.4 — Plan Mode vs. Direct Execution
questions.question: A task's complexity is already clearly stated upfront as "architectural, affecting many files, with multiple valid implementation strategies." What is the correct sequencing?

options.A: Start in direct execution and switch to plan mode only once complexity becomes apparent, when the complexity is already stated upfront
options.B: Start in plan mode from the beginning, since the complexity is already known
options.C: Alternate between plan mode and direct execution every few minutes, switching modes without any clear trigger for doing so
options.D: Skip planning entirely since it wastes time, despite the task explicitly involving multiple valid architectural approaches

questions.rationale: When complexity is already known upfront, starting in plan mode is correct; waiting to "discover" already-stated complexity is the wrong sequencing.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.4 — Plan Mode vs. Direct Execution
questions.question: What is the role of the Explore subagent during a multi-phase plan-mode task?

options.A: It writes the final production code directly, committing changes to the codebase as soon as its investigation is complete
options.B: It isolates verbose discovery/exploration output, returning a summary, to prevent context window exhaustion in the main session
options.C: It replaces the need for plan mode, since exploration alone is sufficient without any separate planning step
options.D: It only works with MCP servers, since built-in tools like Read and Grep aren't available to the Explore subagent

questions.rationale: The Explore subagent's purpose is specifically to protect the main session's context during verbose discovery phases.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.4 — Plan Mode vs. Direct Execution
questions.question: A developer uses plan mode to investigate and design a library migration approach, gets team sign-off on the plan, then switches to direct execution to implement it. Is this an appropriate use of both modes?

options.A: No — you must use only one mode per task, since switching between plan mode and direct execution partway through is not supported
options.B: Yes — combining plan mode for investigation/design with direct execution for implementing an already-agreed plan is a normal, correct sequence
options.C: No — direct execution can never follow plan mode, since plan mode's output is meant only for team review, not for implementation
options.D: Yes, but only if no subagents are involved, since plan mode followed by direct execution is incompatible with any multi-agent workflow

questions.rationale: This combination is explicitly described as a valid and common pattern.

questions.task_statement: Task 3.4 — Plan Mode vs. Direct Execution
questions.question: Which factor is NOT part of the criteria for choosing plan mode?

options.A: Multiple valid architectural approaches exist, which is a legitimate reason to favor plan mode's exploration phase
options.B: The change spans many files, which is a legitimate factor supporting the use of plan mode before committing to changes
options.C: The task requires an urgent, same-minute hotfix regardless of scope
options.D: There are real consequences if the wrong design decision is made, which legitimately favors plan mode's upfront exploration

questions.rationale: Urgency alone isn't the deciding factor; complexity/architectural stakes are. An urgent hotfix that's still simple and well-scoped would still favor direct execution; urgency doesn't override the complexity criteria.

questions.question: A developer's prose description of a data transformation keeps producing inconsistent results across attempts. What is the most effective next step?

options.A: Write an even longer paragraph of prose explaining the transformation, expanding on an approach that's already proven inconsistent
options.B: Provide 2-3 concrete input/output examples showing the exact expected transformation
options.C: Lower the model's temperature setting, adjusting randomness rather than clarifying what the transformation should actually produce
options.D: Split the task across three different sessions, fragmenting the work rather than clarifying the expected transformation itself

questions.rationale: Concrete examples are explicitly more effective than more prose when natural-language descriptions produce inconsistent results.

questions.question: What is the recommended sequencing for test-driven iterative refinement?

options.A: Write the implementation first, then write tests to match whatever was built, since tests should reflect the final behavior as implemented
options.B: Write the test suite (behavior, edge cases, performance) first, then iterate by sharing test failures with the agent to guide improvement
options.C: Skip tests entirely and rely on manual review, since manual verification is more thorough than automated test-driven iteration
options.D: Write tests only after the feature ships, since pre-launch iteration should focus solely on functionality, not test coverage

questions.rationale: Test-first, then iterate against failures, is the documented pattern for progressive improvement.

questions.question: A developer is implementing a caching layer in an unfamiliar domain and isn't sure what edge cases to specify upfront (e.g., invalidation strategy). What technique helps surface these considerations before implementation begins?

options.A: The interview pattern — having Claude ask clarifying questions before implementing
options.B: Immediately generating code and fixing issues after the fact, discovering edge cases only once problems already exist in the implementation
options.C: Avoiding caching altogether, sidestepping the unfamiliar domain rather than surfacing its important design considerations
options.D: Providing the vaguest possible prompt to let the model fill in gaps silently, leaving key decisions unexamined rather than surfaced

questions.rationale: The interview pattern is specifically designed to surface unanticipated design considerations before implementation in unfamiliar domains.

questions.question: A code review surfaces five issues in a file, several of which interact (fixing one changes what the correct fix for another looks like). How should feedback be provided?

options.A: One issue at a time, in five separate sequential messages, addressing each in isolation regardless of how they interact
options.B: All interacting issues together in a single detailed message, since fixing them independently risks contradictory or incomplete fixes
options.C: Randomly ordered, one per session, spreading interacting fixes across multiple unrelated sessions
options.D: None of the issues should be raised until all five are independently confirmed, delaying all feedback until every issue is separately verified

questions.rationale: Interacting issues should be addressed together; only genuinely independent issues suit sequential, one-at-a-time iteration.

questions.question: A migration script has an edge case around null values that keeps being handled incorrectly despite a prose description saying "handle nulls gracefully." What's the more effective fix?

options.A: Repeat the same prose instruction more forcefully, restating "handle nulls gracefully" in stronger language
options.B: Provide a specific test case with example null input and the exact expected output
options.C: Remove null handling from scope entirely, leaving the edge case unaddressed rather than clarifying the expected behavior
options.D: Switch to a different programming language, assuming the language itself is the source of the inconsistent handling

questions.rationale: Concrete input/output test cases are more effective than repeated vague prose for pinning down specific edge-case behavior.

questions.question: A pipeline script runs `claude "Review this PR for security issues"` and the job hangs indefinitely, with logs showing it's waiting for interactive input. What's the fix?

options.A: Add the `-p` (or `--print`) flag to run in non-interactive mode
options.B: Increase the pipeline timeout, giving the interactive prompt more time to eventually receive input that will never arrive
options.C: Run the command twice, hoping the second invocation somehow avoids waiting for interactive input
options.D: Switch to the Batches API, since asynchronous processing inherently bypasses the need for any interactive input

questions.rationale: This is the documented fix for exactly this symptom: `-p`/`--print` for non-interactive CI execution.

questions.question: A team wants automated review findings posted as individual inline PR comments by a script, requiring machine-parseable output. What CLI flags help achieve this?

options.A: `-p` alone is sufficient, since non-interactive execution by itself also guarantees machine-parseable structured findings
options.B: `--output-format json` combined with `--json-schema` to enforce structured, parseable findings
options.C: `--verbose`, since more detailed console output is what a script would parse to extract individual findings
options.D: There is no way to get structured output from Claude Code CLI, making this kind of automated PR commenting impossible

questions.rationale: These flags are specifically for producing machine-parseable structured CI output.

questions.question: Why does providing testing standards, fixture conventions, and review criteria in CLAUDE.md matter for CI-invoked Claude Code specifically?

options.A: It doesn't matter for CI — CLAUDE.md is only read in interactive sessions, not when invoked via the `-p` flag
options.B: It's exactly the mechanism that gives CI-invoked Claude Code project context, improving the quality and relevance of generated tests/reviews
options.C: CI pipelines ignore CLAUDE.md by design, relying instead solely on the prompt passed directly to the `-p` invocation
options.D: It only affects the `-p` flag's behavior, not content quality, since `-p` and CLAUDE.md operate on entirely separate concerns

questions.rationale: CLAUDE.md is the documented mechanism for supplying project context to CI-invoked sessions, directly affecting output quality.

questions.question: Why is a second, independent Claude Code invocation generally a better reviewer of generated code than the same session that generated it?

options.A: Independent instances are always faster, since a fresh session has less accumulated context to process before producing a review
options.B: The generating session retains the reasoning context that led to its decisions, making it less likely to question them, even with explicit self-critique instructions
options.C: The same session cannot access the code it just wrote, since prior tool outputs are purged once a turn completes
options.D: There is no meaningful difference between the two approaches; both produce equivalent review quality regardless of shared reasoning history

questions.rationale: Self-review is structurally weaker due to retained reasoning bias; independent review lacks that bias and catches more issues.

questions.question: A review agent re-runs after new commits are pushed to a PR. Without any special handling, it re-flags issues from the previous run that haven't been addressed yet, creating duplicate PR comments. What's the fix?

options.A: Disable review entirely after the first run, forgoing any further automated feedback on subsequent commits
options.B: Include prior review findings in context on re-runs, instructing the agent to report only new or still-unaddressed issues
options.C: Always start with a completely fresh session with no memory of prior findings, guaranteeing every re-run repeats the same flagged issues
options.D: Increase the PR comment rate limit, allowing more duplicate comments to be posted rather than preventing them

questions.rationale: Including prior findings and instructing the agent to report only new/unresolved issues is the documented fix for duplicate-comment re-runs.

questions.question: A test-generation agent in CI keeps suggesting tests that duplicate existing test coverage. What's the most direct fix?

options.A: Provide the existing test files in context so generation avoids suggesting already-covered scenarios
options.B: Increase the model's context window, since a larger window is what allows the model to recall which tests already exist
options.C: Run test generation less frequently, since reducing how often the agent runs is what would prevent duplicate suggestions
options.D: Switch to the Batches API, since asynchronous processing inherently cross-references against previously generated test files

questions.rationale: Providing existing tests as context directly prevents duplicate-scenario generation, per the exam guide's skill list for this task.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a real Claude Code CLI mechanism (i.e., is a distractor you should recognize as fabricated)?

options.A: `-p` / `--print`, the flag documented for running Claude Code non-interactively so it doesn't wait for input
options.B: `--output-format json`, the flag documented for producing machine-parseable structured output in CI contexts
options.C: `CLAUDE_HEADLESS` environment variable to enable non-interactive mode
options.D: `--json-schema`, the flag documented for enforcing a specific JSON structure on non-interactive output

questions.rationale: This environment variable does not exist per the exam guide; it's the classic distractor pattern in the official sample questions.

questions.question: A team wants: (1) universal conventions always loaded, (2) a reusable `/deploy-check` command, (3) test-file-specific conventions regardless of directory, and (4) an isolated codebase-analysis workflow. Which four mechanisms correctly map to these needs, in order?

options.A: CLAUDE.md; `.claude/commands/`; `.claude/rules/` with glob paths; a skill with `context: fork`
options.B: `.claude/rules/`; CLAUDE.md; `.claude/commands/`; `argument-hint`, mismatching each mechanism to a need it doesn't actually address
options.C: All four needs should use CLAUDE.md, relying on a single always-loaded file to cover on-demand, path-specific, and isolated needs alike
options.D: All four needs should use `~/.claude/commands/`, placing every requirement into a personal, non-shared configuration location

questions.rationale: This correctly matches each need to its purpose-built mechanism: always-loaded standards → CLAUDE.md; reusable team command → project commands; file-type-scoped conventions → rules with glob paths; isolated analysis → forked skill context.

questions.question: A CI pipeline needs Claude Code to (1) run non-interactively, (2) produce structured findings, and (3) avoid duplicate comments on re-runs. Which combination addresses all three?

options.A: `-p` alone, since non-interactive execution by itself also guarantees structured, duplicate-free findings across re-runs
options.B: `-p` + `--output-format json`/`--json-schema` + including prior findings in context on re-runs
options.C: `--verbose` + `fork_session`, since more detailed logging combined with session branching addresses all three requirements
options.D: CLAUDE.md alone, with no CLI flags, since project context by itself is sufficient to produce structured, non-interactive output

questions.rationale: Each requirement maps to a specific, distinct mechanism; all three are needed together for the full CI workflow.

questions.question: A developer is unsure whether a large refactor should use plan mode. The refactor touches 6 files but each change is mechanical and identical (renaming one function call site everywhere). What's the better call?

options.A: Plan mode, since it touches multiple files, and file count alone should always determine whether plan mode is used
options.B: Direct execution — despite touching several files, the change is mechanical, well-understood, and has no real architectural ambiguity
options.C: This requires a coordinator-subagent architecture, since any change spanning more than one file needs multi-agent orchestration
options.D: This should be split across multiple sessions using `fork_session`, since each file's rename should happen in an isolated branch

questions.rationale: File count alone doesn't trigger plan mode; the deciding factor is architectural ambiguity/complexity, which is absent here despite the multi-file scope.

questions.question: A `.claude/skills/deep-audit/SKILL.md` has `context: fork` and `allowed-tools: [Read, Grep, Glob]`. What does this configuration collectively achieve?

options.A: The skill can modify files and its output pollutes the main session, since `allowed-tools` and `context: fork` don't restrict either behavior
options.B: The skill runs read-only/analysis-only, in an isolated context that won't pollute the main conversation with its verbose findings
options.C: The skill is disabled by this configuration, since combining `context: fork` with a restricted `allowed-tools` list prevents invocation entirely
options.D: The skill can only be invoked by the coordinator, since `context: fork` restricts which role is permitted to call it

questions.rationale: `context: fork` isolates output; `allowed-tools` restricted to read/search tools scopes it to non-destructive analysis only.

questions.question: Which best explains why `.claude/rules/` with `paths` frontmatter is preferred over cramming all conventions into one root CLAUDE.md, even for a small project?

options.A: It's always strictly required by Claude Code, which will not load any configuration unless `.claude/rules/` is present in the project
options.B: It keeps irrelevant conventions out of context when they don't apply to the file currently being edited, saving tokens even at small scale
options.C: Root CLAUDE.md files are limited to 100 lines, so anything beyond that threshold must be moved into `.claude/rules/`
options.D: `.claude/rules/` is required for any project using MCP servers, regardless of how conventions are otherwise organized

questions.rationale: The token/context efficiency benefit applies regardless of project size, though the maintainability benefit becomes more pronounced as conventions grow.

questions.question: A CI review agent's system prompt says "flag anything that seems off." Reviewers report high false-positive rates and low trust in the findings. Which domain's principle most directly explains the fix here, and what is it?

options.A: Domain 3 — add more CLAUDE.md content, since expanding project-level configuration is what governs review-agent behavior in CI
options.B: Domain 4 — replace vague criteria like "seems off" with explicit, categorical criteria for what counts as a finding
options.C: Domain 2 — this is a tool description problem, since the review agent's own capabilities, not its prompt criteria, are causing the false positives
options.D: Domain 1 — this requires a hook, since deterministic enforcement is the only way to reduce a review agent's false-positive rate

questions.rationale: This is a Domain 4 (Prompt Engineering) issue tested here in a Domain 3/CI scenario context — recognizing cross-domain application is part of scenario-based testing.

questions.question: A developer wants Claude Code to explore a legacy module, understand its structure, and propose (but not yet implement) a modernization plan. Which mode is appropriate, and why?

options.A: Direct execution, because exploration doesn't require planning, treating investigation and implementation as needing no separate design phase
options.B: Plan mode, because it enables safe exploration and design before any commitment to changes
options.C: Neither — this requires a coordinator-subagent system instead, treating a single-session exploration task as needing multi-agent orchestration
options.D: `fork_session`, because no other mode supports exploration, when session forking addresses a different concern entirely

questions.rationale: "Explore and propose without committing to implementation" is exactly plan mode's core value proposition.

questions.question: A skill's `SKILL.md` omits `allowed-tools` entirely. What is the practical implication?

options.A: The skill cannot run at all, since `allowed-tools` is a mandatory field required for any skill to be invoked
options.B: Without an explicit restriction, the skill isn't scoped down from the broader toolset available to the session — an omission worth reviewing for skills with any risk of destructive action
options.C: The skill automatically gets `context: fork` applied by default whenever `allowed-tools` is left unspecified
options.D: `allowed-tools` is required syntax, and omitting it will cause a validation error the next time the skill is invoked

questions.rationale: Omitting `allowed-tools` means no tool restriction is applied via that mechanism; for skills capable of destructive actions, this is a design gap worth closing.

questions.question: A team's CI review prompt was originally written for a small project and doesn't mention project-specific testing fixtures. As the codebase and test suite have grown, review quality has degraded. What is the most likely fix?

options.A: Reduce the frequency of CI reviews, since running fewer reviews naturally lowers the rate of context-related quality issues
options.B: Update CLAUDE.md to document current testing standards and available fixtures, since this context isn't automatically inferred and needs to stay current
options.C: Switch review generation to the Batches API, since asynchronous processing inherently produces more thorough, higher-quality reviews
options.D: Add more `Bash` tool access, since broader execution capability compensates for outdated project context in the review prompt

questions.rationale: CLAUDE.md content needs to be actively maintained as the project evolves; stale project context degrades CI output quality over time.

questions.question: Overall, which best summarizes Domain 3's central theme?

options.A: Configuration is a one-time setup task with no ongoing maintenance, since CLAUDE.md and rules files rarely need revision once written
options.B: Reliable, scalable Claude Code workflows depend on correctly scoping configuration (user/project/directory/path-based), choosing the right mode for task complexity, and maintaining project context over time
options.C: All configuration should default to user-level for simplicity, since project-level configuration adds unnecessary complexity for most teams
options.D: Plan mode should always be used regardless of task size, since exploring before any change reduces risk universally across every task

questions.rationale: This captures the throughline across CLAUDE.md hierarchy, commands/skills scoping, path rules, plan mode judgment, and CI context maintenance.

questions.question: A review agent's prompt says "only report high-confidence findings" to reduce false positives. False positive rates remain high. Why didn't this help?

options.A: The instruction was too long, and shortening it to something more direct would have produced the intended reduction in false positives
options.B: General confidence-based instructions like this don't provide a concrete boundary the model can apply consistently — explicit categorical criteria are needed instead
options.C: The model ignores all system prompt instructions related to confidence, treating them as suggestions rather than binding constraints
options.D: This requires a hook, not a prompt change, since confidence-based filtering can only be enforced through deterministic tool-call interception

questions.rationale: Vague instructions like "high-confidence" or "be conservative" don't meaningfully improve precision; explicit, categorical criteria do.

questions.question: Which instruction is most likely to reduce false positives in a comment-accuracy checker?

options.A: "Check that comments are accurate," since a direct, general instruction naturally gives the model a clear standard to apply consistently
options.B: "Flag a comment only when the claimed behavior explicitly contradicts the actual code behavior; do not flag comments that are merely incomplete or stylistically imprecise."
options.C: "Be very careful and conservative," since caution-oriented instructions are the most reliable way to reduce over-flagging in review tasks
options.D: "Only flag comments you're very confident about," since self-reported confidence reliably correlates with true accuracy for this kind of judgment

questions.rationale: This gives an explicit, categorical, testable boundary rather than a vague quality descriptor.

questions.question: A "security" finding category has a 60% false-positive rate, which is eroding developer trust in the review tool overall, including in accurate categories like "syntax errors." What's a reasonable interim step while the security prompt is being improved?

options.A: Nothing — keep the category active regardless of trust impact, since removing any category risks missing a genuine future finding
options.B: Temporarily disable the high-false-positive security category to restore developer trust, while iterating on its prompt separately
options.C: Disable the entire review tool, including accurate categories, since one unreliable category undermines confidence in every category equally
options.D: Increase the false-positive threshold for all categories equally, since a uniform adjustment addresses the root cause across the board

questions.rationale: Because high false-positive rates in one category erode trust across all categories, temporarily disabling just that category while fixing it is a reasonable interim measure.

questions.question: How should severity levels (critical/high/medium/low) be defined for consistent classification?

options.A: Using adjectives only, e.g., "critical means very bad", relying on subjective descriptors with no concrete anchor
options.B: With concrete code examples illustrating each severity level
options.C: By letting the model decide severity however it prefers each time, producing inconsistent classification across different findings
options.D: Severity should not be used at all, discarding a useful prioritization signal rather than defining it more concretely

questions.rationale: Concrete examples per severity level produce consistent classification; adjectives alone don't.

questions.question: Detailed prose instructions for handling documents with inline citations versus separate bibliographies still produce inconsistent extraction. What technique is most likely to help?

options.A: Making the prose instructions even longer, adding more descriptive detail to the same natural-language explanation
options.B: Adding 2-4 few-shot examples demonstrating correct extraction from each document structure variant
options.C: Switching to a different model, assuming a different underlying model would resolve the inconsistency without any prompt change
options.D: Removing the ambiguous document types from the pipeline, narrowing scope rather than improving handling of the variation

questions.rationale: Few-shot examples are the documented fix when detailed instructions alone still produce inconsistent output, especially for structurally varied inputs.

questions.question: An escalation-decision prompt struggles with borderline cases (e.g., a frustrated customer with a resolvable issue vs. one with a genuine policy gap). What's the most effective addition?

options.A: A longer definition of "complex case", since more detailed prose description alone resolves ambiguity in borderline scenarios
options.B: Few-shot examples showing reasoning for ambiguous scenarios — why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives
options.C: A confidence threshold on the model's own self-rating, since numeric self-assessment reliably distinguishes genuine policy gaps from resolvable frustration
options.D: Removing escalation as an option entirely, forcing the agent to resolve every case autonomously regardless of complexity

questions.rationale: Few-shot examples that demonstrate reasoning on genuinely ambiguous cases are the effective lever here, more than either more prose or self-rated confidence.

questions.question: What is the value of including examples that distinguish acceptable code patterns from genuine issues, rather than only examples of clear-cut violations?

options.A: None — only clear violations need examples, since ambiguous cases are rare enough that dedicated examples add little practical value
options.B: It reduces false positives by teaching the model to recognize benign patterns, while still letting it generalize judgment to novel cases it hasn't seen before
options.C: It increases token usage with no benefit, since the added examples don't meaningfully change how the model handles borderline cases
options.D: It only matters for style-related findings, since correctness-related findings don't have genuinely ambiguous cases to learn from

questions.rationale: Examples of acceptable patterns (not just violations) are what let the model generalize judgment correctly, reducing false positives on borderline cases.

questions.question: How many few-shot examples are generally recommended for an ambiguous extraction scenario, according to best practice?

options.A: As many as possible, ideally 50+, since a larger number of examples always produces more reliable generalization
options.B: 2-4 targeted examples showing reasoning, rather than a large number repeating the same pattern
options.C: Exactly 1, to avoid confusing the model, since even a second example risks introducing conflicting signals
options.D: Few-shot examples should never be used for extraction tasks, since they add token overhead without improving accuracy

questions.rationale: A small number of targeted, reasoning-rich examples outperforms a large number of repetitive ones.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.3 — Structured Output via Tool Use and JSON Schemas
questions.question: What does enforcing output via `tool_use` with a JSON schema guarantee?

options.A: Both syntactic validity and full semantic/factual correctness, overstating what schema enforcement alone actually guarantees
options.B: Syntactic validity (schema-compliant structure) only — not semantic correctness
options.C: Neither syntactic nor semantic correctness, understating the real syntactic guarantee that `tool_use` does provide
options.D: Only that the output will be shorter than free text, describing a side effect unrelated to what schema enforcement actually guarantees

questions.rationale: This is the central, repeatedly tested limitation: schema enforcement via `tool_use` eliminates syntax errors but cannot catch semantic errors like a total that doesn't sum correctly.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.3 — Structured Output via Tool Use and JSON Schemas
questions.question: An invoice extraction schema marks `late_fee` as a required field. Many invoices genuinely have no late fee. What risk does this create?

options.A: No risk — the tool will simply fail cleanly on those invoices, returning a clear error rather than any fabricated value
options.B: The model may fabricate a value (e.g., "$0" or a guessed number) to satisfy the required field, since it cannot express "not applicable" otherwise
options.C: This risk only applies to optional fields, since required fields are validated strictly enough to prevent any fabrication from occurring
options.D: `tool_use` schemas cannot include required fields, so this scenario would not be possible to construct in practice

questions.rationale: Required fields for genuinely-absent information push the model toward fabrication; the field should be nullable/optional instead.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.3 — Structured Output via Tool Use and JSON Schemas
questions.question: You have three extraction schemas for three document types and don't know the type in advance. Which `tool_choice` setting is correct?

options.A: `"auto"`, since the model should decide everything freely, which risks the model returning text instead of calling any extraction tool
options.B: `"any"`, guaranteeing a tool call while letting the model pick the fitting schema
options.C: A forced call to one specific schema tool, which would incorrectly commit to a single document type before it's known
options.D: No `tool_choice` is needed for multi-schema situations, relying on default behavior to guarantee a tool call happens

questions.rationale: `"any"` guarantees structured output while accommodating uncertainty about which of several valid schemas fits (same principle as Domain 2, tested here in structured-output context).

questions.task_statement: Task 4.3 — Structured Output via Tool Use and JSON Schemas
questions.question: Why include an `"unclear"` value in an enum field alongside the substantive categories?

options.A: It's purely decorative and has no functional benefit, serving no purpose beyond making the schema look more complete
options.B: It avoids forcing a false-precision choice among fixed categories when the source document is genuinely ambiguous
options.C: It disables the field from being required, since including "unclear" as an enum value automatically makes the field optional
options.D: `tool_use` schemas require at least one `"unclear"`-type value by specification, mandating this pattern for every enum field

questions.rationale: This prevents the model from being forced into an inaccurate category selection when genuine ambiguity exists in the source.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.3 — Structured Output via Tool Use and JSON Schemas
questions.question: A pipeline needs `extract_metadata` to run before any enrichment tool is even considered. Which mechanism enforces this ordering?

options.A: `tool_choice: "auto"`, since giving the model full discretion is what best guarantees `extract_metadata` runs before any other tool
options.B: Forced tool selection: `{"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}`, followed by handling enrichment in subsequent turns
options.C: A longer system prompt asking politely for this order, since sufficiently detailed prose instructions reliably enforce strict tool-call sequencing
options.D: `tool_choice: "any"`, since forcing the model to call *some* tool is equivalent to forcing it to call `extract_metadata` specifically

questions.rationale: Forced tool selection is the mechanism that guarantees a specific tool call happens, useful for enforcing required-first steps.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.3 — Structured Output via Tool Use and JSON Schemas
questions.question: Besides the JSON schema itself, what else should be included in the prompt to handle inconsistent source formatting (e.g., varying date formats across documents)?

options.A: Nothing — the schema alone handles all formatting variation, since structural enforcement alone doesn't resolve inconsistent formatting
options.B: Explicit format normalization rules alongside the strict output schema
options.C: A separate tool call just for date parsing, mandatory for every document, adding overhead beyond what's actually needed
options.D: Formatting rules should never be described in the prompt, leaving inconsistent source formatting entirely unaddressed

questions.rationale: Format normalization guidance in the prompt, alongside the schema, addresses formatting inconsistency that schema structure alone doesn't resolve.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.4 — Validation, Retry, and Feedback Loops
questions.question: An extraction fails JSON schema validation due to a malformed date field. What should the retry request include?

options.A: Only a generic instruction to "try again", since restating the request alone is enough for the model to self-correct the malformed field
options.B: The original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error, so the model has concrete correction targets
options.C: A completely new, unrelated document to test the model, since introducing fresh content helps isolate whether the original document was the issue
options.D: No retry should be attempted for any validation failure, since a single failed attempt should always be treated as unrecoverable

questions.rationale: Retry-with-error-feedback requires including the original document, the failed attempt, and the specific error for effective self-correction.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.4 — Validation, Retry, and Feedback Loops
questions.question: An extraction repeatedly fails to populate a `contract_expiration_date` field because the source document simply never states this date anywhere. Will retrying with error feedback fix this?

options.A: Yes, retrying always eventually succeeds, since enough attempts will eventually surface the correct value even if it isn't in the source
options.B: No — retries are ineffective when the required information is genuinely absent from the source; this isn't a format/structural problem
options.C: Yes, but only after exactly 3 attempts, since that's the standard number of retries before a value is guaranteed to be found
options.D: This should be resolved by switching to `tool_choice: "any"`, since forced tool selection improves the model's ability to locate missing fields

questions.rationale: Recognizing information-absence versus format-error is the key skill; retries only help with the latter category of failure.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.4 — Validation, Retry, and Feedback Loops
questions.question: A review tool tracks a `detected_pattern` field on every finding a developer dismisses. What is the value of this field over time?

options.A: None — dismissed findings should simply be deleted, since retaining data about rejected findings serves no ongoing analytical purpose
options.B: It enables systematic analysis of which code constructs most often trigger dismissed (likely false-positive) findings, informing future prompt improvements
options.C: It is required by MCP tool schemas, which mandate a `detected_pattern` field on every structured finding returned by a tool
options.D: It replaces the need for severity levels, since pattern tracking alone is sufficient to prioritize which findings matter most

questions.rationale: This creates a feedback loop for systematically identifying and fixing recurring false-positive patterns.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.4 — Validation, Retry, and Feedback Loops
questions.question: An extraction tool outputs both `calculated_total` (computed by summing extracted line items) and `stated_total` (extracted directly from the document). Why is this useful?

options.A: It's redundant and should be simplified to just one field, since either total alone provides equivalent information for downstream use
options.B: The discrepancy between the two can be automatically flagged, surfacing potential extraction or source-document errors without requiring a human to notice manually
options.C: It doubles the token cost with no benefit, since the two totals will always match exactly and provide no additional signal
options.D: It is required whenever using `tool_choice: "any"`, since forced tool selection mandates redundant numeric fields for validation

questions.rationale: This redundant-computed-field pattern is a self-correction/self-validation design technique explicitly recommended for catching inconsistencies.

questions.question: A team runs both a blocking pre-merge check and a nightly technical debt report. A manager proposes switching both to the Message Batches API for the 50% savings. What's the correct evaluation?

options.A: Switch both — savings apply regardless of workflow type, since the 50% cost reduction outweighs any latency difference for either use case
options.B: Use batch processing only for the nightly report; keep real-time calls for the blocking pre-merge check, since batch has no guaranteed latency SLA and can take up to 24 hours
options.C: Keep both real-time to avoid any batch complexity, since introducing asynchronous processing anywhere adds more risk than the savings justify
options.D: Switch both to batch with a real-time fallback if the batch is slow, since a fallback path fully resolves the SLA risk for the blocking check

questions.rationale: This is the core batch-fit-assessment pattern: split by latency tolerance, never batch a blocking workflow regardless of cost savings.

questions.question: Which workflow characteristic makes the Message Batches API a good fit?

options.A: A developer is actively waiting for the result before proceeding, a blocking use case poorly suited to batch's lack of latency guarantee
options.B: The workload is non-blocking and latency-tolerant, such as an overnight or weekly report
options.C: The workflow requires multi-turn tool calling within a single request, a capability the Batches API doesn't support
options.D: The workflow requires a guaranteed sub-second response time, directly conflicting with the Batches API's up-to-24-hour window

questions.rationale: Non-blocking, latency-tolerant workloads are exactly the batch API's intended use case.

questions.question: A batch submission of 500 documents completes with 23 documents failing due to a document-size limit being exceeded. What's the correct remediation?

options.A: Resubmit all 500 documents unchanged, since resubmitting the full batch guarantees the 23 failures will be resolved along with everything else
options.B: Resubmit only the 23 failed documents (identified via `custom_id`), after applying an appropriate fix such as chunking the oversized documents
options.C: Discard the 23 failures permanently, since a small failure rate within a 500-document batch is not worth the effort of remediation
options.D: Switch the entire remaining pipeline to real-time calls, since batch failures indicate the API is fundamentally unsuitable for this workload

questions.rationale: `custom_id`-based targeted resubmission of only the failures, with an appropriate fix, is the correct remediation pattern.

questions.question: Which capability is NOT supported by the Message Batches API?

options.A: 50% cost savings compared to real-time calls, a real capability the Batches API does support
options.B: Multi-turn tool calling within a single batched request
options.C: Up to a 24-hour processing window, a real characteristic of how the Batches API operates
options.D: Correlating requests and responses via `custom_id`, a real, supported mechanism of the Batches API

questions.rationale: The Batches API explicitly does not support executing a tool mid-request and returning results within that same request.

questions.question: Before submitting 10,000 documents to the Batches API, what's a cost-efficient best practice?

options.A: Submit the full 10,000 immediately to save time, accepting whatever first-pass success rate the untested prompt happens to produce
options.B: Refine the prompt against a small sample set first to maximize first-pass success and reduce costly iterative resubmission
options.C: Submit in batches of exactly 100 with no testing, splitting the volume without addressing the underlying prompt quality
options.D: Skip prompt testing since batch processing self-corrects errors automatically, relying on the API to fix any prompt weaknesses

questions.rationale: Sample-testing before a large batch run reduces the cost of iteratively fixing prompt issues across a huge volume.

questions.question: A team needs a 30-hour SLA for a report that uses the Batches API, which has up to a 24-hour processing window. How should submission frequency be calculated?

options.A: Submit once and hope it completes in time, since the Batches API's processing window is close enough to guaranteed for planning purposes
options.B: Calculate submission frequency based on the SLA constraint — e.g., submitting within a window that guarantees the 24-hour batch processing still meets the overall 30-hour SLA
options.C: This SLA cannot be met using the Batches API under any circumstances, since a 24-hour processing window can never fit inside a 30-hour SLA
options.D: Switch to `tool_choice: "any"` to speed up batch processing, since forcing tool selection reduces the time each batch request takes to process

questions.rationale: SLA-aware submission scheduling (accounting for the batch window against the total time budget) is the correct approach.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.6 — Multi-Instance and Multi-Pass Review Architectures
questions.question: Why does asking the same Claude Code session that generated code to "review your work critically" tend to be less effective than using a separate instance?

options.A: The same session cannot technically re-read its own output, since prior turns are excluded from what a self-review pass can access
options.B: The generating session retains the reasoning context behind its decisions, making it structurally less likely to question them, even with explicit self-critique instructions
options.C: Self-review always produces syntactically invalid output, since a single session cannot both generate and evaluate code in the same context
options.D: There is no real difference between the two approaches; either produces equivalent review quality regardless of shared reasoning context

questions.rationale: This is the core self-review limitation: retained reasoning context biases the session against catching its own subtle mistakes.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.6 — Multi-Instance and Multi-Pass Review Architectures
questions.question: A single-pass review of a large multi-file PR produces contradictory findings — approving a pattern in one file, flagging the same pattern in another. What's the fix?

options.A: Use a bigger context window model in a single pass, since more capacity alone resolves inconsistent per-file attention
options.B: Split into focused per-file local analysis passes, plus a separate cross-file integration pass
options.C: Randomly discard half the findings to reduce noise, reducing the contradiction count without addressing its actual cause
options.D: Run the review three times and average the results numerically, treating contradictory findings as something to average away

questions.rationale: Attention dilution across many files causes inconsistency; splitting into per-file + integration passes is the documented fix.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.6 — Multi-Instance and Multi-Pass Review Architectures
questions.question: A verification pass has the model output a confidence score (1-10) alongside each extracted field. What is this designed to enable?

options.A: Faster extraction only, describing a speed benefit rather than the actual purpose of confidence-based routing
options.B: Calibrated routing — e.g., sending low-confidence extractions to human review
