options.C: Replacing the JSON schema entirely, when confidence scoring is a complementary layer, not a substitute for schema enforcement
options.D: Skipping validation for high-confidence fields automatically with no human oversight ever, removing review entirely rather than calibrating it

questions.rationale: Self-reported confidence, when calibrated, enables routing decisions like directing attention to lower-confidence extractions.

questions.task_statement: Task 4.6 — Multi-Instance and Multi-Pass Review Architectures
questions.question: Which review architecture is best suited to catching cross-file issues, like a change in file A silently breaking an assumption in file B?

options.A: A single per-file pass only, with no integration step, which is exactly the setup that misses cross-file issues
options.B: A dedicated cross-file integration pass, run separately from (and in addition to) per-file local analysis passes
options.C: Skipping review of files under 50 lines, reducing coverage rather than adding a step to catch cross-file interactions
options.D: A single, very long combined prompt containing all files with no structural separation, the setup prone to attention dilution

questions.rationale: Cross-file issues specifically require a dedicated integration pass that per-file analysis alone cannot catch.

questions.question: An extraction pipeline correctly uses `tool_use` with a JSON schema, includes few-shot examples for varied document formats, and adds a validation-retry loop with specific error feedback. What critical gap might still remain?

options.A: None — this pipeline is complete and error-proof, since schema enforcement combined with retries eliminates all categories of extraction error
options.B: Semantic validation (e.g., checking that extracted totals sum correctly) still needs to be explicitly designed in, since schema enforcement alone doesn't catch semantic errors
options.C: This pipeline cannot use the Batches API, since validation-retry loops are fundamentally incompatible with asynchronous batch processing
options.D: Few-shot examples are unnecessary once a schema is in place, since schema enforcement alone determines the accuracy of extracted values

questions.rationale: Even a well-built pipeline with schema + few-shot + retry still needs explicit semantic checks (like redundant computed fields) since schema compliance never guarantees semantic correctness.

questions.question: A CI review tool has explicit severity criteria with code examples, few-shot examples distinguishing acceptable patterns from real issues, and structured JSON output. Reviewers still complain about excessive comments on trivial style issues. What's the most targeted next fix?

options.A: Disable the tool entirely, since persistent complaints about comment volume indicate the underlying approach cannot be salvaged
options.B: Add explicit criteria narrowing what counts as reportable (e.g., excluding minor style/local pattern preferences), rather than relying on confidence-based filtering
options.C: Switch to the Batches API, since asynchronous processing inherently produces more selective, higher-quality findings
options.D: Remove all severity levels, since a flat, unranked list of findings is easier for reviewers to skim quickly

questions.rationale: This is a precision problem needing explicit scope criteria (what to report vs. skip), consistent with Task 4.1's core lesson, applied here as a targeted refinement.

questions.question: A batch job processes 1,000 mixed-format documents. Which combination of Domain 4 techniques together minimizes cost and maximizes first-pass accuracy?

options.A: No schema and no few-shot examples, since adding either would slow down the initial submission of a 1,000-document batch unnecessarily
options.B: Nullable/optional fields where information may be absent, few-shot examples covering format variety, prompt refinement on a small sample before the full batch submission, and `custom_id`-based failure remediation
options.C: A single rigid required-fields-only schema with no examples, since strict schemas alone are sufficient to guarantee both cost efficiency and first-pass accuracy
options.D: Real-time processing instead of batch, since latency tolerance has no bearing on cost or accuracy for a job of this size

questions.rationale: This combines the domain's core techniques (schema design, few-shot, sample testing, structured failure handling) into one coherent, cost-effective pipeline.

questions.question: An agent's refund-eligibility decision uses `tool_choice: "any"` across three possible response tools (approve, deny, escalate) with few-shot examples for ambiguous cases. What does `"any"` guarantee here that `"auto"` would not?

options.A: That the response will always be "approve", since forcing tool selection biases the model toward the most common, positive outcome
options.B: That the model will call one of the three tools rather than returning free-form conversational text with no structured decision
options.C: That escalation will never be triggered, since `"any"` restricts the model from selecting a tool associated with deferring a decision
options.D: That the response will be faster, since forcing tool selection reduces the number of reasoning tokens the model generates before responding

questions.rationale: `"any"` guarantees some structured tool call happens, avoiding the risk of `"auto"` allowing an unstructured text-only response when a decision must be made.

questions.question: A team wants to both (a) reduce false positives and (b) catch cross-file issues in their review pipeline. Which two Domain 4 techniques directly address each, respectively?

options.A: (a) Batch processing; (b) `tool_choice: "auto"`, neither of which directly addresses false positives or cross-file issues
options.B: (a) Explicit criteria + few-shot examples distinguishing patterns; (b) a separate cross-file integration pass
options.C: (a) Nullable fields; (b) `custom_id` correlation, both of which are extraction-pipeline techniques unrelated to review false positives
options.D: (a) Confidence scores alone; (b) more prose in the system prompt, neither of which reliably addresses either problem

questions.rationale: Each technique maps precisely to its named problem: explicit criteria/few-shot for precision, integration passes for cross-file issues.

questions.question: A schema requires an `industry` field with enum values `["tech", "finance", "retail"]`. A healthcare company's document appears in the pipeline. What happens without an `"other"` option, and what's the fix?

options.A: Nothing happens — this isn't a real concern, since the model will simply leave the field blank when no category truly fits
options.B: The model is forced to select an inaccurate category since none genuinely fits; the fix is adding `"other"` with a free-text detail field
options.C: The schema will automatically reject the document, refusing to process it at all when no enum value accurately applies
options.D: This can only be fixed by using `tool_choice: "auto"` instead of a schema, abandoning enum constraints altogether

questions.rationale: This is the exact scenario the `"other"` + detail pattern exists to prevent: forced false-precision when the fixed enum doesn't cover a real case.

questions.question: Which best distinguishes a "syntax error" from a "semantic error" in structured extraction, and which does `tool_use` eliminate?

options.A: Syntax errors are about meaning; semantic errors are about JSON formatting; `tool_use` eliminates semantic errors
options.B: Syntax errors are malformed/non-schema-compliant output; semantic errors are logically incorrect but structurally valid output (e.g., wrong values); `tool_use` eliminates only syntax errors
options.C: There is no meaningful distinction between the two, since both ultimately just mean the extraction failed
options.D: `tool_use` eliminates both syntax and semantic errors equally, since schema enforcement guarantees end-to-end correctness

questions.rationale: This is the correctly reversed and precise version of the key distinction tested repeatedly across this domain.

questions.question: A support agent's tone/style preferences are specified via prompt instructions, while its refund-approval-threshold logic is enforced via a hook. Why the different approaches for these two things?

options.A: This is inconsistent and should be unified — either both should be enforced via hooks for guaranteed compliance, or both should rely on prompt instructions for flexibility
options.B: Tone/style is a soft preference suited to probabilistic prompt guidance; refund thresholds are a compliance-critical rule needing deterministic enforcement — matching Domain 1's guaranteed-vs-probabilistic distinction, tested here in a Domain 4 prompting context
options.C: Hooks are reserved specifically for financial operations like refunds and cannot be configured to intercept any other category of tool call
options.D: Prompts are only suited to instructing the model on formatting and syntax, not on any subjective or stylistic quality of a response

questions.rationale: This question tests recognizing when prompt-based guidance (Domain 4 territory) is appropriate versus when Domain 1's hook-based enforcement is needed — matching technique to stakes.

questions.question: An extraction schema for medical records includes a `diagnosis_confidence` field, required, alongside the diagnosis text itself. Why might this specific field benefit from being nullable rather than required?

options.A: It never should be nullable under any circumstances, since a confidence field is critical enough to always require a value
options.B: If the source document doesn't itself express a confidence level, forcing a required numeric value invites fabrication of unstated certainty
options.C: Nullable fields are not permitted in medical data schemas, since regulatory requirements mandate every field be populated
options.D: This field should never appear in a schema at all, since confidence is inherently too subjective to be worth extracting

questions.rationale: Same fabrication-prevention logic as Q10, applied to a new field/domain — testing pattern transfer, not memorization of one example.

questions.question: A team's few-shot examples for a review agent only show clear-cut, obvious bugs. Reviewers report the tool struggles specifically on borderline/ambiguous cases. What's missing?

options.A: Nothing — obvious-case examples are sufficient for all scenarios, since the model generalizes equally well regardless of example difficulty
options.B: Examples specifically demonstrating reasoning on ambiguous/borderline cases, since generalization to novel edge cases depends on seeing how the model should reason through uncertainty, not just clear-cut cases
options.C: The examples should be replaced with a numeric confidence threshold instead, since thresholds handle ambiguity more reliably than examples do
options.D: This requires switching to the Batches API, since asynchronous processing naturally improves handling of ambiguous cases

questions.rationale: Few-shot value comes disproportionately from ambiguous-case coverage, not obvious cases the model would likely get right anyway.

questions.question: A `contract_type` enum field has values `["employment", "vendor", "nda"]` with no `"other"` or `"unclear"` option, and no nullable fallback. A batch run processes 5,000 documents. What downstream risk does this schema design create at scale?

options.A: None — enums are always safe regardless of coverage, since the schema itself prevents any value outside the three listed categories
options.B: A systematic pattern of forced misclassification across every document that doesn't cleanly fit one of the three categories, potentially affecting a meaningful fraction of a 5,000-document batch
options.C: The batch will simply fail to run, since Claude cannot produce output for an enum field without a matching category available
options.D: This only matters for real-time processing, since batch requests apply a different, more lenient enum validation rule

questions.rationale: At scale, a poorly-designed enum without escape valves compounds into a systematic, hard-to-detect misclassification problem across the whole batch.

questions.question: Which best describes an appropriate use of `tool_choice: "auto"` in a support agent?

options.A: When deciding whether to process a refund, which must always result in a structured decision, making `"auto"` inappropriate there
options.B: When the agent might either need to call a tool (e.g., look something up) or simply respond conversationally, and both are valid outcomes
options.C: When guaranteed structured output is required for compliance logging, a case better served by forced tool selection than `"auto"`
options.D: `"auto"` should never be used in customer-facing agents, since any customer-facing interaction requires guaranteed structured output

questions.rationale: `"auto"`'s flexibility fits situations where free-form conversational response is a legitimate valid outcome, unlike a required structured decision.

questions.question: A batch-based weekly technical debt report occasionally needs to look up related PRs mid-analysis via a tool before finalizing findings for a given file. Is the Batches API suitable for this specific step?

options.A: Yes, the Batches API supports `tool_use` calls mid-request just like the standard Messages API, since batching only affects request scheduling, not per-request capabilities
options.B: Not directly for that step — the Batches API doesn't support multi-turn tool calling within a single request, so this would need to be handled via separate real-time calls or restructured into a single-shot request with all needed context provided upfront
options.C: No, but only because this particular report runs overnight — if it ran during business hours, mid-request tool calls would be supported
options.D: `custom_id` allows the batch to pause execution, call the required tool, and resume the same request once results are available

questions.rationale: This tests recognizing the specific "no multi-turn tool calling within a batch request" limitation and its practical implication for pipeline design.

questions.question: A validation-retry loop keeps failing on the same document after 3 attempts, always citing "missing field: signature_date." What diagnostic question should be asked before attempting a 4th retry?

options.A: None — always retry indefinitely until it succeeds, since persistence alone will eventually produce a schema-compliant extraction
options.B: Does the source document actually contain a signature date anywhere? If not, retrying further is futile; the field should be nullable and this document should return null for it
options.C: Increase `max_tokens` and retry again, since insufficient token budget is the most common cause of a persistently missing required field
options.D: Switch `tool_choice` to `"auto"` and retry, since forcing a specific tool may be preventing the model from finding the missing field

questions.rationale: This directly applies the retry-limits principle: diagnosing information-absence versus fixable-format-error before continuing to retry.

questions.question: Which is the more effective fix for a review agent producing verbose, inconsistent finding descriptions across different files in the same PR?

options.A: Ask the model to "be more concise" in the system prompt, since a general brevity instruction reliably produces consistent formatting across files
options.B: Provide few-shot examples showing the exact desired output format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix) for consistency
options.C: Reduce the number of files reviewed per PR, since limiting scope is what actually drives consistency in finding descriptions
options.D: Disable structured output and use free text instead, since removing the schema gives the model more room to self-correct its own formatting

questions.rationale: Concrete format examples produce format consistency far more reliably than a vague conciseness instruction.

questions.question: In a redundant-field self-correction design, a `conflict_detected` boolean is set to `true`. What should happen next in a well-designed pipeline?

options.A: The document should be silently discarded, since a detected conflict means the extraction attempt is fundamentally unusable
options.B: The flagged case should be routed for further review/attention (e.g., human review or a targeted retry), since it signals inconsistent source data or an extraction issue worth investigating
options.C: The boolean should simply be ignored, since `conflict_detected` is informational metadata with no required downstream action
options.D: This should trigger an immediate full-batch resubmission, since one conflicting document indicates the entire batch is compromised

questions.rationale: Redundant-field conflict signals are only useful if they route to appropriate follow-up action, connecting Task 4.4's self-correction design to Task 5.5's human-review routing.

questions.question: A team uses `tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "flag_finding"}` for every single review call, forcing a finding to always be reported even when the code is clean. What's wrong with this configuration?

options.A: Nothing — forcing structured output is always correct, since a structured response is preferable to free-form text regardless of context
options.B: Forcing a specific tool call on every turn means the model cannot express "no issues found," likely producing fabricated or trivial findings on clean code
options.C: `tool_choice` cannot be used with review agents, since forced tool selection is only supported for extraction and synthesis workflows
options.D: This is required to satisfy JSON schema validation, since a schema cannot be enforced unless a specific tool is forced on every call

questions.rationale: Forced tool selection should be reserved for genuinely required steps; forcing a "finding" tool on every call removes the model's ability to correctly report a clean result, likely causing false positives.

questions.question: Which best describes the relationship between few-shot examples and JSON schema enforcement in a well-designed extraction pipeline?

options.A: They are redundant — a well-designed JSON schema alone guarantees both correct structure and correct extracted values, making few-shot examples unnecessary
options.B: They address different failure modes: schema enforcement guarantees structural validity, while few-shot examples improve consistency and accuracy of the actual extracted values, especially across varied formats
options.C: Few-shot examples replace the need for a schema entirely, since the examples alone are sufficient to constrain the model's output format
options.D: Schema enforcement replaces the need for few-shot examples entirely, since `tool_use` inherently teaches the model how to handle format variation

questions.rationale: These are complementary techniques addressing different problems (structure vs. content quality/consistency), not substitutes for each other.

questions.question: A weekly batch-based technical debt report and a blocking pre-merge security check share the exact same underlying review prompt and schema. Is this appropriate?

options.A: Yes, always — prompts and schemas should never differ by workflow, since consistency in review criteria matters more than latency requirements
options.B: The prompt/schema content can reasonably be shared, but the *API approach* (batch vs. real-time) must still match each workflow's latency requirements — sharing prompt logic doesn't override the batch-fit assessment
options.C: No — batch and real-time workflows must always use entirely different schemas, since the two APIs are fundamentally incompatible at the schema level
options.D: This is not possible; the Batches API and the standard Messages API cannot share any prompt or schema content between them

questions.rationale: Distinguishes prompt/schema reuse (fine) from API-approach selection (must still match latency needs) — a nuance worth testing since it's easy to conflate the two.

questions.question: A team's confidence-score-based routing sends anything below 7/10 to human review, calibrated using a labeled validation set. What is the purpose of calibrating against a labeled set rather than trusting raw self-reported scores?

options.A: Calibration is unnecessary — raw model confidence scores are always accurate representations of true correctness likelihood
options.B: Raw self-reported confidence isn't inherently well-calibrated to actual accuracy; validating against known-correct labels establishes what threshold actually correlates with real error rates
options.C: Calibration is only relevant for the Batches API, since confidence-score routing doesn't apply to real-time, synchronous processing
options.D: This is purely a cosmetic step with no functional benefit, since any consistent threshold produces the same real-world review outcomes

questions.rationale: This connects Task 4.6/5.5's confidence-calibration principle: raw scores need validation against ground truth before being trusted for routing decisions.

questions.question: A code-generation agent produces working code, and a second independent Claude Code instance reviews it without access to the first instance's reasoning trace. The second instance flags an edge case the first missed. What does this demonstrate?

options.A: The second instance is a fundamentally more capable model, since only a stronger model could catch something the first one missed
options.B: Independent review, unburdened by the generating session's prior reasoning and commitment to its own decisions, catches issues self-review tends to miss
options.C: This is a coincidence unrelated to review architecture, since either instance was equally likely to catch or miss the edge case
options.D: The first instance's code was necessarily low quality, since a missed edge case always indicates a poorly written implementation

questions.rationale: This is the practical demonstration of the self-review-limitation principle in action, not a claim about relative model capability.

questions.question: Overall, which best captures Domain 4's central theme?

options.A: More rigid rules and required fields always produce more reliable structured output, since eliminating optional or ambiguous fields removes any opportunity for the model to introduce inconsistency
options.B: Reliable structured output comes from combining schema-enforced structure (for syntax), few-shot examples (for consistency and edge cases), explicit criteria (for precision), and validation/retry loops with error feedback (for correctable failures) — while recognizing none of these alone guarantees semantic correctness
options.C: Structured output is only reliably achievable through the Batches API, since real-time synchronous calls don't support `tool_use` with JSON schemas the way batch requests do
options.D: Prompt engineering becomes unnecessary once `tool_use` schemas are in place, since schema enforcement alone guarantees both syntactic and semantic correctness of extracted values

questions.rationale: This synthesizes the domain's throughline: multiple complementary techniques, each addressing a distinct failure mode, none sufficient alone.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.1 — Preserving Critical Information Across Long Interactions
questions.question: A long customer support conversation gets progressively summarized to save tokens. By turn 20, the agent describes the refund amount as "a moderate refund" instead of the exact figure stated earlier. What went wrong?

options.A: This is expected and harmless behavior, since vague qualitative descriptions are an acceptable substitute for exact figures
options.B: Progressive summarization eroded a precise numerical detail that mattered operationally
options.C: The customer changed their story, and the vague phrasing reflects a genuine shift in what they reported
options.D: This indicates a tool_use schema error, since imprecise language in a summary points to a malformed structured-output call

questions.rationale: This is the named risk of progressive summarization: precise figures, dates, and stated expectations get smoothed into vague language over repeated summarization passes.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.1 — Preserving Critical Information Across Long Interactions
questions.question: A synthesis agent receives a very long aggregated input from multiple subagents. It reliably references findings from the first and last sections but consistently omits a well-supported finding buried in the middle. What effect explains this?

options.A: The finding was factually incorrect, since inconsistent referencing typically indicates the model judged that content unreliable
options.B: The "lost in the middle" effect — models process beginning and end content more reliably than middle content in long inputs
options.C: The finding used an unsupported data format, since structurally different content is more likely to be skipped during synthesis
options.D: This indicates a tool_choice misconfiguration, since forcing the wrong tool would cause synthesis to skip certain input sections

questions.rationale: This is the direct, named "lost in the middle" phenomenon affecting long aggregated inputs.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.1 — Preserving Critical Information Across Long Interactions
questions.question: A `lookup_order` tool result includes 40+ fields (warehouse codes, internal SKUs, carrier metadata) when only 5 are relevant to the current return request. What's the recommended fix?

options.A: Leave all fields in context since more information is always better, disregarding the token cost of irrelevant data
options.B: Trim the tool output to only relevant fields before it accumulates in context
options.C: Increase the context window size instead, compensating for noise rather than reducing the irrelevant data itself
options.D: Remove the tool entirely, eliminating needed functionality rather than trimming its output to relevant fields

questions.rationale: Verbose tool outputs consume disproportionate context relative to their relevance; trimming to relevant fields is the direct fix.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.1 — Preserving Critical Information Across Long Interactions
questions.question: What is the purpose of maintaining a persistent "case facts" block (order numbers, amounts, dates, statuses) included in every prompt, separate from the summarized conversation history?

options.A: It has no functional purpose beyond formatting preference, since the same information is already present in the summarized history
options.B: It ensures hard transactional facts survive even if the narrative history gets summarized/compressed over a long conversation
options.C: It replaces the need for tool calls entirely, since the case-facts block alone is sufficient to answer any follow-up customer question
options.D: It is required by the MCP `isError` specification, which mandates a persistent facts block for any tool that can fail

questions.rationale: This directly counters the progressive-summarization risk by keeping critical facts outside the part of context that gets compressed.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.1 — Preserving Critical Information Across Long Interactions
questions.question: A downstream synthesis agent has a limited context budget. Upstream subagents currently return full verbose reasoning chains and prose. What change would better respect the downstream budget?

options.A: Have upstream agents return structured key facts, citations, and relevance scores instead of full prose and reasoning chains
options.B: Increase the downstream agent's context window instead, leaving the upstream agents' verbose output unchanged
options.C: Have upstream agents stop returning any information at all, removing their contribution to the pipeline entirely
options.D: Have upstream agents write directly to a shared file the downstream agent never reads, disconnecting the two stages entirely

questions.rationale: Structured, condensed output from upstream agents (facts + citations + relevance scores) respects a downstream agent's limited context budget far better than verbose prose.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.1 — Preserving Critical Information Across Long Interactions
questions.question: Where should key findings/summaries be placed within a long aggregated input to mitigate position effects?

options.A: Buried in the middle, surrounded by supporting detail, since burying key findings preserves the natural narrative flow of the input
options.B: At the beginning of the aggregated input, with detailed results organized under explicit section headers
options.C: Only at the very end, after all raw data, relying solely on end-of-input attention to surface the most important conclusions
options.D: Position within the input has no effect on model attention, so findings can be placed anywhere without any practical consequence

questions.rationale: Placing key findings at the start (plus explicit headers for detail) directly mitigates the lost-in-the-middle effect.

questions.question: A customer says: "I want to speak to a human right now." The issue itself looks straightforward and resolvable by the agent. What should happen?

options.A: Attempt to resolve the issue first, and only escalate if the customer insists again, delaying an explicit request for a human
options.B: Honor the explicit request and escalate immediately, without first attempting an unrequested investigation
options.C: Explain to the customer why a human isn't necessary, overriding their explicit preference rather than honoring it
options.D: Ignore the request since the issue is simple, disregarding the customer's explicit preference for human assistance

questions.rationale: Explicit requests for a human should be honored immediately, distinct from the case of a merely frustrated customer with a resolvable issue.

questions.question: A customer is visibly frustrated but their issue (a standard, policy-covered replacement) is well within the agent's capability to resolve. What's the appropriate response?

options.A: Escalate immediately due to the frustration, treating visible emotion as sufficient grounds on its own to hand off to a human
options.B: Acknowledge the frustration, offer to resolve the issue, and escalate only if the customer reiterates a preference for a human
options.C: Ignore the emotional tone entirely and proceed mechanically, addressing the issue without any acknowledgment of the customer's frustration
options.D: Use a sentiment classifier to auto-escalate based on a frustration threshold, treating detected negative tone as the primary escalation signal

questions.rationale: Frustration alone (without an explicit request or genuine complexity) doesn't warrant automatic escalation; acknowledge and offer resolution first.

questions.question: A customer asks for a price match against a competitor's price. The company's policy document addresses only same-site price adjustments and is silent on competitor price matching. What should the agent do?

options.A: Deny the request, assuming silence means "no", treating the absence of an explicit rule as an automatic rejection
options.B: Approve the request, assuming silence means "yes", treating the absence of an explicit rule as an automatic approval
options.C: Escalate, since this is a genuine policy gap rather than something the agent should decide unilaterally
options.D: Make up a plausible-sounding policy to tell the customer, inventing a rule that isn't actually documented anywhere

questions.rationale: Policy silence/gaps on the specific request are an explicit legitimate escalation trigger, distinct from cases where policy clearly does or doesn't cover the situation.

questions.question: A team proposes using the agent's self-reported confidence score (1-10) as the primary signal for escalation, escalating anything below 6. What is the main risk?

options.A: None — self-reported confidence is a reliable, well-calibrated proxy for case difficulty, and can safely be used as the primary escalation signal
options.B: The model can be confidently wrong on exactly the hardest cases, meaning low raw self-reported confidence isn't a reliable proxy for actual complexity
options.C: This approach requires the Batches API, since confidence-based escalation can only be computed in an asynchronous processing context
options.D: Confidence scores can only be produced via hooks, not prompts, so this approach wouldn't be technically possible to implement

questions.rationale: Self-reported confidence is explicitly called out as an unreliable escalation proxy, since the model can be miscalibrated exactly where it matters most.

questions.question: A `get_customer` lookup for "John Smith" returns three matching records. What should the agent do?

options.A: Select the most recently active record, using account activity as a heuristic to resolve the ambiguity automatically
options.B: Ask the customer for an additional identifying detail (e.g., email, order number, zip code) rather than guessing
options.C: Merge all three records and proceed, combining potentially unrelated customer accounts into a single working record
options.D: Escalate to a human immediately without attempting clarification, bypassing the simple identifier request that could resolve this directly

questions.rationale: Multiple ambiguous matches call for requesting additional identifiers, not heuristic-based selection.

questions.question: Which is NOT a reliable escalation trigger per Domain 5 principles?

options.A: The customer explicitly asks for a human agent, a clear and reliable trigger for escalation
options.B: A genuine gap or exception in stated policy, a legitimate reason to escalate rather than guess
options.C: Detected negative sentiment in the customer's message, used as the primary trigger
options.D: The agent genuinely being unable to make further progress, a legitimate signal that escalation is warranted

questions.rationale: Sentiment-based escalation is explicitly named as unreliable; the other three are legitimate, named triggers.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.3 — Error Propagation Across Multi-Agent Systems
questions.question: A search subagent times out. Its error response to the coordinator includes only `{"status": "search unavailable"}`. What is the problem, and what should be included instead?

options.A: No problem — a status message is sufficient, since the coordinator only needs to know that something went wrong, not why
options.B: This generic status hides valuable context; the coordinator needs failure type, what was attempted, any partial results, and possible alternatives to make an intelligent recovery decision
options.C: The subagent should instead terminate the entire workflow immediately rather than reporting a timeout back to the coordinator at all
options.D: The subagent should retry silently forever without informing the coordinator, since surfacing transient errors adds unnecessary noise

questions.rationale: Structured error context (not a generic status string) is what enables intelligent coordinator recovery decisions.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.3 — Error Propagation Across Multi-Agent Systems
questions.question: A document-analysis subagent's search for a specific topic returns zero matching documents — a legitimate, successful query with no results. How should this be distinguished from a timeout failure in the returned data?

options.A: They should be reported identically, since both result in "no data" being available to the coordinator either way
options.B: They should be clearly distinguished — a valid empty result is a success; a timeout is an access failure requiring a different response
options.C: Empty results should always be treated as failures, since a search returning nothing usually indicates something went wrong
options.D: Timeouts should always be treated as successes with empty data, since presenting a clean result avoids alarming the coordinator unnecessarily

questions.rationale: Conflating access failures with valid empty results prevents the coordinator from making the correct distinction between "nothing to find" and "something went wrong."

questions.task_statement: Task 5.3 — Error Propagation Across Multi-Agent Systems
questions.question: A subagent catches a failure internally and returns an empty result marked `success: true` to avoid "bothering" the coordinator. What anti-pattern is this?

options.A: Appropriate local error recovery, since converting any internal failure into a clean empty result is the standard recommended pattern
options.B: Silent suppression — hiding a real failure from the coordinator by masking it as a successful empty result
options.C: The correct way to handle all transient errors, since presenting success prevents unnecessary noise from reaching the coordinator
options.D: A required MCP behavior, since the protocol mandates that subagents always report success regardless of internal outcome

questions.rationale: This is explicitly named as an anti-pattern; failures that can't be locally resolved should be surfaced, not disguised as success.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.3 — Error Propagation Across Multi-Agent Systems
questions.question: One of four subagents in a research pipeline fails irrecoverably. What should the coordinator generally do?

options.A: Immediately terminate the entire workflow, discarding all other subagents' completed work regardless of its usefulness
options.B: Proceed with partial results from the successful subagents, annotating the final output with the coverage gap caused by the failure
options.C: Silently present the report as fully complete with no annotation, hiding the fact that one subagent's contribution is missing
options.D: Retry the entire pipeline from scratch indefinitely, repeating all four subagents' work rather than proceeding with what succeeded

questions.rationale: Full workflow termination on a single failure is an anti-pattern; proceeding with annotated partial results is preferred over both termination and silent gaps.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.3 — Error Propagation Across Multi-Agent Systems
questions.question: A subagent hits a rate-limit error (clearly transient and retryable). Per best practice, what should it do before escalating to the coordinator?

options.A: Immediately escalate without any local handling, since only the coordinator has the authority to decide how to respond to any error
options.B: Attempt local recovery (e.g., retry after a delay), escalating only if it cannot resolve the issue locally, and including partial results plus what was attempted if it does escalate
options.C: Silently drop the task and report success, since a rate-limit error usually resolves on its own without any explicit handling
options.D: Terminate the whole multi-agent workflow itself, since a single subagent's error should be treated as a critical, unrecoverable failure

questions.rationale: Local recovery for transient, retryable errors should happen before escalation; only unresolvable errors should be propagated, with context.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.4 — Context Management in Large Codebase Exploration
questions.question: In a long exploration session, the agent starts saying things like "typical error-handling classes in this codebase usually..." instead of referencing the specific classes it identified earlier in the same session. What does this indicate?

options.A: The codebase changed during the session, since references to "typical" patterns indicate the agent detected new files being added mid-session
options.B: Context degradation — earlier concrete findings have effectively been pushed out of effective attention as the session grew
options.C: A tool_choice misconfiguration, since forcing the wrong tool would cause the agent to generalize rather than cite specific findings
options.D: The MCP server disconnected, since loss of connection would cause the agent to fall back to generic, non-specific language

questions.rationale: Vague "typical pattern" references replacing specific earlier findings is the named symptom of context degradation in long sessions.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.4 — Context Management in Large Codebase Exploration
questions.question: What technique directly counters context degradation in long exploration sessions?

options.A: Increasing the iteration cap, since allowing the loop to run longer gives the agent more opportunities to recall earlier findings
options.B: Having the agent maintain a scratchpad file recording key findings, and referencing it for later questions
options.C: Switching to `tool_choice: "any"`, since forcing tool calls keeps the model actively engaged with fresh information throughout the session
options.D: Disabling all MCP servers, since fewer available tools reduces the amount of context competing for the model's attention

questions.rationale: Scratchpad files persist key findings across context boundaries, directly counteracting degradation from losing track of earlier discoveries.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.4 — Context Management in Large Codebase Exploration
questions.question: A main coordinating agent needs to trace refund-flow dependencies across a large codebase without flooding its own context with verbose exploration output. What's the recommended pattern?

options.A: Have the main agent perform all exploration itself, in full detail, since keeping investigation centralized improves coordination
options.B: Spawn a subagent to investigate the specific question, isolating verbose exploration output while the main agent stays at a high level
options.C: Skip exploration entirely and guess at the dependencies, since tracing refund-flow logic manually would take too long to be practical
options.D: Use `fork_session` to duplicate the main agent's entire context, giving the fork the same context budget pressure as the original

questions.rationale: Subagent delegation for specific exploration questions isolates verbose output from the main agent's context, per the documented pattern.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.4 — Context Management in Large Codebase Exploration
questions.question: Before spawning subagents for the next phase of a multi-phase investigation, what should happen with the findings from the phase just completed?

options.A: Nothing — the raw exploration history should be carried forward unchanged, preserving every detail for the next phase
options.B: Key findings should be summarized and injected as initial context for the next phase, rather than carrying forward the full raw history
options.C: The findings should be discarded entirely, since each phase of a multi-phase investigation should start with no prior context
options.D: The findings should be sent directly to a human for review before continuing, pausing the investigation at every phase boundary

questions.rationale: Summarizing between phases and injecting the summary (not raw history) into the next phase's context is the documented pattern.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.4 — Context Management in Large Codebase Exploration
questions.question: A long-running multi-agent process needs to support crash recovery. What is the recommended structural approach?

options.A: Simply restart from the very beginning after any crash, since re-exploration guarantees the most accurate and up-to-date state
options.B: Each agent exports state to a known location; the coordinator loads a manifest summarizing progress on resume and injects relevant parts into each agent's prompt
options.C: Crash recovery is not possible with the Agent SDK, since there's no built-in mechanism for persisting or resuming multi-agent progress
options.D: Use `--resume` with no additional structure needed, since named session resumption alone reconstructs full multi-agent progress automatically

questions.rationale: Structured state manifests, loaded and injected on resume, are the documented crash-recovery pattern — distinct from simple session resumption.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.4 — Context Management in Large Codebase Exploration
questions.question: What does the `/compact` command do, and when is it useful?

options.A: It permanently deletes the session, since compacting removes all prior conversation history beyond recovery
options.B: It reduces context usage mid-session, useful when context has filled with verbose discovery output during extended exploration
options.C: It forks the session into two branches, letting you explore two different approaches from the current point independently
options.D: It converts the session into a batch job, deferring further processing to run asynchronously instead of interactively

questions.rationale: `/compact` is specifically for reducing accumulated context usage without ending the session.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.5 — Human Review Workflows and Confidence Calibration
questions.question: An extraction system reports 97% overall accuracy. Should this be trusted as sufficient to reduce human review across the board?

options.A: Yes — a 97% aggregate figure is always sufficient justification, regardless of how that accuracy is distributed across document types or fields
options.B: Not without further validation — aggregate accuracy can mask poor performance on a specific document type or field; accuracy should be checked broken down by type and field first
options.C: No — 97% is too low to ever reduce human review, since accuracy below 99% should always trigger full manual review regardless of breakdown
options.D: Aggregate accuracy is irrelevant to review workflow decisions, since review routing should instead be based solely on document volume

questions.rationale: This is the named risk: a good-looking aggregate number can hide a real, isolated weak spot that only breakdown analysis reveals.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.5 — Human Review Workflows and Confidence Calibration
questions.question: What is the purpose of stratified random sampling (across document types/confidence bands) in a quality-monitoring workflow?

options.A: To reduce the total amount of data processed, since sampling only a fraction of documents lowers overall pipeline compute cost
options.B: To measure error rates specifically within categories like "high-confidence extractions" and catch novel error patterns a single overall sample might miss
options.C: To eliminate the need for confidence scores entirely, since sampling alone can determine which extractions are trustworthy
options.D: To replace the JSON schema validation step, since sampling accuracy checks make structural validation unnecessary

questions.rationale: Stratified sampling targets specific segments (e.g., high-confidence bucket) precisely because uniform overall sampling can miss segment-specific problems.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.5 — Human Review Workflows and Confidence Calibration
questions.question: A model outputs field-level confidence scores. Before using these scores to set a human-review threshold, what should happen?

options.A: Nothing — raw scores can be trusted immediately at face value, since model-reported confidence is inherently well-calibrated
options.B: The scores should be calibrated against a labeled validation set to establish what threshold actually correlates with real accuracy
options.C: The scores should be discarded and ignored entirely, since uncalibrated confidence provides no useful signal whatsoever
options.D: The scores should be averaged into a single document-level number and nothing else, discarding the more granular field-level detail

questions.rationale: Calibration against labeled ground truth is required before raw confidence scores can be trusted for routing decisions.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.5 — Human Review Workflows and Confidence Calibration
questions.question: Besides low model confidence, what other case type should be prioritized for human review?

options.A: Cases that took the longest to process, using processing time as a proxy rather than actual source-data ambiguity
options.B: Cases with ambiguous or contradictory source documents
options.C: Cases from the largest file size documents only, using document size as an unrelated proxy for review priority
options.D: All cases should be reviewed equally regardless of any signal, ignoring available signals that should inform prioritization

questions.rationale: Ambiguous/contradictory source material is named alongside low confidence as a trigger for prioritized human review.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.6 — Information Provenance and Uncertainty in Synthesis
questions.question: A synthesis agent produces a well-written report, but none of its claims can be traced back to which source supports them. What went wrong upstream?

options.A: Nothing — synthesis output never needs traceable sourcing, since a well-written report is sufficient on its own
options.B: Findings were likely compressed during summarization without preserving explicit claim-to-source mappings, losing provenance
options.C: The synthesis agent used the wrong `tool_choice` setting, causing it to lose track of which claims came from which source
options.D: This can only be fixed by re-running the entire pipeline from scratch with a different model, rather than adjusting how findings are structured

questions.rationale: Provenance loss during summarization, when claim-source mappings aren't explicitly preserved, is the named root cause.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.6 — Information Provenance and Uncertainty in Synthesis
questions.question: Two credible sources report different statistics for the same metric. How should the synthesis agent handle this?

options.A: Silently choose the more recent-sounding source and discard the other, presenting only the newer figure as fact
options.B: Annotate the conflict explicitly, attributing each value to its respective source, rather than arbitrarily selecting one
options.C: Average the two numbers together and present the average as fact, blending the two disagreeing figures into one
options.D: Omit both statistics entirely, leaving the disagreement out of the report rather than surfacing it to the reader

questions.rationale: Explicit conflict annotation with source attribution is the correct handling; arbitrary selection or averaging misrepresents the actual state of evidence.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.6 — Information Provenance and Uncertainty in Synthesis
questions.question: Two sources disagree on a company's market share — one from 2022, one from 2024. Without publication dates included in the structured output, what risk arises?

options.A: No risk — market share figures never change over time, so any apparent disagreement must reflect a data error
options.B: The synthesis agent might misinterpret a legitimate temporal difference as a genuine contradiction between the sources
options.C: This can only be resolved via `tool_choice: "any"`, forcing the model to reconcile the two figures during tool selection
options.D: This risk only applies to financial data, not other types of statistics, since only numeric fields are sensitive to temporal context

questions.rationale: Requiring publication/collection dates prevents exactly this kind of misread — temporal difference mistaken for contradiction.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.6 — Information Provenance and Uncertainty in Synthesis
questions.question: What structured data should subagents output to preserve attribution as findings move downstream to synthesis?

options.A: Just the raw claim text, with no additional metadata, leaving attribution to be reconstructed later if needed
options.B: Claim-source mappings including source URL, document name, and relevant excerpt, kept separate from the claim content itself
options.C: A single combined block of unstructured text mixing claims and sources together, without separating the two into distinct fields
options.D: Nothing — synthesis agents should re-derive sourcing themselves from scratch, independently locating the original source for each claim

questions.rationale: Structured claim-source mappings, explicitly separated from content, are what allow downstream preservation of attribution.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.6 — Information Provenance and Uncertainty in Synthesis
questions.question: A final research report presents both a well-established scientific consensus and a single contested preliminary study with equal weight and identical framing. What issue does this illustrate?

options.A: This is the correct, neutral way to present all findings, since giving every source equal framing avoids introducing reviewer bias
options.B: The report fails to structure content to distinguish well-established findings from contested ones, losing important context about confidence/reliability
options.C: This can only be fixed by adding more citations, since additional sources alone would resolve the lack of distinction between claim types
options.D: This is a `tool_choice` configuration issue, since forcing a specific synthesis tool would have preserved the distinction automatically

questions.rationale: Reports should structurally distinguish confidence tiers (well-established vs. contested), not present all findings as equally authoritative.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.6 — Information Provenance and Uncertainty in Synthesis
questions.question: A synthesis report converts a set of financial figures into flowing narrative prose, rather than presenting them as a table. What issue does this raise?

options.A: None — prose is always the best format for all content types, since it reads more naturally to a human reviewer regardless of what data is being presented
options.B: Financial/tabular data often loses clarity and precision when force-converted to prose; format should match content type (tables for financial data, prose for narrative news, structured lists for technical findings)
options.C: This is required by the MCP resource specification, which mandates a single content format across an entire synthesis report
options.D: This can only be fixed by switching from a single synthesis pass to a multi-pass review architecture, regardless of the underlying formatting issue

questions.rationale: Matching output format to content type (rather than uniform prose) is an explicit best practice for synthesis output design.

questions.question: A support session spans 30 turns. By the end, the agent both retains exact dollar figures (via a persistent case-facts block) and correctly declines to escalate despite mild customer frustration on an issue it's actively resolving. Which two Domain 5 techniques are being applied correctly here?

options.A: Stratified sampling and provenance tracking, since both techniques apply to how information is validated and attributed across a session
options.B: The case-facts persistence pattern (5.1) and correct escalation-trigger judgment, i.e., not treating sentiment alone as an escalation signal (5.2)
options.C: Crash recovery manifests and `/compact`, since both techniques help the agent manage a long-running session's state efficiently
options.D: Claim-source mapping and confidence calibration, since both are needed to justify not escalating despite the customer's frustration

questions.rationale: This scenario combines the two relevant task-statement techniques correctly: precise fact retention and appropriate (non-sentiment-driven) escalation judgment.

questions.question: A research pipeline experiences a subagent timeout mid-investigation. The coordinator receives structured error context, proceeds with partial results, and the final synthesis explicitly notes which sections have full source support versus coverage gaps. Which two Domain 5 task areas does this demonstrate together?

options.A: Error propagation (5.3) and provenance/coverage annotation (5.6)
options.B: Escalation resolution (5.2) and human review routing (5.5), tasks concerned with different aspects of the workflow than what's described
options.C: Context degradation handling (5.4) and case-facts persistence (5.1), tasks about long-session memory rather than error handling and provenance
options.D: None of these areas apply here, despite the scenario directly matching two specific Domain 5 task areas

questions.rationale: Structured error handling with partial-results continuation is 5.3; explicitly annotating coverage confidence in the final report is 5.6.

questions.question: A multi-phase codebase exploration uses scratchpad files, subagent delegation for specific questions, and inter-phase summarization. Midway through, the process crashes. What additional Domain 5 mechanism would best support recovery?

options.A: A structured state manifest that the coordinator can load on resume and inject into agent prompts
options.B: Simply restarting from scratch with no memory of prior work, discarding everything discovered before the crash
options.C: Switching immediately to the Batches API, moving the entire exploration workflow to asynchronous processing
options.D: Disabling all subagents going forward, reverting to a single-agent approach for the remainder of the investigation

questions.rationale: Manifest-based crash recovery is the specific mechanism designed for exactly this situation, complementing (but distinct from) the other context-management techniques already in use.

questions.question: A pipeline uses field-level confidence scores calibrated against a labeled set, routes low-confidence and ambiguous-source cases to human review, and validates accuracy broken down by document type. What Domain 5 principle unifies all three practices?

options.A: Provenance preservation, since calibrating confidence and validating by document type are both examples of tracking where information originated
options.B: Rigorous, evidence-based human-review workflow design that doesn't over-trust aggregate metrics or raw uncalibrated model outputs
options.C: Error propagation across multi-agent systems, since routing low-confidence cases to review is fundamentally an error-handling mechanism
options.D: Context window management, since confidence calibration is primarily about managing how much information fits in a single request

questions.rationale: All three practices are facets of Task 5.5's core theme: don't trust surface-level signals (aggregate accuracy, raw confidence) without validation.

questions.question: A support agent correctly (a) asks for an additional identifier when multiple customer records match, and (b) escalates immediately when a customer explicitly requests a human, without first investigating. What do both behaviors have in common from a Domain 5 perspective?

options.A: Both are examples of provenance tracking, since each behavior involves preserving a record of where information originated
options.B: Both reflect correctly recognizing specific, well-defined triggers (ambiguous match, explicit request) rather than defaulting to a guess or a blanket policy
options.C: Both require the Batches API, since asynchronous processing is what enables an agent to pause and request clarification
options.D: Both are unrelated to escalation/ambiguity resolution, since neither behavior involves handing the conversation off to a human

questions.rationale: Both are concrete applications of Task 5.2's principle: respond to specific, legitimate triggers rather than heuristics or blanket rules.

questions.question: Which combination of failures would be worst for a research pipeline's reliability, combining two separate Domain 5 anti-patterns?

options.A: A subagent silently suppresses a real failure as a success (5.3), and the final synthesis presents the resulting incomplete findings as fully comprehensive with no coverage annotation (5.6)
options.B: A subagent correctly retries a transient error, and the synthesis correctly annotates a coverage gap, representing two reliability best practices working as intended
options.C: A subagent escalates a policy gap, and the coordinator asks for a customer identifier, both of which are appropriate, well-defined escalation triggers
options.D: The coordinator uses `/compact` and a scratchpad file, both standard techniques for managing context in a long-running session

questions.rationale: This combines two named anti-patterns (silent suppression, and failing to annotate coverage gaps) compounding into a report that appears complete but is actually silently incomplete and unflagged.

questions.question: A developer resumes a named session after two days without mentioning that three files were modified externally in the meantime. The agent proceeds to make changes based on its stale understanding of those files. Which Domain 5 (and cross-domain, Task 1.7) principle was violated?

options.A: Provenance preservation, since the issue here is fundamentally about tracking where the file changes originated from
options.B: The requirement to explicitly inform a resumed session about file changes, since it won't automatically detect them
options.C: Stratified sampling, since verifying file state after a gap is a form of sampling the codebase for consistency
options.D: The `/memory` command's function, since `/memory` is what would have surfaced the external file changes automatically

questions.rationale: This is a direct real-world consequence of not following the resume-with-file-change-notification pattern (Task 1.7, closely tied to Domain 5's context-currency concerns).

questions.question: A batch of documents is processed with confidence scores, but the scores were never validated against any labeled data — they're used as-is straight from the model. Six months later, an audit reveals the "high-confidence" bucket actually had a 15% error rate. What was skipped?

options.A: Nothing was skipped; this is expected variance, since a 15% error rate within a high-confidence bucket is well within normal tolerances
options.B: Calibration of confidence scores against a labeled validation set, which would have revealed the miscalibration before it caused six months of under-reviewed errors
options.C: The Batches API's built-in calibration feature, which automatically adjusts confidence scores against historical accuracy without manual validation
options.D: `tool_choice: "any"` configuration, which ensures confidence scores are calibrated correctly as part of the tool-selection process

questions.rationale: This is a real-world consequence of skipping the calibration step described in Task 5.5 — trusting raw scores led to a hidden, costly error rate.

questions.question: A report states a statistic with no source, no date, and doesn't indicate whether it's well-established or preliminary. A reader has no way to assess its reliability. Which three Domain 5.6 practices, if all had been followed, would have prevented this?

options.A: Claim-source mapping preservation, requiring publication dates, and structuring reports to distinguish confidence tiers
options.B: Case-facts persistence, scratchpad files, and `/compact`, since these context-management techniques govern how facts are retained
options.C: Escalation criteria, stratified sampling, and manifest-based recovery, since these reliability techniques govern how errors are handled
options.D: None of these practices are relevant to this problem, since missing source attribution is purely a formatting concern

questions.rationale: All three named 5.6 practices, working together, directly address exactly this failure: unsourced, undated, unqualified claims.

questions.question: A 25-turn support conversation reaches a point where the agent needs to recall the exact order number mentioned in turn 2. Assuming no case-facts block was used, what's the most likely outcome, and why?

options.A: Perfect recall, since models never lose track of details in long conversations regardless of how much summarization has occurred
options.B: A risk of imprecise or lost recall, since the detail may have been compressed away during progressive summarization and is deep in the "middle" of a long conversation, away from the more reliably attended beginning/end
options.C: The conversation would fail to continue entirely once turn 25 is reached, since there's a hard structural limit tied to turn count
options.D: The order number would automatically be moved to a separate database by the API without any explicit extraction step required

questions.rationale: Without the case-facts persistence pattern, this scenario combines both named Task 5.1 risks: summarization erosion and lost-in-the-middle positioning.

questions.question: A coordinator's error-handling code distinguishes between `errorCategory: "transient"` (retry locally) and structural failures needing escalation, and separately, its synthesis step distinguishes well-supported findings from contested ones. Which two domains' principles are both being applied here, and how do they relate?

options.A: Domain 2 (structured MCP errors) and Domain 5 (provenance/confidence-tier reporting) — both rely on structured metadata to enable better downstream decisions, one for errors, one for findings
options.B: Domain 3 (Claude Code configuration) and Domain 4 (prompt engineering), since both practices involve giving the model explicit written guidance
options.C: This only reflects Domain 1 principles, since both examples involve a coordinator agent making a decision about how to proceed
options.D: These two practices are unrelated design choices that happen to appear together in the same system by coincidence

questions.rationale: This question tests recognizing a shared underlying pattern (structured metadata enabling better downstream decisions) across two different domains and use cases.

questions.question: Which best distinguishes Task 5.5 (human review workflows) from Task 4.4 (validation/retry loops), given both deal with handling extraction problems?

options.A: They are functionally identical, since both ultimately result in a corrected or reviewed final output for the affected document
options.B: 4.4 is about automatically correcting recoverable extraction failures via retry; 5.5 is about routing genuinely uncertain or low-confidence cases to human judgment when automated correction isn't appropriate or sufficient
options.C: 5.5 only applies to batch-processed documents, while 4.4 only applies to documents processed through the synchronous, real-time API
options.D: 4.4 requires human involvement at every retry attempt, while 5.5 is a fully automated process with no human review step

questions.rationale: This distinguishes two complementary but distinct reliability mechanisms: automated self-correction (4.4) versus human-in-the-loop routing for genuine uncertainty (5.5).

questions.question: A coordinator receives partial results after a subagent failure, with structured context on what was attempted. It decides to proceed with synthesis rather than retry, since the missing information isn't critical to the report's core conclusions. Is this decision consistent with Domain 5 principles?

options.A: No — the coordinator must always retry regardless of context, since proceeding without complete information is never acceptable
options.B: Yes — this is exactly the kind of intelligent recovery decision that structured error context (rather than a generic failure message) is designed to enable
options.C: No — the coordinator must always terminate the workflow on any subagent failure, regardless of whether the missing data is critical
options.D: This decision is irrelevant to Domain 5, since it concerns synthesis quality rather than reliability or error handling

questions.rationale: This demonstrates the coordinator using structured error context correctly to make a judgment call, rather than defaulting to either blind retry or full termination.

questions.question: A support agent's tool outputs are trimmed to relevant fields, its case facts persist across turns, and its escalation logic uses explicit criteria rather than sentiment. Which Domain 5 tasks does this combination draw from?

options.A: 5.1 (context preservation) and 5.2 (escalation) only
options.B: 5.3, 5.4, and 5.5 only, task areas concerned with error propagation, context degradation, and human review rather than what's described
options.C: 5.6 only, a task area about provenance and multi-source synthesis rather than context preservation and escalation
options.D: None — this combination isn't coherent, despite directly reflecting two specific, well-matched Domain 5 task areas

questions.rationale: This correctly identifies that trimmed tool outputs and case-facts persistence are 5.1, while explicit non-sentiment-based escalation criteria are 5.2.

questions.question: A team's crash-recovery manifest includes each agent's completed steps and key findings but omits any note about which files were still being actively modified at the time of the crash. What risk does this omission create?

options.A: None — the manifest is already sufficient for full recovery, since completed steps and findings capture everything needed to resume safely
options.B: On resume, the coordinator may not know which files require re-verification for consistency with in-progress changes at the time of the crash, risking incorrect assumptions about file state
options.C: This can only be resolved by discarding the manifest entirely and having every agent restart its exploration completely from scratch
options.D: This is unrelated to the manifest's purpose, since file-modification state is tracked separately by the file system, not the manifest

questions.rationale: This extends the manifest concept to a realistic gap: manifests need to capture enough state detail to support genuinely safe resumption, not just high-level progress.

questions.question: A pipeline correctly implements nullable fields (Domain 4) to avoid fabrication, and separately implements stratified sampling by document type (Domain 5) to catch accuracy issues. How do these two techniques complement each other?

options.A: They don't relate to each other at all — nullable fields address extraction-time schema design, while stratified sampling is a completely separate, unrelated auditing practice
options.B: Nullable fields reduce one source of extraction error (fabrication under forced-required fields); stratified sampling helps detect remaining accuracy issues (including ones nullable fields alone wouldn't prevent) across specific segments
options.C: Once nullable fields are implemented, fabrication is fully eliminated, making stratified sampling useful only for catching formatting errors
options.D: Stratified sampling replaces the need for nullable fields, since sampling alone can catch any fabricated values that appear in the extracted output

questions.rationale: This tests recognizing that these are complementary, not redundant, reliability techniques addressing different failure modes at different pipeline stages.

questions.question: Overall, which best captures Domain 5's central theme across all six task statements?

options.A: Reliability is achieved primarily by using models with larger context windows, since more capacity to hold conversation history eliminates the need for active context curation or escalation criteria
options.B: Reliability comes from actively managing what information survives across context boundaries, applying well-defined (not proxy-based) triggers for escalation and review, structuring errors and findings with enough metadata for good downstream decisions, and never over-trusting aggregate or self-reported signals without validation
options.C: Reliability only matters for customer-facing agents, since internal research or coding tools don't carry the same accuracy or trust requirements as external-facing systems
options.D: Domain 5 is primarily about reducing API costs through batching and caching, with escalation and provenance tracking serving mainly as cost-control mechanisms rather than reliability concerns

questions.rationale: This synthesizes the domain's throughline across preservation, escalation, error propagation, codebase context, human review, and provenance: deliberate information management and validated, non-proxy signals drive reliability.

questions.question: A coordinator's loop checks whether Claude's response contains conversational phrases like "I have finished researching" to decide whether to stop invoking tools. What is the correct, reliable replacement for this check?

options.A: Check the `stop_reason` field: continue on "tool_use", terminate on "end_turn"
options.B: Add more phrase variants to the keyword list to catch edge cases, extending an approach that remains fundamentally unreliable
options.C: Ask Claude to output a special JSON flag `{"done": true}` in its text and parse that instead, still relying on parsing free-form text
options.D: Cap the loop at a fixed number of iterations and stop regardless of content, a safety net rather than a real completion signal

questions.rationale: `stop_reason` is the structured signal the API provides specifically for this purpose. Natural-language parsing (B, C) is inherently unreliable regardless of the exact keyword or format chosen, and a fixed iteration cap (D) doesn't reflect whether the task actually finished.

questions.question: When `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`, what must happen before the next request is sent to Claude?

options.A: The requested tool must be executed and its result appended to the conversation history
options.B: The conversation should be summarized before continuing, an unrelated step that doesn't address executing the requested tool
options.C: The loop should pause and wait for human confirmation on every call, an unnecessary manual step not required by the loop's design
options.D: The system prompt should be regenerated with updated instructions, an unrelated action that doesn't fulfill the pending tool request

questions.rationale: The agentic loop's core mechanism is: execute the requested tool, then feed the result back into conversation history so Claude can reason about the next action.

questions.question: In a hub-and-spoke multi-agent architecture, which statement is accurate?

options.A: Subagents communicate directly with each other to save latency, bypassing the coordinator's central routing role
options.B: The coordinator routes all inter-subagent communication, error handling, and information flow
options.C: Each subagent independently decides which other subagents to invoke, decentralizing a decision that belongs to the coordinator
options.D: The coordinator only aggregates final results and has no role in task decomposition, understating its actual responsibilities

questions.rationale: Hub-and-spoke means the coordinator is the single point managing communication and routing between subagents, which supports observability and consistent error handling — direct subagent-to-subagent communication (A) defeats this pattern.

questions.question: A coordinator invokes all four available subagents (search, analysis, synthesis, citation-check) on every query regardless of complexity, even for simple factual lookups. What's the main downside of this design?

options.A: It reduces the risk of incomplete research coverage, since invoking every subagent guarantees maximal breadth on every query
options.B: It adds unnecessary latency and cost for queries that didn't need the full pipeline
options.C: It violates the hub-and-spoke pattern, since routing all four subagents through the coordinator breaks that architecture
options.D: It prevents parallel subagent execution, since always invoking every subagent forces them to run one at a time

questions.rationale: A well-designed coordinator dynamically selects which subagents to invoke based on query complexity rather than always routing through the full pipeline — always invoking everything wastes latency and cost on simple queries.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: What must be true of a coordinator agent's configuration for it to be able to spawn subagents at all?

options.A: Its `allowedTools` list must include "Task"
options.B: It must have a `context: fork` setting in its own definition, a skill-specific option unrelated to spawning subagents
options.C: It must be running in plan mode, an execution mode unrelated to whether the Task tool is available
options.D: It must be invoked via a custom slash command, an unrelated invocation method that doesn't affect Task tool access

questions.rationale: The Task tool is the mechanism for spawning subagents, and the coordinator's `allowedTools` must explicitly include "Task" for this to be available.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: A synthesis subagent produces vague, generic conclusions instead of using the specific findings from the web-search and document-analysis subagents. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The synthesis subagent's model is not capable enough for the task, requiring a stronger model to produce specific conclusions
options.B: The coordinator did not explicitly include the prior agents' findings in the synthesis subagent's prompt
options.C: The subagents should have been run sequentially instead of in parallel, since parallel execution is what caused the vague output
options.D: The Task tool has a hidden limit on how much context it can pass, silently truncating the findings before synthesis received them

questions.rationale: Subagents do not automatically inherit the coordinator's or other subagents' conversation history — findings must be explicitly included in the prompt when spawning the subagent, or it has nothing concrete to synthesize from.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: You want two subagents to run concurrently rather than one after another. How should the coordinator's response be structured to achieve this?

options.A: Emit both Task tool calls within a single coordinator response
options.B: Emit one Task call, wait for its result, then emit the second in a following turn, which produces sequential rather than concurrent execution
options.C: Use `fork_session` to duplicate the coordinator's context for each subagent, a mechanism intended for a different purpose
options.D: Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the coordinator, which affects whether a tool is called at all, not whether calls run concurrently

questions.rationale: Parallel subagent execution is achieved by emitting multiple Task tool calls within a single coordinator response, rather than issuing them across separate sequential turns.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.4 — Multi-Step Workflow Enforcement and Handoff
questions.question: A refund workflow must never execute unless customer identity has already been verified. Which approach guarantees this ordering?

options.A: A system prompt instruction stating verification must happen first, relying on the model to consistently follow that written rule
options.B: A programmatic prerequisite gate that blocks the refund tool until the verification tool has returned a confirmed result
options.C: Few-shot examples demonstrating the correct order, relying on demonstrated patterns rather than any structural guarantee
