options.D: A reminder appended to each user turn about the required order, restating the same prompt-based rule on every message

questions.rationale: Prompt-based guidance (A, C, D) is probabilistic and has a non-zero failure rate. Only a programmatic gate — blocking the dependent tool call until the prerequisite has actually completed — gives a deterministic guarantee, which matters when consequences (like an unverified refund) are financial.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.4 — Multi-Step Workflow Enforcement and Handoff
questions.question: When an agent escalates a complex case mid-conversation to a human who has no access to the chat transcript, what should the handoff include?

options.A: Just the customer's original message, verbatim, omitting everything the agent discovered during its own investigation
options.B: A structured summary with customer details, root cause analysis, and recommended next action
options.C: The full raw tool call history with no synthesis, requiring the human to sift through unprocessed detail unassisted
options.D: Nothing — the human agent should re-investigate from scratch for accuracy, discarding the agent's investigation entirely

questions.rationale: Since the receiving human has no transcript access, a structured handoff summary (customer details, root cause, recommended action) is what allows them to act quickly without re-doing the investigation.

questions.question: Different MCP tools return dates in inconsistent formats (Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings, etc.), causing the agent to misinterpret ordering. What's the best fix?

options.A: Add a `PostToolUse` hook that normalizes all date formats before the agent processes tool results
options.B: Instruct the agent in the system prompt to convert dates itself before reasoning, relying on the model to correctly infer each format
options.C: Add few-shot examples showing correctly ordered dates, relying on demonstrated patterns rather than resolving the format inconsistency directly
options.D: Ask each MCP server owner to agree on a shared date format over time, an external, uncontrolled fix rather than a technical one

questions.rationale: A `PostToolUse` hook can deterministically normalize heterogeneous data formats before the model ever sees them, which is more reliable than hoping the model correctly interprets and converts inconsistent formats itself.

questions.question: You want to guarantee that refunds above $500 are never processed automatically, no matter what the model decides. What's the most reliable mechanism?

options.A: A system prompt rule stating refunds above $500 require escalation, relying on the model to consistently apply that written threshold
options.B: A hook that intercepts the outgoing `process_refund` tool call and blocks it above the threshold, redirecting to escalation
options.C: A few-shot example showing a refund being escalated at $600, relying on a single demonstrated case to establish the threshold
options.D: Trusting the agent's self-reported confidence score before allowing large refunds, relying on the model's own uncalibrated judgment

questions.rationale: Hooks intercepting outgoing tool calls provide deterministic enforcement of business rules. Prompt-based rules (A, C) and self-reported confidence (D) are all probabilistic and insufficient when a hard guarantee is required.

questions.question: A code review needs to check each of 14 changed files for local issues, then separately check for issues that only appear when files interact. Which decomposition pattern fits best?

options.A: A single pass reading all 14 files together, the setup most prone to attention dilution and contradictory findings
options.B: Prompt chaining: a per-file analysis pass, followed by a separate cross-file integration pass
options.C: One dynamic, adaptively-generated subtask per file discovered at runtime, over-engineering a review with a known, fixed file set
options.D: A single subagent given all 14 files and unlimited time, still processing everything in one undifferentiated pass

questions.rationale: This is a predictable, multi-aspect review — well suited to prompt chaining (fixed sequential steps: per-file pass, then integration pass) rather than dynamic decomposition, which is better suited to open-ended, less predictable investigation tasks.

questions.question: You're asked to "add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase" with no further detail. What decomposition approach is most appropriate?

options.A: A fixed prompt chain with the same steps regardless of what's discovered, applied uniformly regardless of what the codebase exploration reveals
options.B: Dynamic decomposition: first map the codebase structure, identify high-impact areas, then build a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered
options.C: Immediately generate tests for every file in alphabetical order, without first assessing which areas are highest-impact or highest-risk
options.D: Ask a single subagent to write all tests in one pass with no exploration step, relying entirely on the codebase being already well understood

questions.rationale: Open-ended, under-specified tasks benefit from dynamic decomposition, where subtasks are generated based on what's discovered during exploration, rather than a fixed pipeline decided upfront.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.7 — Session State, Resumption, and Forking
questions.question: You want to explore two different refactoring approaches starting from the same point in an analysis, without either exploration affecting the other. What should you use?

options.A: `--resume` with the same session name for both explorations, which continues one session rather than branching into two independent ones
options.B: `fork_session` to create two independent branches from the shared baseline
options.C: Start two completely fresh sessions with no shared context, losing the already-completed research baseline entirely
options.D: Use `/compact` twice to create two condensed copies, a context-reduction command not intended for branching explorations

questions.rationale: `fork_session` is designed exactly for this: creating independent branches from a shared analysis baseline so divergent approaches can be explored without interfering with each other.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.7 — Session State, Resumption, and Forking
questions.question: You resume a named session to continue investigating a codebase, but several files have since been modified by teammates. What should you do?

options.A: Trust the resumed session's prior tool results without changes, since resumption preserves everything needed, risking stale assumptions
options.B: Inform the agent about the specific file changes so it can perform targeted re-analysis
options.C: Start an entirely new session and re-explore the whole codebase from scratch every time, discarding useful prior context unnecessarily
options.D: Use `fork_session` instead, since it automatically detects file changes, when forking doesn't provide automatic change detection

questions.rationale: Resumed sessions can hold stale tool results. Explicitly informing the agent about specific changes enables targeted re-analysis, which is more reliable than assuming old results are still valid or over-correcting with a full re-exploration.

questions.question: A research coordinator produces a synthesis with confident, unified conclusions even though two of its subagents reported partial failures (one search timed out, one document was inaccessible). What's the most likely design flaw?

options.A: The synthesis subagent is not capable enough for the task, requiring a stronger underlying model to produce accurate conclusions
options.B: Subagent errors were suppressed or not propagated with enough context for the coordinator to annotate coverage gaps
options.C: The system should have used a single agent instead of multiple, since multi-agent architectures inherently obscure partial failures
options.D: The web search subagent needs a larger context window, since insufficient capacity is what caused the search to time out

questions.rationale: When partial failures occur, structured error propagation should let the coordinator annotate the final synthesis with coverage gaps rather than presenting an artificially confident, complete-looking result.

questions.question: A customer's message raises three unrelated issues at once (a billing question, a shipping delay, and a product defect). What's the best way for the agent to handle this?

options.A: Only address the first issue mentioned and ask the customer to submit separate requests for the rest of their concerns
options.B: Decompose the message into distinct items, investigate each using shared context, then synthesize a single unified resolution
options.C: Escalate immediately since multi-issue messages are inherently too complex, treating any multi-concern message as automatically unresolvable
options.D: Pick the issue that seems most urgent and ignore the others, addressing only part of what the customer raised

questions.rationale: Multi-concern requests should be decomposed into distinct items and investigated in parallel using shared context, then synthesized into one coherent response — not dropped, escalated by default, or handled one at a time in isolation.

questions.question: Which of the following is an anti-pattern for determining when an agentic loop should stop?

options.A: Checking `stop_reason == "end_turn"`, which is the correct, structured signal for loop termination
options.B: Checking for the presence of assistant text content as a completion indicator
options.C: Continuing the loop while `stop_reason == "tool_use"`, which correctly reflects that a requested tool still needs to be executed
options.D: Feeding tool results back into conversation history between iterations, the correct way to carry new information forward

questions.rationale: Checking for the mere presence of assistant text is unreliable — Claude can produce text alongside a tool call. `stop_reason` is the structured, purpose-built signal; text-presence checks are a known anti-pattern.

questions.question: A coordinator decomposes "impact of remote work on urban economies" into subtasks covering only office real estate and commuting patterns, missing retail, housing, and local tax revenue. What's the root cause and fix?

options.A: The subagents under-researched their assigned subtopics — expand their search queries, when each subagent already covered its scope correctly
options.B: The coordinator's initial decomposition was too narrow — it should cover the topic's full breadth before delegating
options.C: The synthesis agent should have caught the gap and requested more data, placing responsibility on synthesis rather than the initial decomposition
options.D: A larger language model would have produced better subagent results, when the issue lies in what subtopics were assigned in the first place

questions.rationale: This is the same failure pattern as narrow topic decomposition seen elsewhere: subagents did their assigned jobs correctly, but the coordinator's initial breakdown didn't cover all relevant domains of the topic in the first place.

questions.question: What are the two `stop_reason` values most relevant to controlling an agentic loop?

options.A: "tool_use" and "end_turn"
options.B: "success" and "failure", values that don't correspond to any actual `stop_reason` field in the API
options.C: "continue" and "stop", values that don't correspond to any actual `stop_reason` field in the API
options.D: "pending" and "complete", values that don't correspond to any actual `stop_reason` field in the API

questions.rationale: These are the two structured signals the API returns: "tool_use" means continue the loop and execute the requested tool; "end_turn" means the model has finished.

questions.question: What is the defining feature of model-driven decision-making in an agentic system, as opposed to a pre-configured decision tree?

options.A: Claude reasons about which tool to call next based on context, rather than following a fixed pre-scripted sequence
options.B: The system never calls the same tool twice, since model-driven reasoning inherently avoids redundant tool calls
options.C: All decisions are made by a separate classifier model, which selects each tool call independently of Claude's own reasoning
options.D: The agent requires human approval before every tool call, since model-driven decision-making depends on a human confirming each step

questions.rationale: Model-driven decision-making means Claude itself reasons about the next action from context, contrasted with rigid, pre-configured tool sequences or decision trees.

questions.question: In coordinator-subagent architectures, do subagents automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history?

options.A: No — subagents operate with isolated context and must be given relevant information explicitly
options.B: Yes, automatically and completely, since the coordinator's full conversation history is passed to every subagent it spawns
options.C: Only the first message is inherited, with all subsequent coordinator turns excluded from the subagent's context
options.D: Only if `fork_session` is used, since forking is what enables context inheritance between a coordinator and its subagents

questions.rationale: Subagents do not automatically inherit context; any information they need must be explicitly included in the prompt when they're spawned.

questions.question: What tool is used to spawn a subagent in the Claude Agent SDK?

options.A: The `Task` tool
options.B: The `Spawn` tool, a tool name that doesn't correspond to any actual mechanism in the Claude Agent SDK
options.C: The `Delegate` tool, a tool name that doesn't correspond to any actual mechanism in the Claude Agent SDK
options.D: The `Fork` tool, a tool name that doesn't correspond to any actual mechanism in the Claude Agent SDK

questions.rationale: The `Task` tool is the mechanism for spawning subagents; a coordinator's `allowedTools` must include "Task" to use it.

questions.question: What is `fork_session` used for?

options.A: Creating independent branches from a shared analysis baseline to explore divergent approaches
options.B: Permanently deleting a session's history, clearing all prior conversation state beyond recovery
options.C: Merging two separate sessions into one, combining their conversation histories into a single unified thread
options.D: Exporting a session transcript to a file, saving the conversation for external review outside of Claude Code

questions.rationale: `fork_session` lets you branch off a shared baseline to explore multiple approaches independently, without one exploration affecting the other.

questions.question: What CLI mechanism lets you continue a specific prior conversation by name?

options.A: `--resume <session-name>`
options.B: `--continue <session-name>`, a flag name that doesn't correspond to any actual Claude Code CLI mechanism
options.C: `--load <session-name>`, a flag name that doesn't correspond to any actual Claude Code CLI mechanism
options.D: `--reopen <session-name>`, a flag name that doesn't correspond to any actual Claude Code CLI mechanism

questions.rationale: `--resume <session-name>` continues a specific named prior conversation.

questions.question: Why is setting an arbitrary iteration cap considered an anti-pattern as the *primary* loop-termination mechanism?

options.A: It doesn't reflect whether the task has actually finished, and can cut off legitimate work or mask runaway loops
options.B: It's not supported by the Claude API at all, since iteration caps cannot technically be implemented in an agentic loop
options.C: It forces the agent to always use the maximum number of tool calls, regardless of how quickly the task could otherwise be completed
options.D: It requires a separate classifier model to configure, adding unnecessary infrastructure just to set a numeric limit

questions.rationale: An iteration cap is a safety net at best, not a substitute for a real completion signal like `stop_reason` — relying on it primarily means stopping for the wrong reason.

questions.question: What's the difference between prompt chaining and dynamic task decomposition?

options.A: Prompt chaining uses a fixed sequence of steps; dynamic decomposition generates subtasks adaptively based on what's discovered
options.B: They are two names for the same technique, describing an identical approach to breaking down a workflow into subtasks
options.C: Prompt chaining only works with subagents, dynamic decomposition only works with a single agent, restricting each technique's applicability
options.D: Dynamic decomposition is always faster than prompt chaining, regardless of how predictable or exploratory the underlying task is

questions.rationale: Prompt chaining is best for predictable, multi-aspect tasks with known steps; dynamic decomposition suits open-ended tasks where subtasks depend on what's found along the way.

questions.question: What should a structured handoff to a human agent typically include?

options.A: Customer details, root cause analysis, and a recommended action
options.B: Only the customer's original message, omitting the agent's own investigation and root cause analysis entirely
options.C: The full internal tool-call log with no summary, requiring the human to interpret unprocessed technical detail unassisted
options.D: Nothing, since the human should investigate independently, discarding everything the agent already discovered

questions.rationale: Since the receiving human often lacks transcript access, a structured summary lets them act quickly on the case.

questions.question: What is a `PostToolUse` hook typically used for?

options.A: Intercepting and transforming tool results before the model processes them
options.B: Blocking a user from sending a new message, a UI-level restriction unrelated to what `PostToolUse` hooks actually do
options.C: Changing the system prompt after every tool call, an unrelated action distinct from transforming tool results themselves
options.D: Logging billing information for the API account, an account-management function unrelated to tool result processing

questions.rationale: `PostToolUse` hooks intercept tool results for transformation (e.g., normalizing inconsistent data formats) before the model reasons over them.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism an LLM uses to decide which tool to call?

options.A: The tool's description
options.B: The tool's internal source code, which the model has no visibility into when deciding whether to call it
options.C: The order tools are listed in, a factor that doesn't meaningfully drive reliable tool selection on its own
options.D: The tool's function name length, an arbitrary property with no real bearing on selection reliability

questions.rationale: Tool descriptions are the primary signal models use for tool selection; minimal or ambiguous descriptions lead to unreliable selection among similar tools.

questions.question: What does the MCP `isError` flag communicate?

options.A: That a tool call failed, allowing the agent to react appropriately
options.B: That the tool is deprecated and should not be used again, a permanent status rather than a per-call failure signal
options.C: That the user made an invalid request, misattributing a tool-level failure to the end user rather than the tool call itself
options.D: That the MCP server is offline, a broader connectivity issue distinct from what the `isError` flag on a single response indicates

questions.rationale: The `isError` flag is the pattern for communicating tool failures back to the agent so it can decide how to proceed.

questions.question: Where should a shared, team-wide MCP server be configured so credentials aren't committed to version control?

options.A: Project-scoped `.mcp.json`, using environment variable expansion (e.g. `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`)
options.B: Hardcoded directly into the tool's source file, embedding the literal credential value into the codebase itself
options.C: User-scoped `~/.claude.json` only, requiring every developer to configure the shared server individually with their own copy
options.D: A shared spreadsheet distributed to the team, tracking the credential value outside of any configuration file entirely

questions.rationale: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` with environment variable expansion allows shared configuration without committing secrets to version control.

questions.question: What's a key risk of giving an agent access to too many tools (e.g. 18 instead of 4-5)?

options.A: Tool selection reliability degrades as decision complexity increases
options.B: The API automatically rejects requests with more than 10 tools, a hard technical limit that doesn't actually exist
options.C: Tool descriptions become mandatory only above a certain tool count, implying descriptions are optional below some threshold
options.D: Latency increases, but selection accuracy is unaffected, understating the real degradation in selection reliability

questions.rationale: Too many available tools — especially outside an agent's specialization — increases the chance of misuse and unreliable tool selection.

questions.question: What does `tool_choice: "any"` guarantee, as opposed to `"auto"`?

options.A: The model must call some tool, though it can choose which one
options.B: The model must call one specific named tool, which is instead the behavior of forced tool selection, not `"any"`
options.C: The model may return plain text instead of calling a tool, which is instead the behavior of `"auto"`, not `"any"`
options.D: The model will call every available tool in sequence, a behavior `tool_choice` settings don't actually produce

questions.rationale: `"any"` forces the model to call a tool (but lets it pick which), whereas `"auto"` allows the model to return text instead, and forced selection names one specific tool.

questions.question: MCP resources are best used for:

options.A: Exposing content catalogs (e.g. schemas, doc hierarchies) to reduce exploratory tool calls
options.B: Executing actions that change state in a backend system, which is instead the defining purpose of an MCP tool
options.C: Replacing the need for tool descriptions, making well-written tool descriptions unnecessary once resources are exposed
options.D: Storing conversation history between sessions, persisting prior turns for later retrieval

questions.rationale: Resources expose content catalogs for visibility, while tools are for taking actions — conflating the two undercuts the point of resources.

questions.question: Which built-in tool is best suited to searching file *contents* for a specific pattern (like a function name)?

options.A: Grep
options.B: Glob, which matches file paths by name or pattern rather than searching the contents of files
options.C: Read, which loads the full contents of a specific known file rather than searching across multiple files for a pattern
options.D: Edit, which modifies existing file content rather than searching the codebase for a pattern

questions.rationale: Grep searches file contents for patterns; Glob matches file paths/names, not content.

questions.question: When `Edit` fails because the target text isn't unique in a file, what's the recommended fallback?

options.A: Use `Read` to load the full file, then `Write` the modified version
options.B: Retry `Edit` with the exact same arguments, repeating a call that will fail again for the same non-uniqueness reason
options.C: Switch to `Bash` to run a sed command instead, reaching for an external tool when a built-in fallback already exists
options.D: Delete and recreate the file from scratch, discarding the rest of its contents just to make one targeted change

questions.rationale: Read + Write is the standard fallback for reliable modification when Edit's unique-text-match requirement can't be satisfied.

questions.question: Why might overlapping or ambiguous tool descriptions (e.g. `analyze_content` vs `analyze_document`) cause problems?

options.A: They cause the agent to misroute requests between similarly-described tools
options.B: They cause the MCP server to crash on startup, an unrelated failure mode distinct from tool-selection confusion
options.C: They are automatically merged into a single tool by the SDK, a behavior the SDK doesn't actually perform
options.D: They only matter if `tool_choice` is set to "auto", when description ambiguity affects selection regardless of that setting

questions.rationale: Near-identical descriptions give the model insufficient signal to differentiate tools, leading to misrouting regardless of `tool_choice` setting.

questions.question: What's the difference between `.mcp.json` and `~/.claude.json` for MCP server configuration?

options.A: `.mcp.json` is project-scoped and shared via version control; `~/.claude.json` is user-scoped and personal
options.B: They are interchangeable and always produce identical behavior, regardless of which one a configuration is placed in
options.C: `~/.claude.json` is only for production servers, `.mcp.json` only for testing, splitting environments rather than scope
options.D: `.mcp.json` cannot use environment variables, requiring all credentials to be hardcoded directly into the file

questions.rationale: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` is for shared team tooling; user-scoped `~/.claude.json` is for personal or experimental servers.

questions.question: What is the correct order of specificity in the CLAUDE.md configuration hierarchy?

options.A: User-level → project-level → directory-level
options.B: Directory-level → user-level → project-level, reversing the actual order of specificity in the hierarchy
options.C: There is no hierarchy; all CLAUDE.md files are equivalent, disregarding the distinct scope of each configuration level
options.D: Project-level always overrides directory-level, reversing which level takes precedence for a given file

questions.rationale: CLAUDE.md configuration flows from broad (user-level, personal) to project-level (shared via version control) to directory-level (most specific).

questions.question: Why might a new team member fail to receive expected coding conventions even though the project's CLAUDE.md looks correct?

options.A: The conventions were placed in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (user-level), which isn't shared via version control
options.B: CLAUDE.md files are cached and take 24 hours to propagate, delaying visibility of new conventions for any team member
options.C: Only the project owner's CLAUDE.md is ever loaded, with all other contributors' CLAUDE.md files being ignored by Claude Code
options.D: New team members must manually copy CLAUDE.md into their home directory, since project-level files aren't loaded automatically

questions.rationale: User-level CLAUDE.md settings apply only to that individual user and are never shared via version control — a common cause of "it works for me but not my teammate."

questions.question: What does the `@import` syntax in CLAUDE.md allow?

options.A: Referencing external files to keep CLAUDE.md modular
options.B: Importing a different AI model for a specific task, a capability unrelated to what `@import` actually references
options.C: Pulling in a teammate's personal settings automatically, when `@import` references specific files, not another user's configuration
options.D: Triggering a CI/CD pipeline run, an unrelated automation action distinct from referencing a file's content

questions.rationale: `@import` references external files so CLAUDE.md doesn't have to be one large monolithic file.

questions.question: What's the advantage of `.claude/rules/` files with glob-pattern frontmatter over directory-level CLAUDE.md files?

options.A: They apply conventions to files by type regardless of where those files live in the directory tree
options.B: They load faster than CLAUDE.md files, reducing the time Claude Code takes to start a session
options.C: They replace the need for a project-level CLAUDE.md entirely, making universal conventions unnecessary
options.D: They only work for test files, and cannot be applied to any other category of file in the codebase

questions.rationale: Glob-pattern rules (e.g. `**/*.test.tsx`) apply based on file type/pattern rather than directory location, which matters when relevant files are scattered throughout a codebase.

questions.question: Where should a custom slash command live so it's shared with the whole team via version control?

options.A: `.claude/commands/` in the project repository
options.B: `~/.claude/commands/` in each developer's home directory, which is personal and not shared via git
options.C: Inside the root CLAUDE.md file, which holds project context and instructions rather than command definitions
options.D: A `.claude/config.json` commands array, a configuration format that isn't how Claude Code defines slash commands

questions.rationale: `.claude/commands/` is version-controlled and project-scoped; `~/.claude/commands/` is personal and not shared.

questions.question: What does the `context: fork` frontmatter option do for a skill?

options.A: Runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so its output doesn't pollute the main conversation
options.B: Forks the entire git repository automatically, creating a separate copy of the codebase for the skill to operate on
options.C: Duplicates the skill for every team member, creating individual personal copies of the same SKILL.md file
options.D: Forces the skill to run twice for verification, executing the same logic in two separate passes to cross-check results

questions.rationale: `context: fork` isolates verbose or exploratory skill output from the main session's context.

questions.question: When is plan mode most appropriate, compared to direct execution?

options.A: For complex tasks with architectural implications, multiple valid approaches, or large-scale multi-file changes
options.B: For any single-line bug fix, since exploring the codebase first is always more valuable than making a direct, well-scoped change
options.C: Only when working with MCP servers, since plan mode's exploration phase is specifically designed around discovering available MCP tools
options.D: Whenever `stop_reason` is "tool_use", since that signal indicates the task has grown complex enough to require upfront design

questions.rationale: Plan mode is designed for exploration and design before committing to complex, high-stakes changes; simple well-scoped changes are better handled with direct execution.

questions.question: What does the `/memory` command help you do?

options.A: Verify which memory (CLAUDE.md) files are currently loaded, to diagnose inconsistent behavior
options.B: Permanently erase all session history, clearing every prior turn beyond recovery
options.C: Switch between different Claude models mid-session, changing which underlying model handles subsequent turns
options.D: Generate a summary of the current git diff, listing uncommitted changes in the working directory

questions.rationale: `/memory` shows which memory files are loaded, which helps diagnose why behavior might differ across sessions or team members.

questions.question: What CLI flag runs Claude Code in non-interactive mode, suitable for CI/CD pipelines?

options.A: `-p` (or `--print`)
options.B: `--headless`, a flag name that doesn't correspond to any actual Claude Code CLI mechanism
options.C: `--batch`, a flag name that doesn't correspond to any actual Claude Code CLI mechanism
options.D: `--ci`, a flag name that doesn't correspond to any actual Claude Code CLI mechanism

questions.rationale: `-p`/`--print` processes the prompt and exits without waiting for interactive input — the documented approach for automated pipelines.

questions.question: What do `--output-format json` and `--json-schema` enable in a CI context?

options.A: Machine-parseable, structured output that can be posted as automated PR comments
options.B: Faster execution time for large codebases, reducing how long Claude Code takes to process a given repository
options.C: Automatic retries on failure, re-running the review command whenever the initial attempt doesn't complete successfully
options.D: Skipping the need for a CLAUDE.md file, removing the requirement for project-level configuration in CI runs

questions.rationale: These flags enforce structured, schema-compliant output so CI tooling can reliably parse and act on Claude Code's findings.

questions.question: What's the most reliable way to guarantee schema-compliant structured output from Claude?

options.A: `tool_use` with a JSON schema as the tool's input parameters
options.B: Asking nicely in the system prompt for valid JSON, relying on the model's free-text output to happen to be well-formed
options.C: Post-processing free-text output with regular expressions, patching around unstructured output rather than enforcing structure upfront
options.D: Increasing `max_tokens`, adjusting an unrelated generation limit rather than enforcing any actual structural guarantee

questions.rationale: Tool use with JSON schemas eliminates JSON syntax errors, unlike relying on the model to freely produce well-formed JSON in text.

questions.question: Does enforcing a strict JSON schema via tool use prevent semantic errors (e.g. line items that don't sum to the stated total)?

options.A: No — it eliminates syntax errors but not semantic/logical errors
options.B: Yes, schemas fully guarantee semantic correctness, overstating what structural enforcement alone actually provides
options.C: Only if `tool_choice` is set to "auto", when the tool_choice setting doesn't affect whether semantic errors are prevented
options.D: Only for numeric fields, an arbitrary restriction schema enforcement doesn't actually apply

questions.rationale: Schema enforcement guarantees structural validity, not semantic correctness — separate validation is needed to catch things like totals that don't add up.

questions.question: Why should extraction schema fields be marked nullable rather than required when the source document may not contain that information?

options.A: To prevent the model from fabricating values just to satisfy a required field
options.B: Because JSON schemas don't support optional fields, when nullable/optional fields are in fact a standard, supported schema feature
options.C: To make the schema smaller and faster to validate, a performance framing unrelated to the actual fabrication risk
options.D: Because nullable fields are always faster to extract, an unrelated performance claim rather than the real underlying reason

questions.rationale: Forcing a required field when the source doesn't express that information invites the model to fabricate a plausible-looking but invented value.

questions.question: What is the most effective technique for achieving consistently formatted output when detailed prose instructions alone produce inconsistent results?

options.A: Few-shot examples
options.B: Increasing the temperature setting, which adjusts output randomness rather than providing concrete formatting guidance
options.C: Adding more adjectives to the instructions, elaborating on prose that has already proven insufficient
options.D: Splitting the prompt into more system messages, restructuring delivery without adding the concrete examples actually needed

questions.rationale: Few-shot examples demonstrate the desired output format and handling of ambiguous cases more reliably than prose instructions alone.

questions.question: What's a key limitation of the Message Batches API?

options.A: No guaranteed latency SLA and no multi-turn tool calling within a single request
options.B: It cannot be used for more than 10 requests at a time, an arbitrary volume limit that doesn't reflect the API's actual constraints
options.C: It costs more than synchronous API calls, the opposite of the Batches API's actual 50% cost-saving characteristic
options.D: It only supports single-field JSON schemas, an arbitrary restriction on schema complexity that doesn't actually exist

questions.rationale: Batches offer cost savings but trade off guaranteed latency and don't support multi-turn tool calling mid-request — making them unsuitable for blocking, time-sensitive workflows.

questions.question: What field is used to correlate a Message Batches API request with its corresponding response?

options.A: `custom_id`
options.B: `request_hash`, a field name that doesn't correspond to any actual Message Batches API mechanism
options.C: `batch_key`, a field name that doesn't correspond to any actual Message Batches API mechanism
options.D: `trace_id`, a field name that doesn't correspond to any actual Message Batches API mechanism

questions.rationale: `custom_id` fields let you match each submitted request to its response, especially useful when resubmitting only failed items.

questions.question: Why do vague instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" often fail to reduce false positives?

options.A: They don't provide the explicit, specific criteria needed for the model to reliably distinguish real issues from false ones
options.B: They cause the model to stop producing output entirely, treating the vague instruction as a directive to remain silent
options.C: They only work when combined with a higher temperature, since more randomness is needed to compensate for the lack of specific criteria
options.D: They are not supported by the API, since the API rejects prompts phrased as general guidance rather than concrete rules

questions.rationale: Specific categorical criteria are far more effective than general instructions to "be careful," which give the model no concrete basis for the judgment call.

questions.question: When a validation-retry loop fails repeatedly on a field, what should you check before retrying again?

options.A: Whether the information is actually present in the source document at all — retries won't help if it's genuinely absent
options.B: Whether `max_tokens` is set high enough, since insufficient token budget is the most common cause of a persistently missing field
options.C: Whether the schema has too many required fields, since reducing the number of required fields typically resolves repeated failures
options.D: Whether the retry request used the same temperature as the original, since a different temperature setting often resolves stuck extractions

questions.rationale: Retries are effective for format/structural errors, but ineffective when the required information simply isn't present in the source — no amount of retrying recovers data that was never there.

questions.question: Why is a second, independent Claude instance often more effective at reviewing generated code than asking the same instance to self-review?

options.A: The generating instance retains reasoning context from creating the code, making it less likely to question its own decisions
options.B: A second instance always uses a larger context window, which is what allows it to catch issues the first instance's smaller window missed
options.C: Self-review is not technically possible with the API, since a session cannot be prompted to evaluate its own prior output
options.D: Independent instances are cheaper to run, and cost — not review quality — is the primary reason a second instance is preferred

questions.rationale: Self-review within the same session inherits the generator's own reasoning and blind spots; an independent instance without that context can catch issues more objectively.

questions.question: What's the purpose of forced tool selection (`tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}`)?

options.A: To guarantee a specific named tool is called, e.g. to enforce a required first step like metadata extraction
options.B: To prevent the model from calling any tool at all, forcing it to respond with conversational text exclusively
options.C: To let the model choose freely among all available tools, exactly matching the behavior of `tool_choice: "auto"`
options.D: To disable JSON schema validation for that call, bypassing structural checks on whichever tool ends up being invoked

questions.rationale: Forced selection ensures one specific tool runs, useful when a particular step (like extracting metadata first) must happen before others.

questions.question: What is the "lost in the middle" effect?

options.A: Models reliably process information at the beginning and end of long inputs but may miss details from middle sections
options.B: Conversations lose their system prompt after 10 turns, requiring it to be manually reinserted into every subsequent request
options.C: Tool results disappear from context after being used once, requiring the same tool to be called again if referenced later
options.D: Claude forgets the user's name partway through a session, unless it's explicitly repeated in every following message

questions.rationale: This describes a known pattern where information placed in the middle of long inputs is more likely to be underweighted or missed compared to the start or end.

questions.question: What's a risk of progressive summarization in long conversations?

options.A: Specific numerical values, dates, and stated expectations can get condensed into vague, lossy summaries
options.B: It always increases token usage instead of reducing it, working directly against the purpose summarization is meant to serve
options.C: It can only be applied once per session, after which no further summarization of the conversation is technically possible
options.D: It automatically deletes the system prompt, removing the agent's core instructions as a side effect of condensing history

questions.rationale: Summarization that isn't careful about preserving concrete facts (amounts, dates, exact expectations) risks losing information that later reasoning depends on.

questions.question: When should an agent escalate to a human, according to reliable escalation design?

options.A: On explicit customer request, when policy is silent/ambiguous on the situation, or when no meaningful progress can be made
options.B: Whenever the conversation exceeds 5 turns, treating conversation length alone as sufficient grounds for escalation
options.C: Whenever sentiment analysis detects any negative tone, treating detected frustration alone as sufficient grounds for escalation
options.D: Only when the agent's self-reported confidence drops below a fixed number, relying solely on the model's own uncalibrated self-assessment

questions.rationale: Sentiment-based and self-reported-confidence triggers are both unreliable proxies for actual complexity; explicit request, policy gaps, and genuine stuckness are the reliable triggers.

questions.question: What should structured error context passed to a coordinator include, beyond a simple failure status?

options.A: Failure type, what was attempted, any partial results, and possible alternative approaches
options.B: Just a boolean indicating success or failure, giving the coordinator no further detail to act on
options.C: The full raw exception stack trace and nothing else, providing low-level technical detail without any recovery-relevant context
options.D: A generic "unavailable" message to keep payloads small, sacrificing detail for brevity

questions.rationale: Rich structured error context lets the coordinator make an informed recovery decision rather than guessing blindly from a generic status.

questions.question: Why is aggregate accuracy (e.g. "97% overall") potentially misleading for an extraction system?

options.A: It can mask poor performance on specific document types or fields that are underrepresented in the aggregate
options.B: Aggregate accuracy is always inflated by at least 10%, systematically overstating true performance regardless of the underlying data
options.C: It only applies to numeric fields, since text-based extractions aren't meaningfully summarized by an aggregate accuracy figure
options.D: It cannot be measured for extraction tasks at all, since extraction accuracy has no well-defined aggregate metric

questions.rationale: A high overall number can hide segments (particular document types or fields) where accuracy is actually much worse — stratified analysis is needed to catch this.

questions.question: What is stratified random sampling used for in this context?

options.A: Measuring error rates within high-confidence extractions and catching novel error patterns that aggregate metrics might hide
options.B: Randomly selecting which MCP server to call, when multiple servers expose overlapping or equivalent tools for the same task
options.C: Choosing which subagent should run first, when a coordinator has multiple equally-valid subagents available for a query
options.D: Deciding the batch size for the Message Batches API, based on random variation in document complexity across a submission

questions.rationale: Stratified sampling across document types/fields helps verify that even "high-confidence" extractions are actually accurate, rather than trusting the aggregate number blindly.

questions.question: Why should information provenance (claim-source mappings) be explicitly preserved during multi-source synthesis?

options.A: Summarization steps can otherwise lose track of which finding came from which source
options.B: It's required by the Claude API for all tool calls, misattributing a content-design best practice to an API-level requirement
options.C: It only matters for numeric data, not qualitative findings, when provenance loss affects any type of claim during compression
options.D: It automatically resolves conflicting data between sources, when preserving provenance surfaces conflicts rather than resolving them

questions.rationale: Without explicit claim-source mappings, compression during summarization can silently erase which source supports which claim, undermining the report's credibility.

questions.question: Two credible sources report different statistics for the same fact. What's the recommended handling?

options.A: Annotate the conflict with source attribution for both values rather than arbitrarily picking one
options.B: Always use the more recently published source and discard the other, treating recency alone as the deciding factor
options.C: Average the two values together, blending the two disagreeing figures into a single blended number
options.D: Omit the fact entirely from the report, leaving the disagreement out rather than surfacing it with attribution

questions.rationale: Arbitrarily selecting one value hides a genuine disagreement between credible sources; annotating both with attribution is more honest and useful to the reader.

questions.question: What's the purpose of a scratchpad file during long codebase-exploration sessions?

options.A: Persisting key findings across context boundaries to counteract context degradation over a long session
options.B: Storing the user's personal preferences, so they persist and are automatically applied across future, unrelated sessions
options.C: Replacing the need for CLAUDE.md, since scratchpad files can hold any project convention that would otherwise live there
options.D: Caching API responses to reduce cost, storing previous tool call results so they don't need to be requested again

questions.rationale: As sessions get long, models can start giving inconsistent answers; a scratchpad of key findings gives the agent something concrete to reference instead of relying on degraded long-context recall.

questions.question: Why is trimming verbose tool outputs to only relevant fields important for context management?

options.A: Full tool outputs (e.g. 40+ fields when only 5 matter) consume context tokens disproportionately to their relevance
options.B: The API rejects tool outputs above a fixed field count, requiring trimming to stay under that structural limit
options.C: It's required for the Message Batches API specifically, and doesn't meaningfully affect real-time, synchronous tool calls
options.D: It has no effect on context usage, only on latency, since token consumption is unrelated to how many fields a tool response contains

questions.rationale: Verbose, unfiltered tool outputs accumulate in context and crowd out room for more relevant reasoning, even when most of the returned data isn't needed for the task at hand.
